Chapter Anchors: The chapter names the five parts as the Pico 2 W, the round display, the microphone, the amplifier with a speaker, and the three buttons.

docs.title: The Brain: Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W is a small circuit board that carries a microcontroller, memory, a wireless chip, and a row of pins you can wire to. It is about the size of a stick of gum. It runs on 3.3 volts and has a micro-USB connector for power and for loading programs. You cannot run a web browser on it, but it has everything an agent terminal needs.

Four things on the board matter for this book.

Feature What the Pico 2 W has Why the book cares Processor RP2350 chip, up to 150 MHz Runs audio code in real time Memory 520 KB of SRAM, 4 MB of flash Holds buffers and your program files Wireless 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (and Bluetooth) Reaches the buddy server Pins 26 usable GPIO pins Connect the display, buttons, and audio parts

Worked example. The Pico's processor makes 150 million clock ticks per second, so one tick lasts about 6.7 nanoseconds. The audio frames in later chapters are 40 ms long, and \( 0.04 \times 150{,}000{,}000 = 6{,}000{,}000 \) ticks. Divide that by the 512 samples in a frame and you get about 11,700 ticks of work available for each sample before the next frame arrives. That is a big number, but MicroPython spends hundreds of ticks on a single line, which is why Chapter 10 teaches faster code.

docs.title: The RP2350 Microcontroller
docs.text: The RP2350 is the chip at the center of the Pico 2 W. A microcontroller is a computer on one chip: processor, memory, and input/output circuits together. The RP2350 adds two features that matter for this book. It has special programmable circuits called PIO blocks, which MicroPython's I2S audio uses to move sound in and out without help from your code. And its processor cores have instructions for fast math, which we use for the FFT.

docs.title: The Cortex-M33 Core and Dual Cores
docs.text:
A core is one processor inside the chip. The RP2350 has two Arm Cortex-M33 cores, so it is a dual core processor. The Cortex-M33 is a 32-bit core that includes a hardware unit for decimal (floating-point) math and instructions for the multiply-and-add operations that signal processing uses constantly.

MicroPython normally runs your program on the first core only. The second core can run a separate task through the _thread module. This book keeps the work on one core, and Chapter 10 shows how to make that single core fast enough.

docs.title: SRAM
docs.text: SRAM is the fast memory that holds your running program's variables. The RP2350 has 520 KB of it, shared by MicroPython itself and your data. It is the "RAM" you counted against in Chapter 2, where a 3-second recording took 150 KB. SRAM loses its contents when power is removed, while the 4 MB of flash keeps your files.

docs.title: The Wi-Fi Radio
docs.text:
The Pico 2 W's Wi-Fi radio is a separate wireless chip (the CYW43439) that sits next to the RP2350 and speaks 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Your MicroPython program controls it through the network module, which Chapter 13 uses to connect to the school network. Because the chip is separate, it uses a few of the Pico's pins for itself: GP23, GP24, GP25, and GP29. The onboard LED hangs off the wireless chip too, which is why you write Pin("LED").

Worked example. A school offers two networks, "School-5G" on the 5 GHz band and "School-2G" on the 2.4 GHz band. The Pico can join only "School-2G", because its radio does not support 5 GHz. If your classroom network is 5 GHz only, the Pico will not see it, and you will need the school's IT team to provide a 2.4 GHz network.

Wi-Fi fact Detail Band 2.4 GHz only Standard 802.11n Pins used by the radio chip GP23, GP24, GP25, GP29 Book chapters that use it 13 (HTTP), 14 (streaming), 15 (MQTT)

docs.title: USB Power
docs.text:
The Pico gets its power from its micro-USB port. A USB port supplies 5 volts, and the Pico has a voltage regulator that turns the 5 V into the 3.3 V the chip and its pins use. Two pins on the board give that power to your parts: VBUS passes the USB 5 V straight through, and 3V3 is the regulated 3.3 V output. A normal computer USB port provides up to about 500 mA, which is enough for this kit at the volumes used in the tests.

The rule for choosing between them is simple: use 3V3 for the display and the microphone, which are 3.3 V parts, and use VBUS or 3V3 for the amplifier. Connecting a 5 V wire to a pin that expects 3.3 V can damage it.

The Microphone Is a 3.3 Volt Part

The INMP441's VDD pin goes to 3V3, never to VBUS. A 5 V wire is an easy mistake because the amplifier next to it is happy on 5 V. Before you power up, trace the microphone's red wire back to the 3V3 pin.

docs.title: Ground Wiring
docs.text:
Ground is the 0 V reference that every voltage in the circuit is measured against. For a signal to mean anything, the sender and the receiver must share the same ground. That is the whole idea of ground wiring: every part's GND pin connects back to a GND pin on the Pico. The Pico has eight GND pins spread around its edges, so you can always find one near the part you are wiring. On a breadboard you usually run one wire from a Pico GND pin to the long blue (or black) rail and then connect each part to that rail.

A missing or loose ground rarely gives a clean "no." It gives strange behavior: a screen that flickers, a microphone that hisses, or a speaker that crackles. When something misbehaves, check the grounds first.

docs.title: Power Supply Noise
docs.text: Power supply noise is the small, fast fluctuation in the voltage that comes from the other parts sharing it. The amplifier is the main source: it draws sudden pulses of current when it plays loud sounds, and those pulses ripple through the shared power and ground wires. The microphone is the most sensitive listener, because it measures tiny changes. Three habits keep the noise down: use short wires, keep the microphone's wires away from the amplifier's, and give the microphone its power from 3V3.

docs.title: The Round Color Display
docs.text:
The kit's round color display is a 2.1 inch screen with 360 by 360 pixels. A pixel is one dot of color, and 360 by 360 gives \( 360 \times 360 = 129{,}600 \) of them. The memory addresses are square, but the glass is circular, so only the circle inscribed in the square can be seen. The corners are hidden under the bezel.

Worked example. The visible circle has radius 180 pixels, so it shows \( \pi \times 180^2 \approx 101{,}788 \) pixels, about 78.5 percent of the square. Because the very edge is also covered by the bezel, the kit's SAFE_RADIUS is 168, and a ring at that radius is the largest circle you can see completely. That circle has about 88,668 pixels, 68.4 percent of the square. Drawing in the corners wastes time on pixels nobody can see.

Display fact Value Size 2.1 inches, round Resolution 360 by 360 pixels (some listings wrongly say 640 by 640) Controller chip GC9B72 Bus SPI, using SPI block 0 Pixel format 16-bit color (RGB565, Chapter 5) Safe drawing radius 168 pixels from the center (180, 180)

docs.title: The Display Controller
docs.text:
The display glass cannot work alone. Behind it is a display controller, a chip that holds the screen's own memory and lights each pixel. In this kit it is the GC9B72. Your Pico sends it commands and pixel data over SPI, and the controller keeps the picture on the screen until you send something new. The Pico does not store the picture.

The controller uses four control wires besides the data and clock.

Pin Name Job CS Chip select Pulled low while the Pico is talking to the display DC Data/command Low means the byte is a command, high means it is data RST Reset A brief low pulse restarts the controller BL Backlight High turns the screen's light on

Worked example. Here is what happens on the wires when you call display.pixel(10, 20, config.RED). The driver sends the "set column" command and then the x range (10 to 10), the "set row" command and the y range (20 to 20), and the "write memory" command, and finally the two bytes of the red color. Every command byte is sent with DC low, and every data byte with DC high.

Step SPI bytes sent DC level Set column command 1 byte (0x2A) low Column range 10 to 10 4 bytes: 00 0A 00 0A high Set row command 1 byte (0x2B) low Row range 20 to 20 4 bytes: 00 14 00 14 high Write memory command 1 byte (0x2C) low The pixel (red, 0xF800) 2 bytes: F8 00 high

That is 13 bytes of traffic to color a single pixel. Keep this number in mind: it is the reason Chapters 5 and 6 teach you to send whole rectangles of pixels at once.

The Display Remembers

The Pico does not keep a copy of the picture, because the controller does. That is why you can draw one small box and leave everything else alone, and it is also why a bad wire can leave the screen showing old pixels instead of an error.

docs.title: The MEMS Microphone
docs.text: A MEMS microphone is a microphone built like a computer chip. MEMS stands for micro-electro-mechanical system: a membrane thinner than a hair is etched into silicon, and sound pressure makes it move, which changes an electrical signal. It is small, cheap, and consistent from one unit to the next, which is why phones use it.

docs.title: The INMP441 Board
docs.text:
The INMP441 is a MEMS microphone with the analog-to-digital converter inside the same package, so it sends finished numbers to the Pico. Its output is 24-bit audio on an I2S bus, and the kit asks for 12,800 samples each second. Its datasheet lists a response from about 60 Hz to 15 kHz, which easily covers the kit's 6,400 Hz limit from Chapter 3.

The board has six pins.

Pin Connects to Job SCK GP10 Serial clock from the Pico WS GP11 Word select from the Pico SD GP12 Serial data, microphone to Pico L/R GND Picks the left channel (3V3 would pick right) VDD 3V3 Power, a 3.3 V part GND GND Ground

Worked example. In a quiet room, test 06 reports a noise floor of about 12.5 bits. As a number, \( 2^{12.5} \approx 5{,}800 \). The largest 24-bit sample is \( 2^{23} = 8{,}388{,}608 \). The room noise is therefore about \( 20 \log_{10}(5800 / 8388608) \approx -63 \) dB below the loudest sound the microphone can report. Your own value will differ with the room, which is why the test calibrates instead of assuming.

Two Wires You Can Swap by Accident

The microphone's SCK and WS wires, and also SCK and SD, are easy to swap because the board's pin labels are tiny. A swapped microphone starts without any error and sends only zeros, so test 02 prints "flat line." Check in this order: SCK on GP10, WS on GP11, SD on GP12.

docs.title: The Speaker
docs.text:
A speaker turns an electrical signal into sound. A coil of wire attached to a paper or plastic cone sits in a magnetic field. When the signal flows through the coil, the cone moves in and out and pushes the air, recreating the pressure wave from Chapter 3. Speakers are rated by impedance in ohms (small ones are usually 4 or 8 ohms; check the label on yours) and by the power they can handle.

Worked example. The power in a speaker is \( P = V^2 / R \). To deliver 1 watt into a 4 ohm speaker the voltage across it must be \( V = \sqrt{P \times R} = \sqrt{1 \times 4} = 2 \) volts. The Pico's pins can only supply a tiny current, so they cannot drive a speaker directly. That is the job of the amplifier.

docs.title: The Class-D Amplifier
docs.text:
A class-D amplifier makes sound with switches. Its output transistors are always either fully on or fully off, and they flip thousands of times each second, varying the width of each pulse to match the sound. Because a transistor that is fully on or off wastes almost no power, class-D amplifiers are very efficient and run cool. That matters in a small USB-powered device.

Worked example. Suppose the speaker needs 1 watt. A class-D amplifier that is 90 percent efficient draws about \( 1 / 0.9 \approx 1.11 \) watts from the supply and wastes about 0.11 W as heat. An older design that is only 50 percent efficient would draw 2 watts and waste a full watt, enough to warm a small board.

docs.title: The MAX98357A Amplifier
docs.text:
The MAX98357A combines a digital-to-analog converter and a class-D amplifier in one chip. It takes digital audio over I2S and drives the speaker directly, so there is no separate converter to wire and no resistor to choose. Its breakout board has these connections.

Pin Connects to Job BCLK GP20 Bit clock from the Pico LRC GP21 Left/right (word select) clock from the Pico DIN GP19 Audio data from the Pico GAIN GP18 Sets loudness: the Pico can float it, pull it low, or push it high VIN VBUS (5 V) or 3V3 Power GND GND Ground Output terminals Speaker The amplified sound

The GAIN pin has three settings, chosen by what the pin is tied to. The kit's set_gain() function picks one in software, and the default is 9 dB.

Pin state Gain Tied high (to the amplifier's VIN) 6 dB (only if VIN is 3.3 V) Left floating (the default) 9 dB Tied to GND 12 dB

BCLK and LRC Must Be Neighbors

MicroPython's I2S needs the left/right clock on the pin right after the bit clock. Here BCLK is GP20 and LRC is GP21. If you move one without the other, I2S() raises an error. The same rule holds for the microphone: SCK on GP10 and WS on GP11.

docs.title: The Push Button
docs.text:
A push button (also called a tactile switch) is a switch that connects two wires only while you press it. The small square ones in the kit have four legs, but they are really two pairs. The two legs on one side are joined inside the button all the time, and pressing the button joins the two sides together.

That construction creates a common mistake. If you wire the button with both of its wires on the same side, the button is always connected and always reads "pressed." Place the button so that the two wires go to legs on opposite sides.

Worked example. To wire MODE, put one leg's wire on GP13 (physical pin 17) and the opposite side's wire on any GND. The kit's config.init_buttons() then sets GP13 as an input with a pull-up. The button reads 1 when released and 0 while pressed. Test 03 confirms it by printing each press and release.

docs.title: The Pull-Up Resistor
docs.text:
A pull-up resistor is a resistor that gently connects a pin to 3.3 V, so the pin has a definite value when nothing else is driving it. Without it, a button that is not pressed leaves the pin floating, which means it picks up stray signals and reads unpredictably. (On the board used to test this book, an unconnected GP16 happened to hold steady at 0, but nothing guarantees that.) With the pull-up, the pin reads 1 until the button connects it to ground, and then reads 0. The Pico has pull-up resistors built in, which Pin.PULL_UP turns on, so the buttons need no extra parts.

A pull-down resistor is the mirror image: it gently connects the pin to ground, so the pin reads 0 until something connects it to 3.3 V. The Pico has these built in too (Pin.PULL_DOWN), but there is a catch on the Pico 2 W. On the test board, GP16 and GP17 kept reading 1 with the pull-down turned on once the pin had been driven or pulled high, and did not fall back to 0. A third pin, GP9, did not do this. Driving the pin low first made it read 0. The pull-ups showed no problem, reading 1 every time. This looks like a known quirk of the RP2350 pads (check Raspberry Pi's RP2350 errata for the details). It is one more reason the kit's buttons use pull-ups, and if you ever need a pull-down, drive the pin low for a moment first or use a real resistor.

Test on GP16 Readings (40 each) Pull-up 40 ones Pull-down, pin driven low first 40 zeros Pull-down, pin driven high first 40 ones (the pull-down did not pull it low)

src/chapters/04-pico-kit-hardware/03-floating-pin-demo.py repeats this test on your board.

docs.title: Diagram: Pull-Up Button Circuit
docs.text:
Pull-Up Button Circuit

Type: microsim sim-id: pull-up-button-circuit Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: infer Learning Objective: The learner will infer the value a GPIO input pin reads for 6 button circuits, given the pin's pull setting, what the button's other leg connects to, and whether the button is pressed, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: push button, pull-up resistor, floating pin, GPIO input (all defined in the sections above this block and in Chapter 2).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 circuits the learner commits to "reads 1", "reads 0", or "unpredictable" before the result is shown. A prediction is correct when it matches the Pin reads column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt. Pressing the button in the example circuit and watching the reading is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A button always reads 1 when pressed. (2) A pin with nothing attached reads 0. (3) The pull-up is what makes the pin read 1 even while the button is pressed to ground. (4) A pull-down always pulls the pin to 0, even after the pin has been high.

Instructional Rationale: An Understand-level inference needs the learner to reason from a circuit's parts to a result. Predicting before the result is shown makes the learner apply the rule that a connected path wins over a pull.

Content:

The circuit shows a Pico input pin, an optional internal pull, and a button whose other leg connects to GND or to 3V3.

# Pin pull setting Button's other leg connects to Button Pin reads Why (shown as feedback) 1 Pull-up GND Released 1 Nothing pulls the pin down, so the pull-up holds it at 1. 2 Pull-up GND Pressed 0 The button connects the pin to GND, which beats the weak pull-up. 3 None (floating) GND Released unpredictable With no pull and no connection, the pin picks up stray signals. 4 Pull-up 3V3 Pressed 1 Both the pull-up and the button push the pin toward 3.3 V. 5 Pull-down 3V3 Pressed 1 The button connects the pin to 3V3, which beats the weak pull-down. 6 Pull-down (pin was low before) 3V3 Released 0 Nothing pulls the pin up, so the pull-down holds it at 0, as long as the pin was low before.

Provenance: The reasoning rule comes from the chapter section "The Pull-Up Resistor." The six circuits are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative." The reality check after circuit 6 comes from the measurement on GP16 and GP17 in the same section.

Rules: A connection from the pin to GND or 3V3 through a pressed button overrides the pin's internal pull (pull-up or pull-down). With a released button and a pull setting, the pin reads the pull's level (1 for pull-up, 0 for pull-down). With a released button and no pull, the pin reads an unpredictable value that the sim shows as alternating 0 and 1. A pull-down only pulls the pin to 0 if the pin was low before; the reality check shows the case where it was high.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores a sample circuit (pull-up, GND, button released) and presses the button to watch the reading change from 1 to 0.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. Circuit 1 is shown with the button state.
  3. The learner picks "reads 1," "reads 0," or "unpredictable."
  4. The sim shows the reading and the Why text, then moves to the next circuit.
  5. After circuit 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that circuit 4 is the wiring mistake that makes a button seem dead.
  6. The sim then shows an unscored reality check: a pin set to pull-down after it was driven high still reads 1 on the test board (GP16 and GP17), while a pull-up always reads 1. The learner is asked to explain, from a choice of two sentences, why the kit uses pull-ups. The correct sentence is "Pull-ups worked every time on the test board, and the pull-down did not." The other sentence is "Pull-ups and pull-downs behaved the same on the test board."

Feedback: 6 circuits, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The pin reads : ". The answer is revealed right after each pick, and a running score "n of 6" is shown. The reality check is not scored: a wrong choice shows the correct sentence and the table of readings.

Starting State: The sample circuit is shown with the button released and the pin reading 1, with the question "What will the pin read when the button is pressed?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that with a pull-up and the button to ground, a released button reads 1 and a pressed button reads 0, and that the kit uses the pull-up built into the Pico. The chapter also states that on the test board a pull-down on GP16 and GP17 kept reading 1 after the pin had been driven high, and that pull-ups were not affected.

docs.title: The Breadboard
docs.text:
A breadboard is a plastic board with rows of small holes. Metal strips under the holes connect them in groups, so you can join parts by pushing wires into the same group instead of soldering. In the middle area, each short row of five holes is connected, and a gap down the center separates the left half from the right. Along the long edges are power rails, which connect all the way along.

Worked example. Place the Pico so that it straddles the center gap, one row of its pins on each side. That leaves four free holes beside every pin, in the same connected group, so you can plug a wire right next to any pin. A wire in a hole beside GP13 is electrically connected to GP13.

Breadboard area How the holes connect Middle rows Groups of five holes in a row are connected Center gap Separates the two halves, so they are not connected Long edge rails All holes in one rail are connected, from end to end

docs.title: Dupont Wires
docs.text: Dupont wires are the thin jumper cables with small plastic ends. Male ends have a pin that pushes into a breadboard hole, and female ends have a socket that slides over the pins on a module. You need male-to-male wires between breadboard holes and male-to-female wires from the breadboard to a module's header. The display wiring in config.py records the color of each wire, which makes tracing a mistake much easier: SCL orange, SDA yellow, RST green, DC blue, CS purple, BL gray, VCC red, and GND black.

docs.title: The Pin Assignment Table
docs.text:
A pin assignment table is a table that lists, for every part, which Pico pin each of its wires goes to. It is the one document you wire from and debug against. Everything in the kit's config.py comes from this table.

Part Part pin Pico pin Physical pin Display SCL GP2 4 Display SDA GP3 5 Display RST GP4 6 Display DC GP5 7 Display CS GP6 9 Display BL GP7 10 Display VCC, GND 3V3, GND 36, any GND Microphone SCK GP10 14 Microphone WS GP11 15 Microphone SD GP12 16 Microphone L/R, GND GND any GND Microphone VDD 3V3 36 Button MODE one leg GP13 17 Button UP one leg GP14 19 Button DOWN one leg GP15 20 Buttons other legs GND any GND Amplifier DIN GP19 25 Amplifier BCLK GP20 26 Amplifier LRC GP21 27 Amplifier GAIN GP18 24 Amplifier VIN VBUS or 3V3 40 or 36 Amplifier GND GND any GND

Three rules hold the table together. First, each GP pin appears once, so no two wires share a pin. Second, the I2S pairs are neighbors: microphone SCK and WS on GP10 and GP11, amplifier BCLK and LRC on GP20 and GP21. Third, nothing connects to GP23, GP24, GP25, or GP29, which belong to the wireless chip.

The kit is built in stages, and each test checks exactly the parts wired so far. That makes any wiring error easy to localize.

Test Wire first What to look for 01 Nothing (just the Pico) The onboard LED blinks 02 Anything you have No warnings for the parts you wired 03 The three buttons Each press and release prints, then "PASS" 04 The display "Hello World!" inside a cyan ring 05 Amplifier and speaker A beep, a scale, three volumes 06 Microphone (with the display) The meter moves when you talk 07 Everything together Hold MODE, talk, hear it back

Wire One Part, Then Test

Do not wire all five parts and then run everything. Add one part, run its test from the table, and only then add the next. When a test fails, you know the problem is in the part you just added.

The last activity of the chapter puts the pin assignment table to work on six wiring listings that each contain one mistake.

docs.title: Diagram: Kit Wiring Fault Finder
docs.text:
Kit Wiring Fault Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: kit-wiring-fault-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine 6 wiring listings against the pin assignment table and identify the one wrong connection in each, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: pin assignment table, ground wiring, pull-up resistor, the I2S neighbor rule, the 3.3 V rule for the microphone (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each listing the learner selects the one line that does not match the pin assignment table. A selection is correct when it equals the Faulty line column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt. Reading the pin assignment table while answering is allowed, and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) A wiring mistake always produces an error message. (2) Any 5 V part can use the 5 V pin. (3) The two I2S pins can be assigned in either order.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level examination requires comparing a whole against a reference and locating the departure. A listing with exactly one fault trains the learner to check each line against the table, which is the same skill used when debugging a real kit.

Content:

Each listing shows the wires of one part as "part pin to Pico pin or rail." The reference is the table "The Pin Assignment Table" in this chapter.

# Part Listing shown Faulty line Correct connection What the learner would see (shown as feedback) 1 Microphone SCK to GP10; WS to GP11; SD to GP12; L/R to GND; VDD to VBUS (5 V); GND to GND VDD to VBUS (5 V) VDD to 3V3 The INMP441 is a 3.3 V part. A 5 V supply can damage it. 2 Microphone SCK to GP10; WS to GP13; SD to GP12; L/R to GND; VDD to 3V3; GND to GND WS to GP13 WS to GP11 I2S() raises "invalid ws (must be sck+1)", and GP13 is also the MODE button. 3 Amplifier BCLK to GP20; LRC to GP22; DIN to GP19; GAIN to GP18; VIN to VBUS; GND to GND LRC to GP22 LRC to GP21 I2S() raises an error because the left/right clock must be the pin right after the bit clock. 4 Button MODE One leg to GP13; the leg on the opposite side to 3V3 Opposite leg to 3V3 Opposite leg to GND With a pull-up, the pin always reads 1, so test 03 never reports a press. 5 Display SCL to GP2; SDA to GP3; RST to GP4; DC to GP5; CS to GP6; BL not connected; VCC to 3V3; GND to GND BL not connected BL to GP7 The screen stays dark in test 04 because the backlight never turns on. 6 Amplifier BCLK to GP20; LRC to GP21; DIN to GP19; GAIN to GP18; VIN to VBUS; GND not connected GND not connected GND to GND Test 05 is silent because the amplifier has no ground return.

Provenance: The listings and symptoms come from the kit README and the headers of tests 03, 04, and 05 in src/kits/study-buddy-base/, and from the table "The Pin Assignment Table" in this chapter.

Rules: Each listing has exactly one faulty line. A selection is correct only if it is the faulty line. The reference table is always available to the learner.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads listing 1 and selects the line that does not match the pin assignment table.
  2. The sim shows whether it was correct, the correct connection, and the symptom text.
  3. The learner continues through listing 6.
  4. After listing 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that only some mistakes produce an error message.

Feedback: 6 listings, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The faulty line is : ". The correct line is revealed right after each selection, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: Listing 1 is shown with the pin assignment table beside it and the question "Which line does not match the table?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the microphone pins SCK GP10, WS GP11, SD GP12, the amplifier pins BCLK GP20, LRC GP21, DIN GP19, GAIN GP18, the display backlight on GP7, and the MODE button on GP13.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
You now have the five parts, the rules that connect them, and a table to check every wire against. The Pico is the brain and the Wi-Fi link. The round display and its controller are the eyes. The INMP441 and its built-in converter are the ears. The MAX98357A and a speaker are the voice. Three buttons wired to ground with built-in pull-ups are the hands.

Key takeaways:

  • The kit has five parts: the Pico 2 W, the round display, the INMP441 microphone, the MAX98357A amplifier with a speaker, and three push buttons.
  • The RP2350 chip has two Cortex-M33 cores, 520 KB of SRAM, and a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radio chip that takes pins GP23, GP24, GP25, and GP29.
  • The display controller keeps the picture; the Pico sends commands and pixels over SPI, using DC to tell them apart.
  • Both the microphone and the amplifier use I2S, and each needs its word-select pin right after its clock pin.
  • The microphone is a 3.3 V part; the amplifier can use 5 V.
  • A push button wired to ground with a pull-up reads 0 when pressed.
  • Every part shares one ground, and wiring one part at a time with its test finds mistakes quickly.

Test yourself with these two questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

Your microphone starts without errors, but test 02 reports a flat line. What do you check first? Click to expand

The SCK, WS, and SD wires: SCK on GP10, WS on GP11, SD on GP12. A swapped microphone sends only zeros without any error. Then check that VDD is on 3V3 and that GND and L/R are both on ground.

Why does coloring one pixel take 13 bytes of SPI traffic? Click to expand

The driver must tell the controller which column and row to write (two commands with four bytes of range each), send the write-memory command, and then send the two bytes of the color. The overhead is far larger than the pixel, so Chapters 5 and 6 send whole rectangles at once.

Kit Wired and Understood

You just learned what each of the five parts does, how they share power and ground, and how to check every wire against the pin assignment table. With a wired kit and passing tests 01 to 07, you are ready to put pictures on that round screen.

In Chapter 5 we start with the display, and find out why drawing a whole frame is so slow.

docs.title: Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size
Summary
docs.text: This chapter shows how the 360 by 360 round display works. Students learn SPI, pixels, and RGB565 color, then calculate the size of a full frame and discover why redrawing everything on each update is too slow. After this chapter, students can draw to the display and explain why the next chapter's region-based approach is needed.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 13 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score SPI Bus 94 Pixel 193 Clock Face Geometry 4 SPI Display Driver 47 RGB565 Color 98 Fonts 2 Polar to Cartesian 2 Backlight Control 1 Frame Buffer 93 Color Themes 2 Frame Size Calculation 92 Full-Frame Update 45 Update Bandwidth 46

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems
  • Chapter 4: The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring

docs.title: Why a Screen Is a Math Problem
docs.text:
Your Study Buddy talks to people through a round screen. Putting a picture on it sounds simple, and in a few lines of code it is. The surprise comes when you ask for something smooth, like a moving level meter, while the microphone is also sending 40 ms of sound that must be handled on time. Then the screen turns out to be the slowest part of the whole device.

Pictures Cost Bytes

In this chapter you will draw on the round screen, and then do the arithmetic that explains why a full redraw is too slow for a device that must also listen. Let's listen closely! You will leave with a number you can calculate for yourself, and it will shape every display decision in the book.

docs.title: The SPI Bus
docs.text:
The display connects to the Pico over an SPI bus. SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is a way for two chips to exchange bytes over a few wires, one bit at a time. One chip is the controller (the Pico), and the other is the peripheral (the display). Four signals make up a full SPI bus.

Signal Also called Direction Display wire SCK Clock Pico to display SCL (GP2) MOSI Controller out, peripheral in Pico to display SDA (GP3) MISO Controller in, peripheral out Display to Pico Not used CS Chip select Pico to display CS (GP6)

The clock wire pulses once for every bit. On each pulse, the Pico puts the next bit on the MOSI wire, and the display reads it. This display never talks back, so the MISO wire (labeled SDO on the display board) is left unconnected.

The speed of the bus is its baud rate, in bits per second. The kit asks for 24 million bits per second, which MicroPython sets up like this.

spi = SPI(0, baudrate=24_000_000, sck=Pin(2), mosi=Pin(3))

The 0 selects SPI block 0, baudrate is the speed you request, and sck and mosi name the two data pins.

The Rate You Ask For Is Not Always the Rate You Get

MicroPython divides a 48 MHz clock and rounds down to the nearest rate it can make, so asking for 20 MHz gives 12 MHz, and nothing exists between 12 and 24 MHz. To see what you really got, print the SPI object. If the picture speckles on long wires, step down to 12,000,000.

The measurements in the kit's config.py show the pattern clearly.

You ask for (Hz) You get (Hz) 10,000,000 8,000,000 16,000,000 12,000,000 20,000,000 12,000,000 24,000,000 24,000,000 (the ceiling) 62,500,000 24,000,000

docs.title: Pixels and Coordinates
docs.text:
A pixel (picture element) is the smallest dot the screen can color. The 360 by 360 display has \( 360 \times 360 = 129{,}600 \) of them. You address each by two numbers, written (x, y). The x number counts columns from the left, and the y number counts rows from the top. The top-left pixel is (0, 0), x increases to the right, and y increases downward, which is the opposite of the graphs you draw in math class. The last pixel is (359, 359) and the center of the round screen is (180, 180).

Only the circle inside the square is visible. The kit stores the center in config.CENTER_X and config.CENTER_Y (both 180), the edge of the glass in config.RADIUS (180), and the largest circle you can see completely in config.SAFE_RADIUS (168).

Worked example. Is the pixel (20, 20) visible? Its distance from the center is \( \sqrt{(20-180)^2 + (20-180)^2} = \sqrt{25600 + 25600} \approx 226 \), which is larger than the radius 180, so it is hidden under the bezel in the corner. The pixel (180, 20) has distance \( |20 - 180| = 160 \), which is less than 168, so it is safely inside the visible ring.

Pixel Distance from center Visible? (180, 180) 0 Yes, the center (180, 20) 160 Yes, inside the safe ring (20, 20) about 226 No, in the corner (359, 180) 179 Barely, at the very edge

docs.title: RGB565 Color
docs.text:
Each pixel needs a color. A computer makes a color by mixing red, green, and blue light, each with a strength. Many systems use one byte (0 to 255) per color, which takes 3 bytes per pixel. This display uses a smaller format called RGB565 to save memory and time: it packs a color into just 16 bits (2 bytes).

The name tells you the split. Red gets 5 bits, green gets 6 bits, and blue gets 5 bits, for \( 5 + 6 + 5 = 16 \) bits. Five bits give 32 levels of red, 6 bits give 64 levels of green, and 5 bits give 32 levels of blue, so the format has \( 2^{16} = 65{,}536 \) colors. Green gets the extra bit because human eyes are most sensitive to green.

The kit builds a color with color565(red, green, blue), where each argument runs from 0 to 255. It keeps the top bits of each value and packs them.

def color565(red, green=0, blue=0):
    return (red & 0xF8) << 8 | (green & 0xFC) << 3 | blue >> 3

The & 0xF8 keeps the top 5 bits of red, & 0xFC keeps the top 6 bits of green, and blue >> 3 drops the low 3 bits of blue so that 5 remain. The shifts << 8 and << 3 slide each part to its place in the 16-bit number.

Worked example. Orange is (255, 128, 0). Red: \( 255 \,\&\, 0xF8 = 0xF8 \), shifted left 8 bits gives 0xF800. Green: \( 128 \,\&\, 0xFC = 0x80 \), shifted left 3 gives 0x0400. Blue is 0. Joining them gives \( 0xF800 + 0x0400 = 0xFC00 \). The driver sends the high byte first, so the two bytes on the wire are FC 00.

Color (R, G, B) RGB565 value Bytes sent Red (255, 0, 0) 0xF800 F8 00 Green (0, 255, 0) 0x07E0 07 E0 Blue (0, 0, 255) 0x001F 00 1F Yellow (255, 255, 0) 0xFFE0 FF E0 Cyan (0, 255, 255) 0x07FF 07 FF Orange (255, 128, 0) 0xFC00 FC 00 Gray (110, 110, 110) 0x6B6D 6B 6D

Try the mixer to see how the bits move.

docs.title: Diagram: RGB565 Color Mixer
docs.text:
RGB565 Color Mixer

Type: microsim sim-id: rgb565-color-mixer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-python/tree/main/docs/sims/rgb-color-mixer Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the 16-bit RGB565 value for 6 given colors, using the packing rule, with at least 5 of 6 correct within two attempts each.

Prerequisites: pixel, RGB565, bit masking and shifting (all defined in the section "RGB565 Color" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 colors the learner types the RGB565 value in hexadecimal. An answer is correct when it equals the RGB565 value column in Content, ignoring upper or lower case and a leading "0x". Mastery is 5 of 6 correct, with up to two attempts per color. Moving the exploration sliders and watching the bits is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) RGB565 stores 8 bits per color. (2) The extra bit goes to blue. (3) The low bits of each color are kept and the high bits are dropped.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation of a bit-packed value needs the learner to follow the masking and shifting rule step by step. Seeing the 16 bits change with the three color strengths gives the learner a way to check the arithmetic.

Content:

For exploration, the learner sets red, green, and blue strengths from 0 to 255 in steps of 1 (unit: none, default 255, 128, 0). The sim shows the color, the three kept bit groups (5, 6, and 5 bits), and the 16-bit value in binary and hexadecimal.

Challenge colors, in this order:

# Color (R, G, B) RGB565 value Why (shown as feedback) 1 Red (255, 0, 0) F800 Red keeps its top 5 bits (11111) in the top of the number. 2 Green (0, 255, 0) 07E0 Green keeps its top 6 bits (111111) in the middle. 3 Blue (0, 0, 255) 001F Blue keeps its top 5 bits (11111) in the bottom. 4 Yellow (255, 255, 0) FFE0 Red 11111 and green 111111 together make FFE0. 5 Orange (255, 128, 0) FC00 Green 128 keeps 100000, so the green bits are 0x0400 and red is 0xF800. 6 Gray (110, 110, 110) 6B6D Red 01101, green 011011, and blue 01101 pack to 0110101101101101.

Provenance: The packing rule is color565 from src/kits/study-buddy-base/lib/gc9b72.py. The values in the table were computed with that function.

Rules: value = ((R AND 0xF8) shifted left 8) OR ((G AND 0xFC) shifted left 3) OR (B shifted right 3), with R, G, and B whole numbers from 0 to 255. The result is a number from 0 to 65535 shown as four hexadecimal digits.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner drags the red, green, and blue controls and sees the color, the kept bit groups, and the 16-bit value update together.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. Challenge 1 shows the color and its (R, G, B) numbers.
  3. The learner types the RGB565 value in hexadecimal and submits.
  4. If it is wrong the first time, the learner may try once more. After a second wrong answer the sim shows the correct value and the Why text.
  5. After challenge 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that the 16-bit value only changes when a color crosses a multiple of 8 (or of 4 for green).

Feedback: 6 challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ". First incorrect: "Not quite. Check which bits each color keeps (5, 6, 5). Try again." Second incorrect: "The value is : ". A running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The mixer shows orange (255, 128, 0) with its bits, and the question "Which bits does each color keep?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that RGB565 uses 5, 6, and 5 bits, has 65,536 colors, and that orange (255, 128, 0) is 0xFC00.

docs.title: The SPI Display Driver
docs.text:
Something has to turn "draw a rectangle" into the right commands and bytes. That something is the SPI display driver, a MicroPython module for the display's controller chip. The kit's driver is lib/gc9b72.py, and its class GC9B72 takes the SPI bus and the control pins.

display = gc9b72.GC9B72(spi, dc=Pin(5, Pin.OUT), cs=Pin(6, Pin.OUT),
                        reset=Pin(4, Pin.OUT), backlight=Pin(7, Pin.OUT),
                        rotation=0)

You do not write this yourself: config.init_display() builds the bus, the pins, and the driver and returns the display object. The dc, cs, and reset arguments are the control wires from Chapter 4, and rotation turns the picture in steps of 90 degrees.

The driver's drawing methods all follow one pattern: they set a window on the screen, then stream the pixels for that window.

Method What it draws pixel(x, y, color) One pixel fill_rect(x, y, width, height, color) A solid rectangle fill(color) The whole screen in one color hline, vline, rect Lines and an outline line(x0, y0, x1, y1, color) A slanted line, one pixel at a time text(font, string, x, y, color, background) Characters from a bitmap font blit_buffer(buffer, x, y, width, height) A block of ready-made pixels

Notice what the table does not contain: a show() method. Many small displays hold a picture in the microcontroller's memory and send it all at once when you call show(). This driver has no such step. Every call streams its bytes to the display immediately, and the display's own memory keeps the result.

Print Your Sizes First

Before you call any draw method with a big rectangle, compute width * height * 2. That is how many bytes it will send, and it tells you in one second whether the call will be quick or slow.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text:
The driver has no built-in letters. Text comes from a font, which is a module that stores a small picture of each character. The kit includes two.

Font module Character size Characters across the screen vga1_8x16 (called SMALL_FONT) 8 by 16 pixels 45 vga1_bold_16x32 (called BIG_FONT) 16 by 32 pixels 22

The width of a string is its length times the character width. Test 04's "Hello World!" has 12 letters in the big font, so it is \( 12 \times 16 = 192 \) pixels wide, and the helper config.centered_text() computes the left edge as \( (360 - 192) / 2 = 84 \).

docs.title: The Frame Buffer Idea
docs.text:
A frame buffer is a block of memory that holds one complete picture, one value per pixel. A program draws into the frame buffer first, in memory, and then copies the whole thing to the screen. This approach is popular because drawing in memory is fast and the screen never shows a half-finished picture. MicroPython even includes a framebuf module for it.

A frame buffer for our display would hold 360 by 360 pixels at 2 bytes each. Whether that is practical depends on a calculation, and the next two sections do it.

docs.title: Frame Size Calculation
docs.text:
The frame size is the number of bytes in one complete picture. The frame size calculation is a single multiplication:

\[ \text{frame bytes} = \text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{bytes per pixel} \]

Worked example. For our display in RGB565, each pixel takes 2 bytes, so a full frame is

\[ 360 \times 360 \times 2 = 259{,}200 \text{ bytes} \approx 253 \text{ KB} \]

The Pico has about 520 KB of SRAM in total. A frame buffer would claim nearly half of all the memory in the chip, and it must be one unbroken block, which Chapter 2 showed is hard to find on a heap that has been in use. MicroPython itself and the audio buffers need the rest. So this kit does not keep a frame buffer on the Pico at all. The display controller already has the picture in its own memory.

The same formula works for any rectangle, and the answers differ enormously.

What is drawn Size Bytes (RGB565) Full frame 360 by 360 259,200 Full frame at 3 bytes per pixel 360 by 360 388,800 Visible circle only about 101,788 pixels about 203,575 Level meter bar in test 06 200 by 22 8,800 A clock-digit box 100 by 30 6,000 One big-font letter 16 by 32 1,024

Use the calculator below to practice the formula and to turn the bytes into a time.

docs.title: Diagram: Frame Size and Update Time Calculator
docs.text:
Frame Size and Update Time Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: frame-size-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the number of bytes in a rectangle of pixels and the time to send it over SPI at a given baud rate, for 6 challenges, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: pixel, RGB565, frame size calculation, baud rate (all defined in the sections above this block). The time formula is given in the Rules field and shown to the learner after the first challenge.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 challenges the learner types one number. An answer is correct when it is within the tolerance in the Content table. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Changing the exploration controls and watching the totals is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A pixel is one byte. (2) Sending data at 24 MHz means 24 million bytes per second. (3) Time depends on how many pixels are visible rather than how many are sent.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation of bytes and time needs repetition with immediate checking. Linking each answer to the same two formulas shows the learner that every display question reduces to a multiplication and a division.

Content:

For exploration, the learner sets the width (1 to 360, step 1, unit pixels, default 360), the height (1 to 360, step 1, unit pixels, default 360), the bytes per pixel (1, 2, or 3, default 2), and the baud rate (8,000,000, 12,000,000, or 24,000,000 bits per second, default 24,000,000). The sim shows the bytes, the bits, and the time in milliseconds.

Challenges, in this order:

# Question Answer Tolerance Why (shown as feedback) 1 Bytes in a full 360 by 360 frame at 2 bytes per pixel 259200 exactly 360 x 360 x 2 = 259,200. 2 Bytes in the 100 by 30 clock-digit box at 2 bytes per pixel 6000 exactly 100 x 30 x 2 = 6,000. 3 Bytes in a full 360 by 360 frame at 3 bytes per pixel 388800 exactly 360 x 360 x 3 = 388,800. 4 Bytes in the 200 by 22 level meter at 2 bytes per pixel 8800 exactly 200 x 22 x 2 = 8,800. 5 Milliseconds to send the 100 by 30 box at 24,000,000 bits per second 2.0 within 0.1 6,000 bytes x 8 = 48,000 bits, divided by 24,000,000 is 0.002 s. 6 Milliseconds to send a full 2-byte frame at 12,000,000 bits per second 172.8 within 0.1 259,200 x 8 = 2,073,600 bits, divided by 12,000,000 is 0.1728 s.

Provenance: The sizes come from the chapter sections "Pixels and Coordinates" and "Frame Size Calculation," and the 200 by 22 meter is the METER_WIDTH by METER_HEIGHT of test 06. The times use the formula in Rules and ignore command overhead.

Rules: bytes = width x height x bytes per pixel. bits = bytes x 8. time in seconds = bits / baud rate. Milliseconds = seconds x 1000. The sim does not include command bytes or Python overhead, and says so.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner changes the width, height, bytes per pixel, and baud rate, and sees the bytes, bits, and milliseconds update.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. Challenge 1 is shown.
  3. The learner types a number and submits.
  4. The sim shows whether it is correct and the Why text, then moves to the next challenge.
  5. After challenge 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that a full frame takes about 86 ms of wire time at 24 MHz with the default settings, while the small box takes about 2 ms. The calculator leaves out Python overhead, and says so.

Feedback: 6 challenges, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The calculator shows the full frame at 2 bytes per pixel and 24,000,000 bits per second, with the question "How long does it take to send this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a full frame is 259,200 bytes, a full frame at 24 MHz takes 86.4 ms, the 100 by 30 box is 6,000 bytes, and the 200 by 22 meter is 8,800 bytes.

docs.title: Update Bandwidth and the Full-Frame Update
docs.text:
The size of a frame tells us how much data there is. The update bandwidth tells us how fast the link can carry it. For SPI, the bandwidth is simply the baud rate: at 24,000,000 bits per second the display can receive at most 3,000,000 bytes per second, because there are 8 bits in a byte.

A full-frame update is a redraw of every pixel. Its minimum time is the bits in a frame divided by the bandwidth.

\[ t = \frac{259{,}200 \times 8}{24{,}000{,}000} = \frac{2{,}073{,}600}{24{,}000{,}000} = 0.0864 \text{ s} = 86.4 \text{ ms} \]

That is the best case, with every bit of the link doing useful work. In MicroPython the real time is longer, because each SPI call has overhead and the driver sends the screen in small chunks (fill_rect sends 256 pixels at a time, so a full screen needs 507 separate data writes). You can measure your own board with a few lines.

import time
import config

display = config.init_display()
config.set_backlight(True)

start = time.ticks_ms()
display.fill(config.RED)
elapsed = time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), start)
print("full-screen fill took", elapsed, "ms")

Your result will be at least 86 ms. At 86.4 ms per frame, the best possible rate is \( 1000 / 86.4 \approx 11.6 \) full frames per second.

The measurements below are from the board used to test this book. The measured times are about 1.5 times the wire time, and the gap is MicroPython's overhead: every SPI call, and every 256-pixel chunk, costs time on top of the bits.

You ask for (Hz) You get (Hz) Best case (ms) Measured (ms) Frames per second 8,000,000 8,000,000 259.2 334.6 3.0 12,000,000 12,000,000 172.8 231.9 4.3 20,000,000 12,000,000 172.8 232.0 4.3 24,000,000 24,000,000 86.4 129.4 7.7

So on this board a full-screen fill at the fastest speed takes about 129 ms, which is 7.7 full frames per second, not 11.6. Your own numbers will differ a little. Run src/chapters/05-display-basics/01-fill-timing.py and compare.

Worked example. Suppose you want the screen to update 10 times a second with full frames. The bandwidth needed is \( 259{,}200 \times 8 \times 10 = 20{,}736{,}000 \) bits per second, which is 86 percent of the 24 MHz link and leaves almost nothing for anything else. At 30 frames per second you would need 62.2 million bits per second, which is more than twice what the bus can carry. Smooth full-screen video is simply not possible on this link.

Now compare with the audio. The microphone frames from Chapter 3 are 40 ms long, and your program must read each one before the next arrives. A single full-frame update takes at least 86.4 ms, and 129 ms when measured, which is more than three whole audio frames. While the Pico is busy pushing pixels to the display, the microphone keeps producing samples that no one is reading.

Update Minimum time at 24 MHz Measured Fits in a 40 ms audio frame? Full frame (259,200 bytes) 86.4 ms 129 ms No, over three frames Level meter (8,800 bytes) 2.9 ms not measured Yes Clock-digit box (6,000 bytes) 2.0 ms not measured (a 100 by 32 box: 3.8 ms) Yes One big-font letter (1,024 bytes) 0.34 ms not measured Yes

Send Only What Changed

A moving meter changes only a small bar, but a full redraw sends every pixel, and nearly all of them are unchanged. The fix is not a faster bus. It is to stop sending pixels that did not change, and that is the whole subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: Clock Face Geometry and Polar to Cartesian
docs.text:
Many round-display designs, including the Chrono Smart Clock family this kit comes from, draw a clock face. A clock face is a good test of coordinate skills, because everything sits on a circle around the center (180, 180). Clock face geometry is the set of angles and distances you use to place marks and hands on that circle.

An hour mark sits every 30 degrees, since \( 360 / 12 = 30 \). Angles on a clock are measured from the 12 o'clock position, going clockwise. To place a point at a distance \( r \) from the center and an angle \( \theta \), you convert from polar coordinates (angle and distance) to Cartesian coordinates (x and y). This is polar to Cartesian conversion.

\[ x = c_x + r \sin\theta, \qquad y = c_y - r \cos\theta \]

Here \( (c_x, c_y) = (180, 180) \). The minus sign in the second formula is there because y grows downward on the screen, as noted earlier.

Worked example. Place the 3 o'clock mark on a ring of radius 150. The angle is 90 degrees, so \( x = 180 + 150 \times 1 = 330 \) and \( y = 180 - 150 \times 0 = 180 \). The 1 o'clock mark has angle 30 degrees: \( x = 180 + 150 \times 0.5 = 255 \) and \( y = 180 - 150 \times 0.866 \approx 50 \).

import math
import config
import shapes

display = config.init_display()
config.set_backlight(True)
display.fill(config.BLACK)

for hour in range(12):
    angle = math.radians(hour * 30)
    x = config.CENTER_X + round(150 * math.sin(angle))
    y = config.CENTER_Y - round(150 * math.cos(angle))
    shapes.circle(display, x, y, 4, config.WHITE, config.FILL)

The loop visits each hour, turns it into an angle in radians with math.radians, converts to x and y, and draws a small filled circle there. Twelve dots appear around the screen.

Hour Angle Position on a radius-150 ring 12 0 degrees (180, 30) 1 30 degrees (255, 50) 3 90 degrees (330, 180) 6 180 degrees (180, 330) 9 270 degrees (30, 180)

docs.title: Backlight Control
docs.text: The display's picture is only visible because of a light behind it, the backlight, which is controlled by the BL wire on GP7. config.set_backlight(True) drives that pin high to turn the light on, and False turns it off. Turning the backlight off does not erase the picture, because the controller still holds it, so turning it back on brings the old image back instantly. That makes it a handy way to implement a screen-off or sleep mode later.

docs.title: Color Themes
docs.text:
A color theme is a named set of colors used together, for example a background, a text color, and an accent. Putting them in one place lets you restyle the whole display by changing a single line, and it will let each school pick its own look in Chapter 16.

NIGHT = {"background": config.BLACK, "text": config.WHITE, "accent": config.CYAN}
DAY = {"background": config.WHITE, "text": config.BLACK, "accent": config.BLUE}
theme = NIGHT
display.fill(theme["background"])

A good theme keeps strong contrast between text and background, so words stay readable in a bright classroom.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
You can now describe the screen from the wires up. The Pico sends bytes over an SPI bus at up to 24 million bits per second. The driver wraps those bytes in commands, and each pixel is a 16-bit RGB565 value. A full frame is 259,200 bytes, which takes at least 86.4 ms to send (129 ms when measured), and that is more than three audio frames. No frame buffer lives on the Pico, because it would use about half of all SRAM.

Key takeaways:

  • SPI is a clocked serial bus; the display uses the clock and data wires only, at up to 24 MHz, but the rate you ask for may be rounded down.
  • A pixel is addressed by (x, y), with (0, 0) at the top left and y increasing downward; the center is (180, 180).
  • RGB565 packs a color into 16 bits (5 red, 6 green, 5 blue), giving 65,536 colors.
  • The frame size formula is width times height times bytes per pixel, so a full frame is 259,200 bytes.
  • The best-case time for a full frame at 24 MHz is 86.4 ms, about 11.6 frames per second; measured on the test board it is 129 ms, about 7.7 frames per second.
  • Update bandwidth, not drawing logic, is what limits the screen, so send only what changed.
  • Polar to Cartesian conversion places clock marks: \( x = c_x + r\sin\theta \), \( y = c_y - r\cos\theta \).

Test yourself with these two questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

How many bytes does a 120 by 50 rectangle take in RGB565, and how long to send it at 24,000,000 bits per second? Click to expand

\( 120 \times 50 \times 2 = 12{,}000 \) bytes, which is 96,000 bits. Divided by 24,000,000 that is 0.004 s, or 4 ms.

Why does the kit not keep a frame buffer on the Pico? Click to expand

A full frame buffer is 259,200 bytes, nearly half of the chip's 520 KB of SRAM, and it needs one unbroken block of memory. The display controller already holds the picture, so the Pico can send only the parts that change.

From Pixels to Bandwidth

You just calculated that a full frame is 259,200 bytes and takes 86.4 ms at best and 129 ms measured, and you packed colors into RGB565. That arithmetic is the reason the next chapter's region updates exist.

In Chapter 6 we stop redrawing everything and write only the pieces that changed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter teaches students to write directly to the display, one region at a time. They set a drawing window, track dirty regions, and use them to render text, icons, sprites, and animation. It ends by loading images and displaying a school mascot inside the round display mask.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 13 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Direct Region Write 44 Drawing Window 19 Dirty Region 17 Text Rendering 1 Hand Drawing 1 Icons 2 Region Layout 14 Sprite 1 Animation 2 Image Loading 4 School Mascot 3 Round Display Mask 1 Display Refresh Rate 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems
  • Chapter 5: Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size

docs.title: Send Only What Changed
docs.text:
Chapter 5 ended with a hard number: a full-frame update costs at least 86.4 ms (129 ms when measured), and your audio frames arrive every 40 ms. The way out is not a faster wire. It is a smarter habit: whenever something on the screen changes, find the smallest rectangle that contains the change, and send only that.

Small Boxes, Fast Screen

By the end of this chapter your screen will update a level meter in a few milliseconds and show a picture of a school mascot inside the round glass. Let's listen closely! Fast displays are mostly about knowing what not to redraw.

docs.title: The Drawing Window
docs.text:
When the display controller receives pixels, it needs to know where they go. The drawing window is a rectangle on the screen that the controller is ready to fill. You set it by sending the column range, the row range, and the "write memory" command, which are exactly the three commands you traced in Chapter 4. After that, every pixel you send lands inside the window, filling it in reading order: left to right along the top row, then the next row down, and so on until the window is full.

Worked example. Set a window of 4 columns and 2 rows with its top-left at (10, 20). The window covers x from 10 to 13 and y from 20 to 21. You then send 8 pixels. They land like this.

Pixel sent Lands at (x, y) 1st (10, 20) 2nd (11, 20) 3rd (12, 20) 4th (13, 20) 5th (10, 21) 6th (11, 21) 7th (12, 21) 8th (13, 21)

The driver hides these steps inside its private _set_window() method. You will rarely call it yourself, but you must know the reading order, because it tells you how to arrange pixels in a buffer.

docs.title: Direct Region Write
docs.text:
A direct region write is the technique built on that window: set the window to the rectangle you want, then stream all of its pixels in one go. Compare the cost of doing the same job two ways. To paint a 100 by 30 box one pixel at a time, you call pixel() 3,000 times, and each call sends 13 bytes (Chapter 4), a total of 39,000 bytes. To paint it with a single fill_rect(), the driver sets the window once (11 bytes of commands and ranges) and then sends 3,000 pixels at 2 bytes each, a total of 6,011 bytes, about one-sixth as much.

Method Calls Bytes on the wire Minimum time at 24 MHz Measured pixel() 3,000 times 3,000 39,000 13 ms 1,593 ms fill_rect() once 1 6,011 2.0 ms 4.3 ms blit_buffer() once 1 6,011 2.0 ms 3.1 ms

The last column was measured on the board used to test this book. The per-pixel loop took about 1.6 seconds, roughly 370 times as long as one fill_rect(), because each pixel() call makes six separate SPI writes and the wire time is a tiny part of it. The two single-call methods were within about 2 ms of their wire-time minimum. You can repeat the measurement with src/chapters/06-display-regions-and-drawing/01-pixel-vs-fillrect.py.

For a region with different colors in it, you build the pixels in a buffer and send them with blit_buffer(buffer, x, y, width, height). The buffer is a bytearray of width * height * 2 bytes, ordered row by row, with each color as two bytes, high byte first.

width, height = 4, 2
pixels = bytearray(width * height * 2)

for i in range(width * height):
    color = config.RED if i % 2 == 0 else config.BLUE
    pixels[i * 2] = color >> 8
    pixels[i * 2 + 1] = color & 0xFF

display.blit_buffer(pixels, 10, 20, width, height)

The loop alternates red and blue pixels, splits each 16-bit color into its two bytes, and sends the whole 4 by 2 block with one call.

A Buffer of the Wrong Size

If the buffer holds fewer bytes than width * height * 2, the last pixels of the window are never filled. If it holds more, the extra pixels wrap into the wrong place. When a picture looks sheared or has stripes, print len(buffer) and compare it with width * height * 2.

docs.title: Dirty Regions
docs.text:
A dirty region is a rectangle whose content on the screen is out of date because the underlying data changed. Updating the screen then becomes a loop of three simple steps: remember what you drew last time, compare it with what you should draw now, and redraw only the regions where the two differ.

The kit's test 06 does this for its level meter. It keeps drawn_width, the width of the bar currently on screen, and only redraws when the new width differs by at least 2 pixels.

width = int(METER_WIDTH * meter_fraction(bits))
if abs(width - drawn_width) >= 2:
    display.fill_rect(METER_X, METER_Y, width, METER_HEIGHT, color)
    display.fill_rect(METER_X + width, METER_Y,
                      METER_WIDTH - width, METER_HEIGHT, TRACK)
    drawn_width = width

The if is the dirty test. If the meter has not moved by 2 pixels, nothing is sent at all. Otherwise two rectangles are drawn: the filled bar and the empty track after it. The 2-pixel margin stops the bar from flickering on tiny changes.

The status line in the same test uses a different dirty test. It stores whether the room was loud on the last frame (heard) and redraws the words "I hear you!" or "Listening..." only when that value flips. Most frames, the status region sends zero bytes.

The meter's savings are easy to measure. src/chapters/06-display-regions-and-drawing/03-dirty-meter.py drives the same meter three ways for 150 frames each. On the test board:

Method Bytes per frame Time per frame Redraw the whole meter every frame 8,822 6.4 ms Test 06's rule (redraw only if the width moved 2 or more pixels) 7,116 5.2 ms Draw only the slice that changed 271 0.8 ms

Test 06's rule helps a little because this wave moves quickly. Drawing only the changed slice cut the bytes by 97 percent and the time by a factor of eight.

Remember, Compare, Redraw

Dirty-region code always has a memory: the last value drawn. Without it, the program cannot tell a change from a repeat. When your display flickers or runs slowly, ask first: what is this code remembering, and when does it compare?

docs.title: Text Rendering
docs.text:
Text rendering draws characters from a font into the window. The driver's text(font, string, x, y, color, background) method draws each glyph with its background color, so a glyph is an opaque rectangle. That means drawing new text over old text covers the old letters, but only inside the cells the new text uses.

If the new text is shorter than the old text, the leftover letters stay on screen. The kit solves this by padding every string to a fixed width, as in this helper from tests 06 and 07.

def put(text, y, font, color, width):
    config.centered_text(display, font, text.center(width), y, color)

The str.center(width) method adds spaces on both sides until the string is width characters long. Drawing "I hear you!" and "Listening..." both at width 14 means the second one fully erases the first, with no separate erase step.

Pad the Text, Skip the Erase

Pick the longest string a text region will ever show, and pad every string to that many characters. One text() call then draws and erases in a single pass, and the region never needs a separate clearing step.

docs.title: Hand Drawing
docs.text: Hand drawing means building a picture from shapes you place yourself in code, instead of loading a stored image. The kit's shapes.py provides the shapes: circle, ring, ellipse, poly, and triangle. Everything is built from horizontal runs, because on this display one hline of forty pixels costs far less than forty calls to pixel(). A face made of two filled circles for eyes and a bottom-half ellipse arc for a smile is a few lines of code, and it sends far fewer bytes than a stored image of the same size would.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text: An icon is a small, simple picture that stands for an idea: a Wi-Fi symbol, a microphone, a speaker. Icons live in fixed boxes, commonly 24 by 24 or 32 by 32 pixels. A 32 by 32 icon is \( 32 \times 32 \times 2 = 2{,}048 \) bytes, so it redraws in under 1 ms. The best habit is to draw each icon once into a buffer and then blit_buffer() it whenever its state changes. A status icon's dirty test is the simplest of all: redraw only when the state flips from, say, "connected" to "disconnected."

docs.title: Sprites
docs.text:
A sprite is a small image that you place and move around, such as a mascot's eye or a bouncing dot. In the kit, shapes.sprite(width, height, background) makes a blank buffer, sprite_pixel() sets a pixel in it, and display.blit_buffer() stamps it on the screen.

The plain blit_buffer() is opaque: it paints the sprite's whole rectangle, including its background. To make part of the sprite transparent, the kit offers shapes.blit_keyed(), which skips every pixel equal to a key color, black by default. It is slower because it sends the sprite in runs of visible pixels, so use it for small sprites and prefer plain blit_buffer() when the sprite can have a solid background.

dot = shapes.sprite(16, 16, config.BLACK)
for y in range(16):
    for x in range(16):
        if (x - 8) ** 2 + (y - 8) ** 2 <= 49:
            shapes.sprite_pixel(dot, 16, x, y, config.CYAN)
shapes.blit_keyed(display, dot, 100, 100, 16, 16)

The loops build a cyan disc of radius 7 inside a black 16 by 16 sprite. The blit_keyed call then stamps only the cyan pixels, leaving whatever was behind the dot visible. A 16 by 16 sprite is 512 bytes.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Animation is a sequence of small updates that look like motion. On this display, the trick is the same as before: do not redraw the picture, redraw only what moved. For a ball that slides to the right by 4 pixels each frame, the pixels that change are a 4-pixel strip left behind by the ball and the new pixels it covers.

BALL = 20
y = 90
x = 40
display.fill_rect(x, y, BALL, BALL, config.CYAN)

while x < 280:
    display.fill_rect(x, y, 4, BALL, config.BLACK)      # erase the strip
    x += 4
    display.fill_rect(x + BALL - 4, y, 4, BALL, config.CYAN)   # new strip
    time.sleep_ms(20)

Each pass erases a 4 by 20 strip on the left and fills a 4 by 20 strip on the right, 80 pixels each, or 160 bytes each, instead of the whole 20 by 20 box. This ball is a square, and a round ball needs shapes.circle, but the dirty-region idea is identical.

The picture changes at most as fast as your loop and your bandwidth allow. Frames that arrive faster than the eye can follow, around 10 to 15 per second for simple motion, are enough to look smooth.

docs.title: Region Layout
docs.text:
A region layout is the plan that divides the screen into named rectangles, each updated on its own. With a layout, "the time changed" becomes "redraw the time region and nothing else." A layout for the Study Buddy needs five regions. The positions below were chosen so that all four corners of every rectangle are inside the safe circle of radius 168 around (180, 180).

Region x y Width Height Bytes (RGB565) Min time at 24 MHz Measured Status bar 120 30 120 20 4,800 1.6 ms 3.0 ms Time 130 72 100 32 6,400 2.1 ms 3.8 ms Mascot 148 112 64 64 8,192 2.7 ms 4.6 ms Spectrum 80 190 200 40 16,000 5.3 ms 8.5 ms Agent message 60 240 240 32 15,360 5.1 ms 8.2 ms All five together 50,752 16.9 ms 28.1 ms

Redrawing every region costs 50,752 bytes: 16.9 ms of wire time, and 28.1 ms when measured on the test board (07-region-layout.py). That is about 4.6 times faster than the 129 ms measured for the 259,200-byte full frame, but it is still 70 percent of one 40 ms audio frame, which is why a frame should redraw only the regions that changed. In practice most frames redraw one or two regions, and the spectrum region alone takes 8.5 ms when measured (5.3 ms of wire time).

Now apply the dirty-region rule to six events. For each, decide which regions need redrawing.

docs.title: Diagram: Dirty Region Planner
docs.text:
Run Dirty Region Planner Fullscreen

Prerequisites: dirty region, region layout, direct region write (all defined in the sections above this block, including the five regions in the table "Region Layout").

Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Viewing the region sizes before answering is allowed and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) Any event requires a full-screen redraw. (2) A region should be redrawn on every frame whether or not its content changed. (3) Changing the mascot's pose does not require redrawing the mascot region.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level use of a rule requires the learner to carry it out on new cases. Deciding the set of dirty regions for each event, and then seeing the byte cost of the choice next to the cost of a full frame, ties the rule to the bandwidth reason for it.

The sim shows the five regions of the table "Region Layout" with their byte sizes: Status bar 4,800; Time 6,400; Mascot 8,192; Spectrum 16,000; Agent message 15,360. A full frame is 259,200 bytes.

docs.title: The Round Display Mask
docs.text:
The round display mask is the shape of the visible area: a circle of radius 180 centered on (180, 180), or radius 168 for the area that is always fully visible. A rectangle that pokes out of the circle wastes pixels on the hidden corners.

For any row, you can compute the width of the visible span from the circle equation. A row at vertical distance \( dy \) from the center has half-width \( \sqrt{r^2 - dy^2} \).

Worked example. Row y = 20 is 160 pixels above the center. With r = 168 the half-width is \( \sqrt{168^2 - 160^2} = \sqrt{2624} \approx 51 \). So only the x range from about 129 to 231 (102 pixels) is visible on that row, not the full 360. Content placed near the top or bottom of the screen has to be narrow. Content near the middle can be wide.

Row y Distance from center Visible x range (r = 168) Visible width 20 160 129 to 231 102 60 120 62 to 298 235 120 60 23 to 337 314 180 0 12 to 348 336

You apply the mask in two ways: by choosing region rectangles whose corners fall inside the circle (as the layout table does), and by shaping images so that their corners are black, as the next section does.

docs.title: Image Loading
docs.text:
An image is just a long list of RGB565 pixels, so image loading means reading those bytes from a file and sending them to a window. The work splits between your computer and the Pico. On your computer, a small Python script resizes the picture, blacks out everything outside a circle, and writes the pixels as raw RGB565 bytes, high byte first. On the Pico, a loader reads the file in chunks and sends each chunk with blit_buffer().

The conversion script uses the Pillow imaging library (pip install pillow) and runs on your computer, not on the Pico.

import sys
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw

def convert(src, dst, size=120):
    image = Image.open(src).convert("RGBA")
    image.thumbnail((size, size))
    canvas = Image.new("RGBA", (size, size), (0, 0, 0, 255))
    offset = ((size - image.width) // 2, (size - image.height) // 2)
    canvas.paste(image, offset, image)
    mask = Image.new("L", (size, size), 0)
    ImageDraw.Draw(mask).ellipse((0, 0, size - 1, size - 1), fill=255)
    black = Image.new("RGBA", (size, size), (0, 0, 0, 255))
    canvas = Image.composite(canvas, black, mask)
    rgb = canvas.convert("RGB").tobytes()
    with open(dst, "wb") as out:
        for i in range(0, len(rgb), 3):
            r, g, b = rgb[i], rgb[i + 1], rgb[i + 2]
            value = (r & 0xF8) << 8 | (g & 0xFC) << 3 | b >> 3
            out.write(value.to_bytes(2, "big"))

convert(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

The function shrinks the picture to fit in a 120 by 120 square, centers it on black, keeps only the pixels inside the inscribed circle, and writes each pixel with the same packing rule as color565. A 120 by 120 image makes a file of \( 120 \times 120 \times 2 = 28{,}800 \) bytes. Copy it to the Pico with mpremote fs cp sage.rgb565 :sage.rgb565.

The loader on the Pico reads the file a few rows at a time so that it never holds the whole image in memory.

def show_image(display, path, x, y, size, rows_per_chunk=10):
    chunk = bytearray(size * rows_per_chunk * 2)
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for row in range(0, size, rows_per_chunk):
            f.readinto(chunk)
            display.blit_buffer(chunk, x, y + row, size, rows_per_chunk)

The buffer chunk holds 10 rows, which is \( 120 \times 10 \times 2 = 2{,}400 \) bytes. readinto fills it from the file with no new allocation, and blit_buffer places it at the right row. Twelve chunks cover the 120 rows. The size must divide evenly by rows_per_chunk, which it does here. A call such as show_image(display, "sage.rgb565", 120, 120, 120) centers the image on the screen.

Loading reads 28,800 bytes from flash and sends them over SPI, a minimum of \( 28{,}800 \times 8 / 24{,}000{,}000 \approx 9.6 \) ms (20 ms when measured on the test board). You do it once when a screen appears, not every frame.

docs.title: The School Mascot
docs.text:
A school mascot is the character that gives each school's device its own identity. In this book the base character is Sage the owl, and Chapter 16 lets each school swap in its own. A mascot image is just an image like the one above, so the same pipeline applies: choose a picture, convert it, copy it, show it in the mascot region.

A mascot needs three design choices for a round display.

  • Keep the important part in the middle. Faces near the corners of the square image are cut by the mask.
  • Use a plain background. A flat color around the character compresses the information and avoids visual noise on a small screen.
  • Keep it small. The layout above gives the mascot a 64 by 64 region (8,192 bytes), and a larger 120 by 120 image costs 28,800 bytes. Bigger pictures are fine for a splash screen, but they should not be redrawn every frame.

docs.title: Display Refresh Rate
docs.text:
The display refresh rate is how many times per second the picture on the screen is updated, measured in hertz. Two different rates are easy to confuse. The panel itself continuously redraws the glass from the controller's memory at a fixed rate that you cannot change. The rate that matters for animation is the update rate: how often your program sends new pixels.

The update rate is limited by the regions you send. If the spectrum region took its wire-time minimum of 5.3 ms, the display could in theory be updated about 190 times a second. Measured, it takes 8.5 ms, about 118 times a second. The audio frame arrives every 40 ms, so the useful rate is 25 per second either way. That is more than enough to look smooth, as long as the loop has time left over for the audio work.

Update Minimum time Measured Maximum rate, measured Full frame 86.4 ms 129 ms 7.7 per second Spectrum region 5.3 ms 8.5 ms 118 per second Time region 2.1 ms 3.8 ms 263 per second Audio frame cadence 40 ms 25 per second

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
You now draw the way a fast embedded display has to: set a window, stream only the pixels that changed, and remember what is on screen so the next frame can tell what changed. Text pads itself to erase old letters, icons and sprites live in small buffers, and images arrive from flash in chunks.

Key takeaways:

  • A drawing window is a rectangle that receives pixels in reading order; a direct region write sets the window and then streams the pixels in one go.
  • A single fill_rect of 100 by 30 pixels sends about one-sixth of the bytes of 3,000 pixel() calls.
  • A dirty region is a rectangle that is out of date; remember what you drew, compare, and redraw only where it differs.
  • Pad text to a fixed width so that one call draws and erases.
  • A region layout names the rectangles; the five-region layout costs 50,752 bytes if all are redrawn, which took 28 ms when measured (16.9 ms of wire time), versus 129 ms measured for a full frame.
  • The round display mask means rectangles near the top or bottom must be narrow; images are masked to a circle when converted.
  • Image loading reads raw RGB565 from flash a few rows at a time and sends each chunk with blit_buffer.

Test yourself with these two questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

A string shows 'Listening...' and is then replaced by 'Done', but part of the old word is still visible. What went wrong and how do you fix it? Click to expand

The new string is shorter, so only its own cells were redrawn. Pad both strings to the same fixed width with str.center(width), so the second call covers every cell the first one used.

Why is the mascot region 8,192 bytes and not 8,192 pixels? Click to expand

The region is 64 by 64 pixels, which is 4,096 pixels, and each RGB565 pixel takes 2 bytes, so \( 4096 \times 2 = 8{,}192 \) bytes.

Regions, Not Frames

You just learned to set a drawing window, track dirty regions, lay out five independent regions that cost about 28 ms instead of 129 ms, and load a masked mascot from flash. Your screen can now keep up with your microphone.

In Chapter 7 we give the device its hands: three buttons, a state machine, and device modes.

docs.title: Buttons, State Machines, and Device Modes
Summary
docs.text: This chapter builds the physical interface for the device. Students read the Mode, Up, and Down buttons reliably with debouncing and edge detection, add long presses and menus, and organize the device's behavior as a state machine. They also learn non-blocking code so button handling never stalls the audio loop later in the book.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:
