If \( j \) and "imaginary" sound intimidating, that is normal, because the word is unfortunate. In the code there is nothing imaginary: each result is two ordinary numbers, re[k] and im[k]. Run 01-dft-by-hand.py and follow the four-number example term by term, and it will click.

docs.title: The FFT: Same Answer, a Hundred Times Less Work
docs.text:
The FFT (fast Fourier transform) is an algorithm that computes exactly the same \( N \) numbers as the DFT with far less arithmetic. The derivation is outside this course, but the shape of the result is easy to see. The FFT splits the job into \( \log_2 N \) stages. In each stage it combines pairs of numbers with a small operation called a butterfly, and each stage needs \( N/2 \) butterflies. The total is \( (N/2)\log_2 N \) butterflies instead of \( N^2 \) multiply-adds.

Worked example. For \( N = 512 \), \( \log_2 512 = 9 \), so the FFT does \( 256 \times 9 = 2{,}304 \) butterflies, against 262,144 for the DFT, a ratio of 113.8. 02-fft-vs-dft.py prints the whole table:

N DFT: \( N^2 \) FFT: \( (N/2)\log_2 N \) Ratio 8 64 12 5.3 64 4,096 192 21.3 256 65,536 1,024 64.0 512 262,144 2,304 113.8 1,024 1,048,576 5,120 204.8

A butterfly is not the same size as a DFT term (a butterfly takes four multiplications and six additions), so read the last column as "about a hundred times less work". The saving grows with \( N \): doubling the frame quadruples the DFT's work but only a little more than doubles the FFT's. This is what makes real-time spectra possible on a microcontroller at all.

Faster, Not Rougher

The FFT is not an approximation of the DFT. It gives the same numbers, to rounding, by reusing partial results instead of recomputing them, like adding a column of figures once and reusing the subtotals.

Before the code, three terms. Each butterfly multiplies one of its two numbers by a twiddle factor; the pairs are found by first reordering the samples with a bit-reversal table; and all of it happens in place. The next three subsections define them.

docs.title: Twiddle Factors
docs.text:
A twiddle factor is the constant that a butterfly multiplies by. It is a point on a circle, \( W_N^k = \cos(2\pi k/N) - j\sin(2\pi k/N) \), the same cosine and sine probes the DFT used. There are only \( N/2 \) different ones, because the rest repeat or are negatives of these. For \( N = 512 \) that is 256 pairs of numbers. Computing a sine takes far longer than looking one up, so make_tables() computes the cosines and sines once, at start-up, into two arrays of 256 entries (1,024 bytes each as 4-byte floats), and the FFT only reads them.

k Angle \( 2\pi k/8 \) Cosine Sine 0 0 degrees 1.0000 0.0000 1 45 degrees 0.7071 0.7071 2 90 degrees 0.0000 1.0000 3 135 degrees -0.7071 0.7071

The table shows the four distinct factors for an 8-point FFT; \( W_8^4 \) to \( W_8^7 \) are the negatives of these. In the code, the sign of the sine is applied inside the butterfly: tr = re[b]*c + im[b]*s and ti = im[b]*c - re[b]*s.

docs.title: The Bit-Reversal Table
docs.text:
The butterflies work most easily when the inputs are in a scrambled order: the sample that belongs at position \( i \) is moved to the position whose binary number is \( i \) written backwards. A bit-reversal table stores that new position for every index, so the reorder is a lookup, and make_tables() builds it once.

Index Binary Reversed New position 0 000 000 0 1 001 100 4 2 010 010 2 3 011 110 6 4 100 001 1 5 101 101 5 6 110 011 3 7 111 111 7

Index 1 and 4 swap, and 3 and 6 swap, while 0, 2, 5, and 7 stay where they are. The code swaps only when rev[i] > i, so every pair swaps exactly once and nothing is swapped back. For \( N = 512 \) the table has 512 entries of 2 bytes, 1,024 bytes in all.

docs.title: In Place, and for Real Input
docs.text:
The FFT is an in-place transform: each butterfly reads two numbers and writes its two results back into the same two slots, so the output overwrites the input and no second buffer is needed. The whole transform for 512 points lives in two arrays of 512 4-byte floats, 4,096 bytes together. The price is that the original samples are gone afterward; keep a copy if you need them. In Chapter 10 this matters for a different reason: an in-place algorithm allocates no memory while it runs.

The microphone samples are real-valued input: ordinary numbers with no imaginary part. The FFT is built for complex input, so you load the samples into the re array and fill the im array with zeros. For real input, the output has a pattern, which you saw in the four-number example: \( X[N-k] \) is the mirror image of \( X[k] \) (its complex conjugate), so the second half of the output repeats the first half. Only bins 0 to \( N/2 \) carry new information. That is why the kit uses 256 of the 512 outputs. (Clever programs use the redundancy to transform two real frames with one complex FFT; this book does not.)

def fft(re, im, tables):
    rev, cos_t, sin_t = tables
    n = len(re)
    for i in range(n):                          # step 1: bit-reversal reorder
        j = rev[i]
        if j > i:
            re[i], re[j] = re[j], re[i]
            im[i], im[j] = im[j], im[i]
    half = 1
    while half < n:                             # step 2: log2(n) stages
        stride = n // (2 * half)                # twiddle step for this stage
        for start in range(0, n, 2 * half):
            for k in range(half):
                a = start + k
                b = a + half
                c = cos_t[k * stride]
                s = sin_t[k * stride]
                tr = re[b] * c + im[b] * s      # twiddle times the second number
                ti = im[b] * c - re[b] * s
                re[b] = re[a] - tr              # the butterfly: difference ...
                im[b] = im[a] - ti
                re[a] += tr                     # ... and sum, written in place
                im[a] += ti
        half *= 2

Read it in two steps. Step 1 is the bit-reversal reorder. Step 2 has three nested loops: the while loop is the stage (half doubles from 1 to 256, giving 9 stages), the for start loop walks across the groups, and the for k loop does the butterflies inside a group. For the 8-point example the stages pair the following positions:

Stage Distance (half) Pairs combined Twiddle indices used (k * stride) 1 1 (0,1) (2,3) (4,5) (6,7) 0 2 2 (0,2) (1,3) (4,6) (5,7) 0, 2 3 4 (0,4) (1,5) (2,6) (3,7) 0, 1, 2, 3

That is 4 butterflies per stage and 3 stages, 12 in all, matching \( (8/2)\log_2 8 = 12 \). 02-fft-vs-dft.py checks this code against naive_dft() on 64 random numbers, and on the machine used to write this chapter the two agreed to within a few parts in ten million.

Size Must Be a Power of Two

The bit-reversal trick only works when N is a power of 2, so make_tables(500) raises a ValueError. If you want a different frame length, pick 128, 256, 512, or 1024, and remember the frame must still be read from the microphone in that many samples.

docs.title: Frequency Bins and Bin Width
docs.text:
Each of the \( N/2 \) useful outputs is a frequency bin: a slot that collects the energy of every sound close to one particular frequency. Bin \( k \) is centered on \( k \) cycles per frame. A frame lasts \( N/R \) seconds, where \( R \) is the sample rate, so \( k \) cycles per frame is \( k \cdot R/N \) cycles per second:

\[ f_k = k\,\frac{R}{N}, \qquad \text{bin width } \Delta f = \frac{R}{N}. \]

The bin width is the gap between neighboring bins. For the kit, \( R = 12{,}800 \) Hz and \( N = 512 \), so the bin width is \( 12{,}800/512 = 25 \) Hz. Bin 0 is 0 Hz (the DC slot), bin 1 is 25 Hz, bin 40 is 1,000 Hz, and bin 255 is 6,375 Hz. Bin 256 would be exactly 6,400 Hz, the Nyquist limit from Chapter 3, which is the top of what 12,800 samples per second can represent. The code uses bins 0 to 255.

To go the other way, a tone of frequency \( f \) lands at \( k = f \cdot N/R = f/25 \), a number that is usually not whole. 03-bin-calculator.py prints the kit's arithmetic:

Tone Bin \( f/25 \) Nearest bin Nearest bin's center Tone minus center 100 Hz 4.00 4 100 Hz 0 Hz 262 Hz (middle C) 10.48 10 250 Hz +12 Hz 440 Hz (concert A) 17.60 18 450 Hz -10 Hz 1,000 Hz 40.00 40 1,000 Hz 0 Hz 1,012.5 Hz 40.50 41 1,025 Hz -12.5 Hz 6,375 Hz 255.00 255 6,375 Hz 0 Hz

The bin width is the finest pitch distinction the frame can make: two tones closer together than about one bin width, 25 Hz, merge into one lump. The worst-case error when you read a pitch off the nearest bin is half a bin, 12.5 Hz. Both numbers come straight from \( R/N \). Use the explorer below to practice the arithmetic.

docs.text:
Run FFT Bin Calculator Fullscreen

FFT Bin Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: fft-bin-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the nearest FFT bin for 4 tone frequencies and the center frequency of 2 bins, using a sample rate of 12,800 Hz and an FFT size of 512, with at least 5 of 6 answers correct.

An answer is correct when it equals the Answer column in Content exactly. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Moving the exploration slider is exploration, not evidence.

The model has a sample rate of 12,800 Hz, an FFT size of 512 samples, a bin width of 25 Hz, and 256 useful bins numbered 0 to 255. The formulas shown on screen are: bin = frequency / 25, and bin center = bin number x 25. The nearest bin is the bin whose center is closest to the tone.

The nearest bin is the bin number rounded to the nearest whole number; a tone exactly halfway between two bins is shown as a tie and is not used in any challenge. Bin center = bin number x 12,800 / 512. Slider values from 0 to 6,400 Hz; at 6,400 Hz the bin is 256, which is outside the 256 useful bins, and the sim says so.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the slider and watches the decimal bin number and the nearest bin change.
  2. The learner notices that a tone at 1,000 Hz lands exactly on bin 40, while 440 Hz lands between bins 17 and 18.
  3. The learner starts the 6 challenges. Challenge 1 is shown.
  4. The learner types a whole number and submits.
  5. The sim shows the correct answer with the Why text, and a running score.

Feedback: 6 challenges, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the bin width is 25 Hz, that there are 256 useful bins (0 to 255, the top bin being 6,375 Hz), that 1,000 Hz is bin 40.0, that 440 Hz is bin 17.6, and that 262 Hz is bin 10.48.

docs.title: The Magnitude Spectrum
docs.text:
Each \( X[k] \) is a pair \( (\text{re}, \text{im}) \). The magnitude spectrum keeps only how big each pair is, by the Pythagorean theorem:

\[ |X[k]| = \sqrt{\text{re}[k]^2 + \text{im}[k]^2}. \]

Plotted against frequency, the magnitudes show which pitches are present and how strongly. The phase, the angle of the pair, says where in its cycle each wave starts, and for loudness displays you throw it away. dsp.magnitudes() is a loop over bins 0 to 255.

def magnitudes(re, im, out):
    for k in range(len(out)):
        out[k] = math.sqrt(re[k] * re[k] + im[k] * im[k])

The magnitudes are not in the same units as the samples. The DFT adds up \( N \) products, so a steady sine of amplitude \( A \) that sits exactly on a bin produces a magnitude of \( A \cdot N/2 \) at that bin. The Fourier worked example near the start of this chapter hinted at this number (8.0 for amplitude 1 in a 16-sample frame), and it is easy to check at full size.

Worked example. A 1,000 Hz sine of amplitude 1,000 sampled at 12,800 Hz fits exactly 40 cycles in 512 samples. The FFT gives a magnitude of \( 1{,}000 \times 512/2 = 256{,}000 \) at bin 40 and zero (to within rounding) at every other bin. A tone half as loud would give 128,000. Reading a spectrum is therefore a two-axis job:

Axis Reads as Units Bin number Pitch: \( k \times 25 \) Hz hertz Magnitude Amplitude: divide by \( N/2 = 256 \) to get the tone's amplitude same as the samples, times 256 Phase (discarded) Where the wave starts in its cycle not used here

Notice that the spectrum answers a different question from RMS. RMS is a single number for the whole frame. The magnitude spectrum is 256 numbers, one per 25 Hz, and its sum of squares is tied to the RMS, because the same energy is just counted by pitch instead of by moment.

One Number Versus 256

RMS squeezes the whole frame into one loudness number. The spectrum spreads the same energy across 256 pitches. Notice that nothing is added: the FFT only re-sorts what the frame already contains.

docs.title: Windowing, the Hann Window, and Spectral Leakage
docs.text:
The test tone above was chosen to fit a whole number of cycles in the frame. Real sounds do not. The FFT quietly assumes that the frame repeats forever, like a loop of tape. If the frame ends part-way through a wave, the end does not join the beginning, and the repeated signal has a jump at every seam. That jump is not part of the sound, but the transform dutifully reports it, as a smear of energy across many bins. This smear is spectral leakage.

Take a 1,012.5 Hz tone, which is bin 40.5, exactly between bins 40 and 41. With no special treatment, 04-leakage-hann.py shows the leakage: bin 40 has 163,903 and bin 41 has 162,059, but there are also 10 bins in total with at least 10% of the peak, and the bin 20 away from the peak is still only 33.5 dB below it.

The fix is windowing: multiply the frame by a smooth curve that fades the samples to zero at both ends before taking the FFT. With the ends at zero, the repeated copies join without a jump. The standard curve is the Hann window, a gentle hill:

\[ w[i] = 0.5 - 0.5\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{N}\right), \qquad i = 0 \ldots N-1. \]

It is 0 at the first sample, rises to 1 in the middle (sample 256), and falls back toward 0. dsp.hann_table() computes the 512 values once; load_frame() multiplies each DC-free sample by its window value as it loads. Windowing costs one multiplication per sample and makes the leakage dramatically smaller, but it has two prices: the peak is half as tall (the window's average height is 0.5), and a tone on a bin center now covers three bins instead of one.

Tone Where Window Bins at least 10% of the peak 20 bins from the peak 1,000 Hz bin 40.0 none 1 below -100 dB (rounding only) 1,000 Hz bin 40.0 Hann 3 below -100 dB (rounding only) 1,006.25 Hz bin 40.25 none 5 -37.0 dB 1,006.25 Hz bin 40.25 Hann 3 -90.3 dB 1,012.5 Hz bin 40.5 none 10 -33.5 dB 1,012.5 Hz bin 40.5 Hann 4 -87.3 dB

All six rows come from running 04-leakage-hann.py on a test tone of amplitude 1,000, no microphone needed. Read the table as a trade: if you know your tone sits on a bin, no window is sharper (1 loud bin, not 3). For real sounds, whose frequencies are anywhere, the Hann window gives a far cleaner picture, about 54 dB less leakage at 20 bins out in the last pair of rows. That is why the display scripts always use it. The 0.5 gain only changes the vertical scale, and dsp.dbfs_reference() includes it.

Unwindowed Frames Look Messy

If your spectrum has a wide skirt around every note, you probably forgot the window. Check that load_frame() received the Hann table, not None, and that the table is built with the same N as the FFT.

Try the explorer to see leakage change as you slide a tone across a bin.

docs.title: Choosing the FFT Size
docs.text:
The FFT size is the number of samples \( N \) in one transform. It sets everything at once. The frame lasts \( N/R \) seconds, the bin width is \( R/N \), and there are \( N/2 \) useful bins. Because bin width times frame length is always 1 (the product of \( R/N \) and \( N/R \)), you cannot improve one without worsening the other: a longer frame resolves finer pitches but reacts more slowly.

FFT size Frame length Bin width Useful bins Butterflies 128 10 ms 100 Hz 64 448 256 20 ms 50 Hz 128 1,024 512 40 ms 25 Hz 256 2,304 1,024 80 ms 12.5 Hz 512 5,120

The kit uses 512, which is config.FFT_SIZE: 25 Hz is fine enough to separate neighboring musical notes above roughly 400 Hz, 40 ms is quick enough for a display that updates 25 times a second, and Chapter 8 already organized the microphone loop around frames of exactly that length.

docs.title: Peak Frequency Detection
docs.text:
Peak frequency detection answers the question "what note is that?" Find the bin with the largest magnitude and report its frequency. For a pure whistle this works well.

best = first_bin                      # start above bin 0 to skip the DC end
for k in range(first_bin, len(mag) - 1):
    if mag[k] > mag[best]:
        best = k
frequency = best * rate / n

The answer can only be a multiple of the bin width, so the error can be up to 12.5 Hz. A 440 Hz tone lands at bin 17.6, the loudest bin is 18, and the reported frequency is 450 Hz, 10 Hz too high. A cheap refinement fits a parabola through the log-magnitudes of the peak bin and its two neighbors and takes the top of the parabola. dsp.peak_frequency(refine=True) does it, and 04-leakage-hann.py shows it recovering 439.7 Hz for the 440 Hz test tone, an error of -0.3 Hz.

Two cautions. In a quiet room the loudest bin is just noise, so the scripts report a peak only when the RMS is above a gate (PEAK_GATE_DBFS, set to -50 dBFS, a guess to tune for your room). And speech has many peaks at once (a voice is a stack of harmonics), so the loudest bin is a poor description of a voice. Later chapters therefore use the whole spectrum, not one peak.

docs.title: Log Magnitude
docs.text:
Magnitudes cover a huge range. The test tone above peaks at 256,000, a quiet room's bins may be near 1,000, and a full-scale sine would reach about \( 1.07 \times 10^9 \). A bar drawn in proportion to magnitude would be invisible for everything except the loudest sounds, and it would not match how the ear hears. The log magnitude is the magnitude converted to decibels, \( 20\log_{10}(|X[k]|/|X|_{\text{ref}}) \), so equal ratios become equal steps.

The reference that makes the scale meaningful is the peak that a full-scale sine would give with the Hann window: \( 2^{23} \times 512/2 \times 0.5 = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824 \). dsp.dbfs_reference() returns it, and it is 180.6 dB on its own scale. With this reference a bin's level reads in dBFS, where 0 means a full-scale tone exactly on that bin.

Worked example. The Hann-windowed 1,000 Hz tone of amplitude 1,000 has a peak magnitude of 128,000 at bin 40. Its level is \( 20\log_{10}(128{,}000/1{,}073{,}741{,}824) = -78.5 \) dBFS. A tone half as loud sits 6 dB lower, at -84.5 dBFS, and a tone ten times quieter sits 20 dB lower. Equal ratios line up as equal distances, which is what a bar chart needs.

docs.title: Band Energy and Log-Spaced Bands
docs.text:
A spectrum of 256 bars does not fit on a round screen as bars you can read, and most of the bars carry nothing you care about. The fix is to group neighboring bins into a few bands and add up their energy. The band energy is the sum of the squared magnitudes of the bins in the band:

\[ E_{\text{band}} = \sum_{k \,\in\, \text{band}} |X[k]|^2. \]

Squaring gives energy, so the decibel form is \( 10\log_{10}(E/E_{\text{ref}}) \), with \( E_{\text{ref}} \) the square of the reference magnitude above.

The next question is where the band edges go. Equal-width bands would give 16 bands of 16 bins (400 Hz) each. The ear does not hear that way: it judges pitch by ratio, so the step from 100 Hz to 200 Hz sounds the same as the step from 1,000 Hz to 2,000 Hz, even though the first is a 100 Hz change and the second a 1,000 Hz one. Log-spaced bands follow the ear. Each band's top edge is a fixed multiple of its bottom edge. For 16 bands from 100 Hz to 6,400 Hz, the total ratio is 64, so each band's edges differ by the factor \( 64^{1/16} = 1.2968 \). dsp.log_band_edges() computes the edges, rounds them to bins, and stretches any band narrower than one bin to one bin. 03-bin-calculator.py prints the result:

Band Bins Frequencies (Hz) Bins in band 0 4 100 to 125 1 1 5 to 6 125 to 175 2 2 7 to 8 175 to 225 2 3 9 to 10 225 to 275 2 4 11 to 14 275 to 375 4 5 15 to 18 375 to 475 4 6 19 to 24 475 to 625 6 7 25 to 31 625 to 800 7 8 32 to 40 800 to 1,025 9 9 41 to 53 1,025 to 1,350 13 10 54 to 69 1,350 to 1,750 16 11 70 to 90 1,750 to 2,275 21 12 91 to 116 2,275 to 2,925 26 13 117 to 151 2,925 to 3,800 35 14 152 to 196 3,800 to 4,925 45 15 197 to 255 4,925 to 6,400 59

The rounding is visible at the bottom: bands 0 to 3 are all one or two bins wide, because a 25 Hz bin is a large share of a 25 to 50 Hz band. The bands start at 100 Hz, not 0, because the lowest bins hold the DC residue and rumble.

Worked example. The 1,000 Hz Hann-windowed test tone of amplitude 1,000 has magnitudes 64,000, 128,000 and 64,000 at bins 39, 40 and 41. Bins 39 and 40 are in band 8 and bin 41 is in band 9. Band 8's energy is \( 64{,}000^2 + 128{,}000^2 = 2.048 \times 10^{10} \) and band 9's is \( 64{,}000^2 = 4.096 \times 10^{9} \). Band 8 is five times stronger, \( 10\log_{10} 5 = 7.0 \) dB. In dBFS, band 8 reads \( 10\log_{10}\left(2.048\times10^{10} / (1.0737\times10^{9})^2\right) = -77.5 \) dBFS: a little higher than the -78.5 dBFS peak because the band also holds a neighbor bin.

docs.title: Diagram: Log Band Layout Explorer
docs.text:
Run Log Band Layout Explorer Fullscreen

Log Band Layout Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: log-band-layout-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use the 16-band log-spaced layout from 100 Hz to 6,400 Hz to find the band that contains 3 tones and the number of bins in 3 bands, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: frequency bin, bin width, band energy, log-spaced bands (all defined in this chapter above the block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 challenges the learner types a whole number (a band number for challenges 1 to 3, a bin count for challenges 4 to 6) and submits. An answer is correct when it equals the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Changing the number of bands or the lowest frequency in exploration is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every band has the same number of bins. (2) Equal-width bands and log-spaced bands put 1,000 Hz in the same band. (3) The highest band is the narrowest.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level use of a layout requires reading a table of edges and mapping a frequency through bins to a band. Changing the number of bands during exploration shows how the layout depends on the ratio between neighboring edges, before the learner uses the fixed 16-band layout for the challenges.

Content:

The fixed layout for the challenges is the 16-band table in the chapter section "Band Energy and Log-Spaced Bands", with bin width 25 Hz. A tone belongs to the band that contains its nearest bin.

# Question shown Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which band contains a 1,000 Hz tone? 8 1,000 / 25 = bin 40, and band 8 holds bins 32 to 40. 2 Which band contains a 440 Hz tone? 5 440 / 25 = 17.6, nearest bin 18, and band 5 holds bins 15 to 18. 3 Which band contains a 3,000 Hz tone? 13 3,000 / 25 = bin 120, and band 13 holds bins 117 to 151. 4 How many bins are in band 10? 16 Band 10 holds bins 54 to 69, which is 69 - 54 + 1 = 16. 5 How many bins are in band 15? 59 Band 15 holds bins 197 to 255, which is 59. 6 How many bins are in band 0? 1 Band 0 holds only bin 4, because the band between 100 and 129.7 Hz is narrower than one 25 Hz bin and is stretched to one bin.

For exploration the learner changes the number of bands and the lowest frequency, and the sim shows the edge in hertz, the bins, and the bin count of every band.

Provenance: The 16-band layout and its bin ranges are printed by src/chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/03-bin-calculator.py, which calls dsp.log_band_edges(16, 100, 6400, 12800, 512). The chapter section reproduces the same table.

Rules: Edge i is round(f_low x r^i x 512 / 12,800) with r = (6,400 / f_low)^(1 / bands); halves round to the nearest even whole number. If an edge is not greater than the previous edge, it is set to the previous edge plus 1. Band i holds bins edge[i] to edge[i+1] - 1. Number of bands: min 4, max 32, step 4, default 16. Lowest frequency: min 50, max 400, step 50, default 100, unit Hz. The highest frequency is always 6,400 Hz.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner changes the number of bands and the lowest frequency and watches the edges and bin counts update.
  2. The learner notices that the lowest bands always shrink to one bin.
  3. The learner starts the 6 challenges with the default layout. Challenge 1 is shown.
  4. The learner types a whole number and submits.
  5. The sim highlights the band or the bins involved and shows the Why text.

Feedback: 6 challenges, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The default 16-band layout is shown, with the question "Which band holds this tone?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the 16 bands run from 100 Hz to 6,400 Hz with a ratio of 1.2968 per band, that band 8 holds bins 32 to 40, that band 10 holds 16 bins, and that band 15 holds 59 bins.

docs.title: The Spectrogram
docs.text:
One spectrum describes one 40 ms frame. A spectrogram stacks the spectra of consecutive frames into a picture: time runs along one axis, frequency along the other, and the level at each point is shown as brightness or color. A steady whistle makes a horizontal line, a rising whistle makes a diagonal, and a clap makes a vertical stripe. At 25 frames per second, a 32-row spectrogram of the 16 bands covers 1.28 seconds and fits in \( 32 \times 16 = 512 \) bytes.

Because this display has no frame buffer, a scrolling picture cannot slide the old rows down. The trick is the one from Chapter 8's ring buffer: write each new row in the next row position and wrap around to the top, so every frame draws only one row. A row of 16 cells that are 12 pixels wide and 6 high is \( 16 \times 12 \times 6 \times 2 = 2{,}304 \) bytes, at least 0.8 ms at 24 MHz. Building this is an extension exercise, not one of the seven scripts.

docs.title: The Spectrum Display
docs.text:
The spectrum display is the live bar chart that this chapter has been building toward. 07-spectrum-display.py does the whole job for every frame: load and window, FFT, magnitudes, band energies, convert each band to decibels, and move each bar to its new height. The bars use the Chapter 6 dirty-region rule: a bar that grows gets a slice of color added on top, and a bar that shrinks gets a slice of black painted over its top.

Part Value Bars 16, each 12 pixels wide with a 3 pixel gap Bar area 237 pixels wide, up to 120 pixels high, baseline at y = 250 Full redraw of the bar area \( 237 \times 120 \times 2 = 56{,}880 \) bytes, at least 19.0 ms at 24 MHz Level scale -90 dBFS (empty bar) to -30 dBFS (full 120-pixel bar), so 2 pixels per decibel; the ends are a starting guess to tune for your room Labels 100, 800, and 6.4k under the bars; the peak frequency below 
def draw_bar(i, height):
    old = shown[i]
    if height == old:
        return
    x = BARS_X + i * (BAR_WIDTH + BAR_GAP)
    if height > old:
        display.fill_rect(x, BASELINE - height, BAR_WIDTH, height - old, colors[i])
    else:
        display.fill_rect(x, BASELINE - old, BAR_WIDTH, old - height, BLACK)
    shown[i] = height

The whole bar area stays inside the visible circle (the corner at the bottom-left of the bars, at x = 61, y = 250, is 119 pixels from the center along one axis and 70 along the other, a distance of 138 pixels, well inside the 168-pixel safe radius from config.py). For each frame, shown[i] remembers what is on the glass, so only the difference travels over the SPI wire.

docs.title: The Whole Pipeline, and What It Costs
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter is one chain, and each stage's cost class is easy to count.

Stage Function in dsp.py Work per 512-sample frame Read the frame readinto() waits for the microphone (up to 40 ms) DC removal, RMS, Hann window load_frame() 3 passes over 512 samples FFT fft() 2,304 butterflies Magnitudes magnitudes() 256 square roots Band energies band_energies() 256 multiply-adds Decibels and bar heights to_db(), scale() 16 logarithms Redraw changed bars fill_rect() only the changed slices

Chapter 8's budget says that all of this must finish within 40 ms. The FFT dominates, and this chapter's FFT is plain Python, which is slow. I expect it to take several frame times: a rough guess from similar boards is somewhere between 100 and 300 ms for the 2,304 butterflies, which would be 3 to 8 frames. That is a guess, not a measurement. The scripts print the real value, in the "work ms" column of 05-mic-spectrum-text.py and the summary line of 07-spectrum-display.py, and Chapter 10 measures it carefully and then makes it faster. Until then, the scripts use dsp.latest_frame() to skip the frames that pile up while the FFT runs, so the display shows the present, a few times a second, instead of a delayed past. The last column of 05 counts the skipped frames.

The files for this chapter:

File Parts needed What it shows 01-dft-by-hand.py none The four-number DFT term by term, then two tones 02-fft-vs-dft.py none FFT equals DFT; operation counts 03-bin-calculator.py none Bin width, bins for tones, the 16 band edges 04-leakage-hann.py none Leakage with and without Hann; peak frequency refinement 05-mic-spectrum-text.py Microphone RMS, dBFS, peak frequency, and band digits as text 06-volume-meter.py Display + microphone RMS volume meter with changed-slice redraw 07-spectrum-display.py Display + microphone 16-band live spectrum on the round screen

Upload and run them as described in src/chapters/README.md; the folder's own README.md says what PASS looks like for each.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
A frame of 512 samples is a 40 ms sound. Remove its average, and the leftover swing is its loudness, which you can measure in RMS and show in decibels as a volume meter. To learn which pitches it contains, window it with Hann, and transform it with the FFT, a fast way to get the DFT's 512 numbers, of which 256 are useful, each a bin of 25 Hz. Take their magnitudes, group them into log-spaced bands, convert to decibels, and draw only the bars that moved.

Key takeaways:

  • RMS loudness is the square root of the mean of the squared, DC-free samples; remove the frame's own average first, because the microphone's offset drifts.
  • Decibels compare amplitudes with \( 20\log_{10} \) (or energies with \( 10\log_{10} \)); relative to full scale (\( 2^{23} \)) they are negative, and every 6 dB is a doubling.
  • The Fourier transform recovers the sine-wave recipe of a signal; the DFT does it for N samples in \( N^2 \) steps; the FFT does it in \( (N/2)\log_2 N \), which is 2,304 butterflies instead of 262,144 for N = 512.
  • Twiddle factors and the bit-reversal table are computed once; the FFT then runs in place, in two 512-entry arrays.
  • Bin \( k \) is at \( k \times 25 \) Hz; the bin width is \( R/N = 25 \) Hz; the useful bins are 0 to 255 because real input mirrors.
  • A tone not on a bin center leaks; the Hann window cuts the leakage by tens of decibels at the price of half the peak and a three-bin-wide peak.
  • The magnitude spectrum is \( \sqrt{\text{re}^2 + \text{im}^2} \); an on-bin sine of amplitude A peaks at \( A \cdot N/2 \) (halved by Hann).
  • Show decibels, not raw magnitudes, and group the 256 bins into log-spaced bands whose edges grow by a constant ratio.
  • Draw by changed slice, and measure the pure-Python pipeline before you trust it to fit in 40 ms.

Test yourself with these questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

A tone of 3,000 Hz is played at 12,800 samples per second with a 512-point FFT. Which bin has the most energy, and which log band is it in? Click to expand

\( 3{,}000/25 = 120 \), so bin 120, which is exactly on a bin center. Band 13 holds bins 117 to 151, so the tone is in band 13.

You move the sample rate to 25,600 Hz but keep N = 512. What happens to the bin width and the frame length? Click to expand

The bin width doubles to \( 25{,}600/512 = 50 \) Hz and the frame length halves to 20 ms. Product of the two stays 1, so a shorter frame always means coarser bins.

Why does a spectrum from a frame that is not windowed show a wide skirt around a pure tone? Click to expand

The FFT treats the frame as if it repeats forever. A tone that does not fit a whole number of cycles leaves a jump where the end meets the start, and the jump spreads energy into many bins. A window that fades the ends to zero removes the jump.

From Samples to a Spectrum

You just learned how RMS and decibels measure loudness, how the DFT and the FFT turn 512 samples into 256 bins of 25 Hz, and how windowing, magnitudes, and log-spaced bands become a live spectrum on the round screen. The spectrum is yours to draw, and the next step is making it fast.

In Chapter 10 we measure how long this pure-Python pipeline really takes on the Pico, and then make it fast enough for the 40 ms budget.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter shows how to make MicroPython fast enough for real-time audio. Students compare pure Python with viper and inline assembly, use typed arrays and pre-allocated buffers, and measure with the cycle counter. They finish able to benchmark code against the frame budget and explain the trade-offs of each speedup.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems
  • Chapter 4: The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring
  • Chapter 8: I2S Audio: Recording and Playing Sound
  • Chapter 9: Signal Processing and the FFT

docs.title: The 40 ms Promise
docs.text:
Chapter 9 ended with an uncomfortable fact: the whole spectrum pipeline is written in plain Python, and the FFT inside it does 2,304 butterflies in every 40 ms frame. This chapter is about keeping the promise from Chapter 8, that every pass of the loop finishes before the next frame arrives. It teaches a method more than a bag of tricks: measure, find the biggest cost, fix that, measure again.

Make It Fit in 40 Milliseconds

In this chapter you will time your own code down to single CPU cycles and learn the tricks that can make a slow loop dramatically faster. Let's listen closely! You will also learn when not to use them.

An honest note before we start. I could not run any of this chapter's benchmarks on the real kit while writing it. Everything that follows is either arithmetic you can check, a fact I verified in the MicroPython source or documentation, a result I computed by running the same integer code on a computer, or a clearly labelled estimate. Every speed that only the Pico can reveal is a blank in the results table near the end, with a script that fills it in. The code was checked in real MicroPython on a computer and against a software model of the Pico's rules, and src/chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/README.md lists exactly what was and was not checked.

docs.title: The Real-Time Constraint and the Frame Overrun
docs.text:
A real-time constraint is a deadline that a result must meet to be useful. A spectrum that arrives 200 ms late is not a slow answer; it is a wrong one, because the sound it describes has already gone. For the Study Buddy the deadline comes from the microphone: a new 512-sample frame arrives every 40 ms whether or not your code is ready for it.

Chapter 8 introduced the budget. In cycles it looks like this, at the Pico 2's 150 MHz clock:

\[ 0.040 \text{ s} \times 150{,}000{,}000 \text{ cycles/s} = 6{,}000{,}000 \text{ cycles per frame}, \qquad \frac{6{,}000{,}000}{512} \approx 11{,}719 \text{ cycles per sample.} \]

A frame overrun is a pass of the loop whose work takes longer than one frame. While your code is busy the microphone keeps filling its ring buffer, so the next readinto() returns at once with an old frame, and the backlog grows. Chapter 8 measured the ring's depth at about 9.8 frames; once the backlog passes that, audio is lost. A loop can therefore be in one of three states, and a program that counts them is much easier to trust than one that only prints an average.

State How the loop sees it What it means On time readinto() waited more than a few milliseconds The frame was not ready yet; there is spare time Behind readinto() returned in under 4 ms The frame was already waiting; the loop has no spare time Overrun The work in this pass was longer than 40 ms The backlog grew by this pass; audio will be lost if it keeps happening

06-frame-loop-budget.py counts all three for a real microphone loop, and it holds back 10 ms of the budget for the screen update, because Chapter 6 measured 8.5 ms for the spectrum region. So the working limit for the audio work is 30 ms.

A Deadline Is Not a Speed

A fast loop is not the same as a loop that meets its deadline. Notice that the average does not matter: one pass in a hundred that takes 90 ms is enough to lose audio. Real-time code is judged by its worst pass.

docs.title: Measure First: Benchmarking
docs.text:
Benchmarking is timing a piece of code in a way you can repeat and trust. A single timing is not trustworthy, because interrupts and garbage collection add random delays. The recipe in bench.py is short:

  1. Call gc.collect() first, so a collection does not strike in the middle of the timing.
  2. Run the code several times.
  3. Report the best time, which is the run that was disturbed least and so measures the code itself.
  4. Separately, look at the spread of times to see how much a single run can vary.
def bench(label, func, args=(), repeat=5, budget_us=40000):
    best_us = None
    for _ in range(repeat):
        gc.collect()
        t0 = time.ticks_us()
        func(*args)
        us = time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_us(), t0)
        if best_us is None or us < best_us:
            best_us = us
    print(label, best_us / 1000, "ms", 100 * best_us / budget_us, "% of a frame")

The real function also reads the cycle counter, described next, and prints a RESULT|... line you can paste into a table. time.ticks_us() counts microseconds, and one microsecond is 150 CPU cycles, so it cannot resolve anything shorter than a few hundred cycles. Time a loop of 512 samples or more, never a single statement.

Best of Five

When a timing jumps around, run the code five times and keep the smallest number. The smallest is the run with the least interference, so it is the closest to what the code itself costs. For a deadline, though, also look at the largest.

docs.title: The Cycle Counter and the DWT Timer
docs.text:
A cycle counter is a hardware register that adds one on every tick of the CPU clock. At 150 MHz one cycle is 6.67 ns, so a counter gives timings 150 times finer than ticks_us() and, better, in the unit that the instruction manuals use. The ARM Cortex-M33 processor in the Pico 2 has such a counter inside a block called the DWT (Data Watchpoint and Trace). The DWT timer is that cycle counter. It sits at fixed addresses and MicroPython reaches it through machine.mem32, which reads and writes any 32-bit address:

Register Address What to do DEMCR 0xE000EDFC Set bit 24 (TRCENA) to switch the DWT block on DWT_CTRL 0xE0001000 Set bit 0 (CYCCNTENA) to start counting; bit 25 (NOCYCCNT) set means there is no counter DWT_CYCCNT 0xE0001004 The count itself, 32 bits 
mem32[DEMCR] = mem32[DEMCR] | (1 << 24)          # allow the DWT block
if mem32[DWT_CTRL] & (1 << 25):                  # NOCYCCNT: this core has no counter
    ...                                          # fall back to ticks_us()
mem32[DWT_CYCCNT] = 0
mem32[DWT_CTRL] = mem32[DWT_CTRL] | 1            # start counting
cycles = mem32[DWT_CYCCNT]                       # read it

This is unverified on the RP2350. The three registers are standard for Cortex-M cores, and I could not confirm that this chip implements the counter or that MicroPython may touch it. 01-cycle-counter.py finds out. It tries the sequence, checks that the counter changes, and compares its rate with ticks_us(): a working counter gives about 150 cycles per microsecond. If it reports no counter, nothing else in the chapter breaks, because bench.py falls back to microseconds and you convert at 150 cycles per microsecond.

Two details matter either way. The counter is 32 bits, so it wraps after \( 2^{32}/150{,}000{,}000 = 28.6 \) seconds, and you must always subtract with (end - start) & 0xFFFFFFFF. And the value is often a number above \( 2^{30} \), which MicroPython cannot hold in a small integer, so a read can allocate a little; 01 measures what one read costs so you can subtract it. A third item: time.ticks_cpu() sounds like a cycle counter, but in the current MicroPython source for this port it returns the microsecond timer, which 01 checks on your build.

docs.title: Profiling and Timing Verification
docs.text:
Profiling is finding out where the time goes inside a loop, so you speed up the part that matters. A profiler at this scale is a few lines: stamp the clock after each section and add the difference to that section's total. The Profiler class in bench.py does it:

prof = Profiler()
while running:
    mic.readinto(frame);        prof.lap("wait")
    dsp.load_frame(...);        prof.lap("load")
    dsp.fft(re, im, tables);    prof.lap("fft")
    ...
prof.report(passes)             # milliseconds per pass, and each section's share

Profile before you optimize. In Chapter 9's pipeline the FFT does 2,304 butterflies while the magnitude and band steps do a few hundred operations each, so the arithmetic predicts that the FFT dominates, and the profile should confirm it. If it did not, there would be no point rewriting the FFT.

Timing verification is proving that the finished loop meets its deadline, by measuring many real passes and checking the worst one. It is different from benchmarking. Benchmarking asks "how fast can this code go?" and reports the best run. Timing verification asks "can this ever be late?" and reports the worst. 06-frame-loop-budget.py runs the live loop for 8 seconds in each of two modes (pure Python and viper) and prints a verdict from three numbers: the mean, the 95th percentile, and the maximum of the work per pass, plus the overrun count. The verdict is a pass only if there were no overruns and the worst pass is within 30 ms.

Two traps make the average misleading. A garbage collection pause strikes only now and then, so it raises the maximum without moving the mean. And the loop must be tested under realistic load: with sound arriving (a quiet room may take a different path through your code than speech) and with the display redrawing. A timing result from an idle bench does not verify a loop that also draws.

docs.title: The Baseline: Pure Python FFT
docs.text:
The pure Python FFT is dsp.fft() from Chapter 9: lists or array('f') buffers, floating-point arithmetic, and every line interpreted. It is correct and readable, and it is the baseline every faster version here is compared with. Count its work first.

Worked example. A 512-point FFT does \( 256 \times 9 = 2{,}304 \) butterflies, and the body of each butterfly in dsp.fft is 10 Python statements (two index calculations, two twiddle lookups, two lines for the twiddle product, four for the sum and difference). That is \( 2{,}304 \times 10 = 23{,}040 \) statements per FFT. If the FFT may use 10 ms, which is a quarter of the frame, each butterfly may take \( 10 \text{ ms} / 2{,}304 = 4.34 \) microseconds, about 651 cycles, and each statement only about 65 cycles. A statement such as tr = re[b]*c + im[b]*s does two array reads, two multiplications and an addition, and each float result is a new heap object (next sections). Fitting that in 65 cycles looks very unlikely for an interpreter.

The table turns the question around: for each cost per butterfly, how long does the whole FFT take?

Cycles per butterfly Microseconds per butterfly FFT of 512 points Share of the 40 ms frame 100 0.67 1.5 ms 4% 300 2.0 4.6 ms 12% 651 4.3 10.0 ms 25% 1,000 6.7 15.4 ms 38% 2,604 17.4 40.0 ms 100% 5,000 33.3 76.8 ms 192% 10,000 66.7 153.6 ms 384%

Every row is arithmetic: cycles \( \times 2{,}304 / 150{,}000 \) gives milliseconds. 02-fft-pure-python-bench.py prints microseconds per butterfly, so multiply by 150 to find your row. Chapter 9 guessed 100 to 300 ms for the FFT; in this table that is 6,500 to 19,500 cycles per butterfly, which is a guess, not a measurement. The real number is a blank in the results table below until someone runs the script on the kit.

docs.title: Why Python Costs So Much Here
docs.text: Four facts explain where the time of pure Python goes, and each points at a fix.

docs.title: Floating Point Cost
docs.text:
The RP2350's ARM cores include a single-precision floating-point unit, so a hardware add or multiply of two floats is cheap. The floating point cost you pay in MicroPython is elsewhere. In the MicroPython source for this port, floats are 32-bit single precision (MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL_FLOAT), and every float result is a new object on the heap (the port uses the default object layout, in which a float is not packed into the value itself). So y = y * 1.0001 runs the interpreter's float multiply and then allocates a small object, and the old object becomes garbage. Whether the C code uses the FPU instructions or software routines I did not verify. Either way, the allocation and the interpreter around the operation cost more than the multiply.

Integers are cheaper: a whole number that fits in 31 bits is stored inside the value, with no allocation. 03-allocation-and-floats.py times 2,000 multiply-adds on integers and on floats so you can see the ratio on your board. The conclusion that matters is the design rule: keep the hot loop on whole numbers where you can.

docs.title: Typed Arrays
docs.text:
A typed array from the array module stores numbers of one kind packed into memory, with no object per element.

Typecode Element Bytes each Range 'b' / 'B' signed / unsigned byte 1 -128..127 / 0..255 'h' / 'H' signed / unsigned 16-bit 2 -32768..32767 / 0..65535 'i' / 'I' signed / unsigned 32-bit 4 about +-2.1 billion / 0..4.29 billion 'f' single-precision float 4 about 7 decimal digits

Worked example. 512 numbers cost these amounts on the Pico, by arithmetic (a list slot is a 4-byte pointer; a float object occupies one 16-byte heap block):

Container Bytes for 512 numbers How list of floats about 10,240 \( 512 \times (4 + 16) \) array('f') 2,048 \( 512 \times 4 \) list of small integers about 2,048 \( 512 \times 4 \) array('h') 1,024 \( 512 \times 2 \)

03 measures the same containers on the board, so you can compare. A typed array has a second benefit: the garbage collector does not need to look inside it, because it holds no pointers. And a third, which matters most for this chapter: a typed array is a block of memory with a fixed layout, so code that works at the machine level can address its elements directly.

docs.title: Array Passed By Address
docs.text: When you pass an array to a function written in viper or assembly, MicroPython does not copy it. It passes the address of the first element, and the function reads and writes your memory in place, exactly as readinto() fills a buffer you own. This is array passed by address, and it is what makes the fast code fast: window_viper(x, w, out, n) takes three arrays and a count and touches no objects at all. It also removes the safety net. The function knows no length except the n you give it, so an n that is too large overwrites memory beyond the array.

docs.title: Avoiding Allocation and Pre-Allocated Buffers
docs.text:
Every allocation uses heap, and heap eventually needs a collection. The MicroPython documentation warns that a collection can take several milliseconds, which is a good fraction of a 40 ms frame. The rule for a real-time loop is therefore avoiding allocation inside it, and the habit that makes it possible is pre-allocated buffers: create every array, table, and buffer once, before the loop, and reuse it on every pass (the Chapter 2 rule, now with a cost attached). Chapter 9's scripts already follow it for re, im, mag, and the tables.

Which statements allocate? The list is not obvious, so 03 tests twelve of them with the garbage collector switched off and reports the bytes used. The first column of the next table is what MicroPython's object model predicts; running 03 on the kit confirms or corrects it.

Statement (run 200 times) Predicted to allocate? Why x = x + 1 no A small integer lives inside the value y = y * 1.0001 yes The float result is a new object arr_f[3] = arr_f[3] * 1.0001 yes Reading makes a float, multiplying makes another arr_h[3] = (arr_h[3] * 3) >> 1 no Whole numbers in a typed array stay small integers buf[0:8] yes A slice of a bytearray is a copy view[0:8] yes A memoryview slice is a new (small) object [0] * 16 yes A new list struct.unpack("<4i", words) yes A new tuple struct.pack_into("<i", words, 0, 7) no Writes into memory you already own "%d" % 12345 yes A new string big + 1 where big is above \( 2^{30} \) yes Too big for a small integer on a 32-bit chip buf[5] = 77 no Stores into an existing byte

Run the allocation quiz to test your own predictions before you look at the table.

docs.title: Diagram: Allocation Classifier
docs.text:
Run Allocation Classifier Fullscreen

Allocation Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: allocation-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish 12 MicroPython statements that allocate heap memory from those that do not, with at least 10 of 12 correct.

Prerequisites: heap, garbage collection, small integer, float object, typed array, pre-allocated buffer, memoryview (defined in Chapter 2 and in this chapter above the block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 12 statements the learner chooses "Allocates" or "Does not allocate" and submits before the answer is shown. A choice is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading the Why text after an answer is feedback, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any arithmetic is free. (2) A slice never copies. (3) Floats are stored inside the value, like small integers. (4) Writing into an array allocates.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level distinction asks the learner to separate cases by a hidden property, whether a new object is created, using the object model rather than memorized examples. Committing before the answer is shown makes the learner apply the model, and the Why text names the object that is created, which is what the learner needs for the next unfamiliar statement.

Content:

The 12 statements are shown one at a time in this order, each with its answer. The answers are what MicroPython's object model predicts for the Pico's 32-bit chip; 03-allocation-and-floats.py measures them on the board.

# Statement Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 x = x + 1 (x is a small whole number) Does not allocate A small integer lives inside the value itself. 2 y = y * 1.0001 (y is a float) Allocates The float result is a new heap object. 3 arr_f[3] = arr_f[3] * 1.0001 (arr_f is array('f')) Allocates Reading an element makes a float object, and so does the product. 4 arr_h[3] = (arr_h[3] * 3) >> 1 (arr_h is array('h')) Does not allocate Every value is a small integer. 5 part = buf[0:8] (buf is a bytearray) Allocates A slice of a bytearray is a new bytearray. 6 part = view[0:8] (view is a memoryview) Allocates A memoryview slice is a new, small memoryview object, though it copies no data. 7 t = [0] * 16 Allocates A new list is created. 8 t = struct.unpack("<4i", words) Allocates A new tuple holds the four results. 9 struct.pack_into("<i", words, 0, 7) Does not allocate It writes into memory the program already owns. 10 s = "%d" % 12345 Allocates A new string is built. 11 z = big + 1 (big is 2**30) Allocates 2**30 does not fit a 31-bit small integer on a 32-bit chip, so the value is a big-integer object. 12 buf[5] = 77 Does not allocate It stores into a byte of an existing bytearray.

Provenance: The answers are predictions from the MicroPython object model on a 32-bit port with the default object layout (source: ports/rp2/mpconfigport.h, which sets single-precision floats and does not override the object representation). They are labelled "expected" in the sim until 03-allocation-and-floats.py has been run on the kit. Statement 11 depends on a 31-bit small integer and is not true on a 64-bit computer; the sim says so.

Rules: A statement allocates when it creates a new object that is not a small integer. A small integer is a whole number from -230 to 230 - 1. Storing into an existing buffer never allocates.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads statement 1 and chooses Allocates or Does not allocate.
  2. The sim shows the answer and the Why text, and a running score.
  3. The learner continues through statement 12.
  4. After statement 12, the sim lists the statements the learner got wrong. The learner should notice that the safe statements either work on small integers or write into an existing buffer.

Feedback: 12 statements, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 12" is shown.

Starting State: Statement 1 is shown with the question "Does this line create a new object?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that floats allocate, small integers do not, a bytearray slice copies, a memoryview slice makes a small object, struct.pack_into writes in place, and that the predictions are confirmed on the kit by 03-allocation-and-floats.py.

docs.title: Table Precomputation
docs.text: Table precomputation is the rule that anything which does not change between frames is computed once, before the loop, and stored. You have used it twice already: the sine table in Chapter 8 and make_tables() in Chapter 9, which fills the Hann window, the twiddle factors, and the bit-reversal table at start-up. The saving is easy to count. Without the twiddle tables, every butterfly would compute a cosine and a sine: \( 2{,}304 \times 2 = 4{,}608 \) trigonometric calls per frame, or \( 4{,}608 \times 25 = 115{,}200 \) per second. With the tables the loop calls none, and the one-time cost is 512 sine and cosine calls, paid at boot. The price is memory, which is small here: 256 cosines and 256 sines in array('f') are 2,048 bytes.

docs.title: Fixed-Point Math
docs.text:
Fixed-point math avoids floats by storing a fraction as a whole number with an agreed scale. In Q15 format a number between -1 and 1 is stored as an integer from -32768 to 32767, with the value equal to the integer divided by 32768. So 16384 means 0.5 and -16384 means -0.5. To multiply two Q15 numbers, multiply the integers and shift right by 15 to remove the extra scale:

\[ (a \times b) \gg 15 \]

Worked example. \( 0.5 \times 0.5 \): \( 16384 \times 16384 = 268{,}435{,}456 \), and \( 268{,}435{,}456 \gg 15 = 8192 \), which is 0.25. 08-q15-fixed-point.py runs six cases on your computer:

a (Q15) b (Q15) \( (a \times b) \gg 15 \) Meaning 16384 16384 8192 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 32767 32767 32766 the largest value squared is just under 1.0 -16384 16384 -8192 -0.5 x 0.5 = -0.25 3 3 0 tiny numbers vanish: \( 9 \gg 15 = 0 \) -3 3 -1 a negative result rounds toward minus infinity -32768 -32768 32768 (-1.0) x (-1.0) = +1.0, which does not fit in 16 bits

Two hazards follow. A result can fall outside the range (the last row), and the intermediate product must fit in the 32-bit register that holds it: two products near \( 32768^2 \) add up to \( 2^{31} \), one more than a signed 32-bit register can hold. The fixed-point FFT later in this chapter avoids both with a scale-down at every stage.

docs.title: Diagram: Q15 Calculator
docs.text:
Run Q15 Calculator Fullscreen

Q15 Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: q15-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the Q15 product (a x b) >> 15 of 6 pairs of Q15 integers, and state whether the result fits in 16 bits, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: fixed-point math, Q15 format, arithmetic shift right (all defined in this chapter above the block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 pairs the learner types the whole-number result and submits. A result is correct when it equals the Answer column in Content. For pair 6 the learner must also choose "Fits in 16 bits" or "Does not fit", and the pair counts as correct only when both are right. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Using the exploration calculator is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The product of two Q15 numbers is already Q15. (2) A shift right always rounds toward zero. (3) Q15 can hold exactly 1.0.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice on cases that differ in kind: a normal product, a vanishing product, a negative rounding case, and an overflow. Committing a number before the result is shown makes the learner carry out the shift, not recognize it.

Content:

The sim shows the formula result = (a x b) >> 15, where >> is an arithmetic shift right that keeps the sign and rounds toward minus infinity. A 16-bit signed Q15 number fits when it is from -32768 to 32767.

# a b Answer Fits in 16 bits? Why (shown as feedback) 1 16384 16384 8192 yes 16384 x 16384 = 268,435,456, and 268,435,456 >> 15 = 8192. 2 32767 32767 32766 yes 32767 x 32767 = 1,073,676,289, and >> 15 gives 32766. 3 -16384 16384 -8192 yes The product -268,435,456 >> 15 is -8192. 4 3 3 0 yes 3 x 3 = 9, and 9 >> 15 is 0: the result is smaller than one Q15 step. 5 -3 3 -1 yes -9 >> 15 rounds toward minus infinity, giving -1, not 0. 6 -32768 -32768 32768 no The product is +1,073,741,824, and >> 15 gives 32768, one more than the largest 16-bit value.

For exploration the learner enters any two Q15 integers from -32768 to 32767 (step 1, default 16384 and 16384) and sees the full product, the shifted result, the real values (integer / 32768) and whether the result fits.

Provenance: The six pairs are the rows of the table in the chapter section "Fixed-Point Math", produced by src/chapters/10-high-performance-micropython/08-q15-fixed-point.py.

Rules: result = floor(a x b / 32768). real value = integer / 32768. A result fits in 16 bits when -32768 <= result <= 32767. Inputs: min -32768, max 32767, step 1, unit none (Q15 integer).

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner enters pairs in the exploration calculator and watches the full product and the shifted result.
  2. The learner tries 32767 x 32767 and -32768 x -32768 and notices that one fits and the other does not.
  3. The learner starts the 6 pairs. Pair 1 is shown.
  4. The learner types the result (and, for pair 6, the fit choice) and submits.
  5. The sim shows the correct answer and the Why text.

Feedback: 6 pairs, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The exploration calculator shows 16384 x 16384 = 8192 with the real values 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25, and the question "What do you get when you multiply two Q15 numbers?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that 16384 stands for 0.5, that 16384 x 16384 >> 15 is 8192, that 3 x 3 >> 15 is 0, and that -32768 x -32768 >> 15 is 32768, which does not fit in 16 bits.

docs.title: Viper: Machine Code from Python
docs.text:
Viper code is Python that MicroPython compiles to real machine instructions for the processor, instead of interpreting it. You mark a function with @micropython.viper and add type hints to its arguments. Inside, integers are plain 32-bit machine words in registers (they wrap around instead of growing), array arguments become pointers into your memory, and nothing is allocated. Three pointer types read arrays of different widths: ptr8 for bytes, ptr16 for 16-bit elements, and ptr32 for 32-bit elements, indexed like lists with no bounds checking.

Here is the windowing loop from Chapter 9 in its viper form (kernels.py). It multiplies each signed 16-bit sample by a Q15 window value:

@micropython.viper
def window_viper(x: ptr16, w: ptr16, out: ptr16, n: int):
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        s = int(x[i])
        if s >= 32768:            # ptr16 reads are unsigned: sign-extend by hand
            s -= 65536
        out[i] = (s * int(w[i])) >> 15
        i += 1

The type hints turn the three arrays into pointers and n into a machine integer. The loop body is the same arithmetic as the Python version out[i] = (x[i] * w[i]) >> 15. The lines about 32768 are the first trap.

ptr16 Reads Are Unsigned

A ptr16 read zero-extends, so a stored -1 comes back as 65535. If your samples are signed, subtract 65536 when the value is 32768 or more, as window_viper does. 04-window-kernels.py prints the raw read so you can see it, and it also checks all four versions give identical answers.

Viper has more rules, from the MicroPython documentation. There are no default argument values. Floating-point works but is not optimized, so keep floats out. Slices are not supported on pointers. And casting one viper value to another viper type costs nothing at run time, but casting a Python object can be slow, so do the casts at the top of the function and not inside a hot loop. Integer division (//) calls a helper function; this chapter's code uses shifts inside loops instead.

I checked the two viper functions in kernels.py in real MicroPython running on a computer (an x86-64 build of the current source), and they produce exactly the same outputs as the plain Python versions over 512 random samples. That checks the code and the ptr16 rule. It says nothing about speed on the Pico.

docs.title: The Viper Q15 FFT
docs.text:
A fixed-point FFT is the Chapter 9 algorithm with whole numbers. fft_viper.py holds it: the same bit-reversal reorder, the same nine stages of butterflies, the same in-place updates, but re and im are array('i'), the twiddle factors are Q15 integers (cosine and sine times 32768), and the functions are viper. After each butterfly both outputs are halved, so a number never grows beyond what it started with. That is how fixed-point FFTs avoid overflow: the 512-point transform's outputs are \( 1/512 \) of the true values, because nine halvings multiply to \( 1/512 \).

tr = (rb * c + ib * s + 16384) >> 15       # twiddle times the second number, Q15
ti = (ib * c - rb * s + 16384) >> 15
re[b] = (ra - tr + 1) >> 1                  # difference, halved
im[b] = (ia - ti + 1) >> 1
re[a] = (ra + tr + 1) >> 1                  # sum, halved
im[a] = (ia + ti + 1) >> 1

The added 16384 and 1 round the result to the nearest integer rather than always down.

Worked example. One butterfly at 45 degrees, where \( c = s = 23{,}170 \) (0.7071 in Q15). Let the first number be \( 4000 + 0j \) and the second \( 3000 + 1000j \):

Step Calculation Result tr \( (3000 \times 23170 + 1000 \times 23170 + 16384) \gg 15 \) 2828 ti \( (1000 \times 23170 - 3000 \times 23170 + 16384) \gg 15 \) -1414 new second number \( ((4000 - 2828 + 1) \gg 1,\; (0 + 1414 + 1) \gg 1) \) 586 + 707j new first number \( ((4000 + 2828 + 1) \gg 1,\; (0 - 1414 + 1) \gg 1) \) 3414 - 707j

The exact answer for the twiddle product is \( (3000 + 1000j)(0.7071 - 0.7071j) = 2828.4 - 1414.2j \), so tr and ti agree to the nearest integer, and the halved outputs are half of \( 4000 \pm 2828.4 \) and so on.

docs.title: How accurate is it?
docs.text:
Precision is the price of whole numbers. The input is cut from 24 bits to 16 (shift=16 in load_frame_q15), and every stage rounds. I measured the effect without the Pico: integer arithmetic gives the same answers on any machine as long as nothing overflows, so I ran the same functions on a computer inside a model that checks every addition and multiplication against 32-bit limits (none overflowed), and compared with the floating-point pipeline on synthetic frames: 48 frames of a single tone (six amplitudes from about -62 to -12 dBFS, four frequencies, two noise seeds) with random noise of about -63 dBFS added.

Question Result of the computer model Largest difference in a band louder than -50 dBFS 0.20 dB (mean 0.03 dB over 48 bands) Largest difference in a band louder than -60 dBFS 0.54 dB (30 bands) Peak bin the same as the float FFT 42 of 42 test tones Rounding-noise floor of the Q15 path, in the bands away from a clean test tone (shift 16) about -65 to -75 dBFS Same, with shift 14 (four times the input gain) about -77 to -90 dBFS Same, with shift 12 (sixteen times the gain) about -91 to -99 dBFS

Read the table as a trade. Where the sound is loud the viper FFT agrees with the float one to within about half a decibel. Where it is quiet, near the room's own noise, rounding in the Q15 path dominates, so the quietest bands read up to roughly 17 dB too high in my noise-only test. Raising the gain (a smaller shift) lowers that floor by 6 dB per factor of two, but a loud sound then clips, because load_frame_q15 clamps at \( \pm 32767 \): at shift 12 any peak louder than about -24 dBFS saturates. For a display of speech and tones the default is fine; for a calibration of the noise floor (Chapter 11) use the float path or a lower shift.

05-fft-viper-bench.py does the same comparison on the Pico, with the real time per stage, and also checks that fft_q15 allocates zero bytes. The speed is not known yet.

docs.title: Inline Assembly
docs.text:
Inline assembly lets you write machine instructions directly inside a Python file with @micropython.asm_thumb. It is the last stop on the road down. Each line is one ARM Thumb instruction, and you decide which register holds what. The function receives up to four arguments in registers r0, r1, r2, r3, and whatever is in r0 when the function ends is the return value. You may use r0 to r7. Arrays arrive as the address of their first element.

The smallest useful loop adds up an array of signed 16-bit numbers. Read it line by line, since there are only eight instructions:

@micropython.asm_thumb
def sum16_asm(r0, r1):            # r0 = address of the array, r1 = count (must be > 0)
    mov(r2, 0)                    # r2 = running total
    label(LOOP)
    ldrh(r3, [r0, 0])             # r3 = next number, zero-extended from 16 bits
    lsl(r3, r3, 16)
    asr(r3, r3, 16)               # sign-extend it to 32 bits
    add(r2, r2, r3)               # total = total + number
    add(r0, r0, 2)                # move to the next 16-bit element
    sub(r1, r1, 1)                # one fewer left
    cmp(r1, 0)
    bgt(LOOP)                     # branch back while the count is greater than 0
    mov(r0, r2)                   # the value in r0 is returned
Instruction What it does ldrh(r3, [r0, 0]) Load 16 bits from the address in r0 plus 0 into r3 lsl, asr by 16 Shift left then arithmetic shift right: copies bit 15 into the upper 16 bits (sign extension) add, sub Add or subtract; r0 moves by 2 bytes because each element is 2 bytes cmp, bgt Compare the count with 0, and branch back to LOOP if it is greater label(LOOP) A name for the position, used by the branch

The windowing loop is the same idea with a multiply: two loads, a sign extension, mul(r4, r5), an arithmetic shift by 15, a store with strh, and three pointer increments. Counting from the source in kernels_asm.py, window_asm runs 13 instructions per sample and sum16_asm 8 per element; I got those by stepping through the code in an emulator written for this chapter, which also confirmed that all three versions of the sum and the window give the same answers. That emulator checks the logic; it does not check the real assembler's encoding rules.

Assembly Looks Scarier Than It Is

A page of mnemonics is hard to take in at first glance, and most people feel that way. Read one instruction at a time, as the table above does, and remember that every line only moves, adds, or compares numbers you have already met.

There are three cautions. The assembler has no safety: a count of 0 still runs the loop once, and a bad address corrupts memory, so pass a count above 0 and no larger than the array. Not every instruction exists on every Pico. The MicroPython source enables the wider ARMv7-M instructions (sdiv, udiv, movw, clz, and others) when the firmware is built for a Thumb-2 core, which the RP2350's Cortex-M33 is; the older RP2040 lacks them. The loops in this chapter use only the basic instructions that both have, so they do not depend on it. And asm_thumb is ARM-only: it works while the Pico 2 runs on its ARM cores (the default), but if you flash firmware for the chip's RISC-V cores it is not available, because that build has a different assembler.

Speed estimate, not measured. Counting 13 instructions in the windowing loop, two of which are loads and one a taken branch, a rough guess for the Cortex-M33 is 15 to 25 cycles per sample. For 512 samples that is 7,700 to 12,800 cycles, or 51 to 85 microseconds. That comes from instruction counts and typical cycle costs, not from a measurement. 04-window-kernels.py measures all four versions on the board, and its numbers replace this paragraph.

docs.title: The Assembly FFT
docs.text:
An assembly FFT puts the butterfly loop into inline assembly. It is the fastest way to run an FFT on this board without leaving MicroPython, and it is a stretch exercise here: I have not written or run one, and I will not pretend to. What I can give you is the design, so you know what is involved.

Part Where it lives Why Bit-reversal reorder viper (fft_q15) It runs once per frame and touches 512 entries The 9 stages and the loop over groups Python or viper There are only 9 stages; but stage 1 has 256 groups, so a Python call per group means 511 calls in total, which is too many The butterflies inside a stage assembly 2,304 per frame; this is where the time is Twiddle factors Q15 arrays read by address Already computed

The assembly function can take only four arguments, so it must be given a small array of parameters (the stage size, the twiddle stride, and the three array addresses) as one of them. Each butterfly needs about six loads, four multiplies, six additions, four shifts, four stores and some pointer arithmetic: roughly 35 to 45 instructions, with r0 to r7 only for all of the values. If a butterfly took 60 cycles, the FFT would take \( 2{,}304 \times 60 = 138{,}240 \) cycles, or 0.92 ms. That is a paper estimate from my own instruction count, not a measurement; treat it as the target to beat when you try the exercise.

Before you attempt it, ask whether you need it. If the viper FFT already meets the deadline with room to spare, the assembly version buys speed you cannot use and costs readability, so the next sections give you the means to decide.

docs.title: Using the Second Core
docs.text:
Dual core use means running a second piece of code at the same time on the Pico's other processor core. MicroPython starts one with _thread.start_new_thread(function, args); on the Pico there are only two threads, one per core, and the new one runs on core 1. In the MicroPython source for this port there is no global interpreter lock, so the two cores run MicroPython code truly in parallel.

The temptation is to read the microphone on core 0 and run the FFT on core 1. It can work, but it comes with hazards, which is why this book keeps the audio work on one core (Chapter 4 said so):

Hazard Why Safe habit Shared heap Both cores allocate from one heap with one garbage collector protected by a lock; a collection started by one core can make the other wait Allocate nothing on core 1: pre-allocate everything, use viper Hardware ownership Starting or stopping I2S, the display's SPI, or a pin from two cores at once is unsafe, and I did not verify how the I2S driver's interrupts behave when its owner is core 1 Do all I2S, SPI, and Pin work on core 0; let core 1 touch only pure data Data races A buffer being rewritten by one core while the other reads it gives garbage Use two buffers and a flag that only one core writes Pauses Flash writes typically pause the other core (the port sets up a lockout for this) Keep file writes out of the real-time loop Latency Doing the FFT on frame \( k \) while frame \( k+1 \) is read means the display is one frame (40 ms) behind Accept it, or avoid the second core

07-dual-core.py measures the safe version of the idea. It runs a worker that touches no hardware, first alone and then beside core 0's counting loop, and reports how much each side slows the other. Pairs A and B are the solo baselines; C uses the allocation-free viper FFT, and D uses the pure-Python float FFT that allocates. My expectation, not a measurement: in C the two sides should run at nearly their solo speeds, and in D at least one should be slower because of the shared garbage collector. The script fills in those four ratios.

docs.title: Choosing: Performance Trade-Offs
docs.text:
Each speed-up buys time and charges something else. Performance trade-offs are the choice of what to pay.

Approach Speed Readability Portability Accuracy Memory Risk Plain Python on lists slowest best any MicroPython float precision most none Python on array slow good any MicroPython float precision less none Fixed-point in Python slow fair any MicroPython limited by bits less overflow Viper much faster (to be measured) fair Pico and other supported ports integer only, limited by bits least no bounds checking, unsigned ptr16 Inline assembly fastest (to be measured) poor ARM Thumb only integer only least crashes, silent corruption Second core up to 2 cores of work poor dual-core ports only unchanged shared heap races, GC stalls

The rule that comes out of the table is to use the simplest approach that keeps the worst pass inside the budget (less the display reserve). Start with plain Python and measure. If the profile shows one loop dominating, move only that loop to viper. Move to assembly or a second core only when viper still does not fit. Stop at the first row that passes timing verification: speed past the deadline is not worth any cost.

docs.title: Diagram: Speed-Up Chooser
docs.text:
Run Speed-Up Chooser Fullscreen

Speed-Up Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: speedup-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend, for 6 scenarios, the simplest implementation whose worst-case pass time fits within the frame budget minus the display reserve, or state that none fits, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: frame budget, display reserve, worst-case pass time, viper code, inline assembly, performance trade-offs (all defined in this chapter above the block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each scenario the learner chooses one of "Plain Python", "Viper", "Assembly", or "None fits" and submits. A choice is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Changing the numbers in the exploration panel is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The fastest implementation is always the best choice. (2) An implementation that fits on average fits the deadline. (3) Assembly is always needed for real-time audio.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level recommendation requires the learner to apply a stated criterion to evidence and justify the choice. The scenarios put a boundary case (an implementation that fits by exactly zero margin), a case where the simplest option already fits, and a case where nothing fits, so the learner cannot recommend by habit.

Content:

The numbers in this activity are illustrative and are not measurements of the kit. Each scenario gives the frame budget, the display reserve, and the worst-case pass time of three implementations, all in milliseconds. The complexity order from simplest to hardest is Plain Python, Viper, Assembly. The fitting limit is the budget minus the reserve; an implementation fits when its worst-case time is less than or equal to the limit.

# Budget (ms) Reserve (ms) Limit (ms) Plain Python Viper Assembly Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 40 10 30 120 6 4 Viper Plain Python is over the limit; viper and assembly both fit, and viper is the simpler. 2 40 10 30 18 5 3 Plain Python Plain Python already fits, so any faster option costs readability for nothing. 3 40 10 30 90 34 12 Assembly Viper at 34 ms is over the 30 ms limit; assembly at 12 ms fits. 4 40 10 30 200 80 45 None fits Even assembly at 45 ms is over the limit, so the work itself must be reduced. 5 20 5 15 60 14 7 Viper Viper at 14 ms is within the 15 ms limit, so assembly is not needed. 6 40 10 30 31 12 9 Viper Plain Python at 31 ms is just over the limit of 30 ms; viper at 12 ms fits.

For exploration the learner sets the budget (10 to 80 ms, step 5, default 40), the reserve (0 to 20 ms, step 5, default 10), and the three times (1 to 300 ms, step 1, defaults 90, 20, 10), and the sim shows which options fit.

Provenance: The scenario numbers are illustrative and invented for this activity. The 40 ms budget and 10 ms reserve are the values used in the chapter section "The Real-Time Constraint and the Frame Overrun". The sim labels all times "illustrative, not measured."

Rules: limit = budget - reserve. An option fits when its time <= limit. The answer is the first option that fits in the order Plain Python, Viper, Assembly; if none fits the answer is None fits. Budget: min 10, max 80, step 5, default 40, unit ms. Reserve: min 0, max 20, step 5, default 10, unit ms. Times: min 1, max 300, step 1, unit ms.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner changes the numbers in the exploration panel and watches which options fit.
  2. The learner notices that raising the reserve can make a fitting option stop fitting.
  3. The learner starts the 6 scenarios. Scenario 1 is shown.
  4. The learner chooses a recommendation and submits.
  5. The sim shows the limit, which options fit, the correct answer, and the Why text.

Feedback: 6 scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The exploration panel shows scenario 1's numbers with the limit of 30 ms and the three options marked fits or does not fit, and the question "Which is the simplest option that fits?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the audio work gets 30 ms of the 40 ms frame after a 10 ms display reserve, that the simplest approach that passes timing verification on the worst pass is the right one, and that the numbers in this activity are illustrative.
