feats is the frame's 16 features and bits is its loudness from Chapter 11's frame_stats(). The method pushes the frame into the window, scores only when the window is full and enough of it was loud, and fires when no cooldown is running and the score reaches the threshold.

docs.title: Testing the Detector
docs.text:
A detector should be able to prove it works before anyone trusts it. This chapter has two tests, one for the math and one for the device.

The detector math test, 01-detector-math-test.py, checks the pure math on synthetic windows and needs no hardware. It checks that every band's mean is 0 after subtraction (the largest was \( 2 \times 10^{-8} \)); that the length after normalizing is 1; that a window scores 1.000000 against its own template; that the score ignores a steady offset and a change of depth; that random windows score near 0; that the running-sums score matches the textbook steps; that the fill percentage goes 0, 4, 20, 40, 80, 96, and 100 percent as expected; that the cooldown and the speech-present rule work; that the template file saves and loads in 1,608 bytes; and that the DCT changes only coefficient 0 when a constant is added. Its last line is PASS or FAIL.

The detector self-test, 06-self-test.py, runs on the Pico against your enrolled template and checks things the math test cannot: that the template scores 1.0000 against itself, how fast the score falls when the window is shifted by 1, 2, or 3 frames (a measure of how fussy your template is), that random windows and a second of your room's noise score low, and, last, the time per frame. It adds up the cost of the features, the window update, and the score and compares the total with the 40 ms budget. That last line is the link to Chapter 8's frame overrun: a detector that is right but too slow loses audio, and the self-test says so.

On a computer, the fake-microphone run of the shift test, on a synthetic smooth pattern, gave 0.891, 0.617, and 0.292 for shifts of 1, 2, and 3 frames. Real speech features change faster, so expect your template to be at least as fussy.

docs.title: False Accepts, False Rejects, and the Trade-Off
docs.text:
A detector can be wrong in two ways. A false accept is a detection when the wake word was not said: the device wakes up for a cough, a similar-sounding phrase, or a classmate's chatter. A false reject is a miss: the student says "Hey Pico" and nothing happens. They are measured differently. A false-reject rate is a fraction of the attempts you made on purpose: say it 20 times and count the misses. A false-accept rate needs a lot of audio that is not the wake word, and it is naturally counted per hour.

Worked example (illustrative arithmetic). Suppose a classroom produces 300 speech-like segments an hour that the level gate opens for (an assumption for the example, not a measurement), and that 1 percent of non-wake segments score above the threshold. That is \( 300 \times 0.01 = 3 \) false accepts an hour, which is a distracting device in a lesson. At 0.1 percent it would be 0.3 an hour. The numbers show why a detector that looks accurate per attempt can be annoying per hour.

The threshold trade-off is that moving the detection threshold changes the two errors in opposite directions. Raise it and the device ignores more imposters (fewer false accepts) but misses more of the real ones (more false rejects). Lower it and the reverse happens. Neither direction is free, and no setting is best for everyone. The table uses synthetic score distributions: 1,000 "Hey Pico" scores drawn near 0.80 and 1,000 other-sound scores drawn near 0.35, from the fixed-seed generator in 01-detector-math-test.py (the shapes are invented to show the effect; real distributions are for 08 to find).

Threshold False rejects (of "Hey Pico") False accepts (of other sounds) 0.50 0.0% 16.6% 0.55 0.1% 9.1% 0.60 0.8% 5.3% 0.65 3.5% 2.4% 0.70 11.2% 0.8% 0.75 26.2% 0.5% 0.80 49.3% 0.1% 0.85 74.3% 0.0% 0.90 90.1% 0.0%

There Is No Free Threshold

The two score distributions overlap, and the threshold only decides which error you accept more of. Lowering the false accepts always costs some false rejects, and the only way to improve both at once is a better detector, not a better number.

docs.title: Diagram: Threshold Trade-Off Explorer
docs.text:
Threshold Trade-Off Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: threshold-tradeoff-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge which detection threshold, if any, meets stated limits on false rejects and false accepts in 4 scenarios, choosing the correct threshold or "none" in at least 3 of 4.

Prerequisites: detection threshold, score, false accept, false reject, threshold trade-off (all defined in this chapter above the block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 4 scenarios the learner chooses one threshold from the table in Content, or "none", before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Answer column. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Moving the threshold control and watching the two error rates in exploration is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A higher threshold is always safer. (2) There is always a threshold that satisfies both limits. (3) A false-accept rate per attempt is the same as per hour.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judgment means deciding against criteria, so each scenario states limits and the learner must test candidate thresholds against them. Scenario 3 has no valid answer, which makes the learner judge rather than pick the middle option.

Content:

The sim shows two score distributions as histograms: 1,000 scores for "Hey Pico" and 1,000 for other sounds, and a threshold line. All scores are synthetic and labelled "synthetic". For each threshold the sim shows the false-reject percentage (wake scores below the threshold) and the false-accept percentage (other scores at or above it).

Threshold False rejects False accepts 0.50 0.0% 16.6% 0.55 0.1% 9.1% 0.60 0.8% 5.3% 0.65 3.5% 2.4% 0.70 11.2% 0.8% 0.75 26.2% 0.5% 0.80 49.3% 0.1% 0.85 74.3% 0.0% 0.90 90.1% 0.0%

Scenarios, in this order. Among the thresholds that meet every limit, the answer is the one with the smallest sum of the two percentages; if no threshold meets every limit, the answer is "none".

# Scenario Limits Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 A quiet bedroom where missing the phrase is annoying False rejects at most 5% 0.65 0.50 to 0.65 meet the limit; 0.65 has the fewest false accepts of them (2.4%). 2 A busy classroom where a false wake-up is disruptive False accepts at most 1% 0.70 0.70 and higher meet the limit; 0.70 has the fewest false rejects of them (11.2%). 3 A demo that must almost never miss and almost never wake by mistake False rejects at most 10% and false accepts at most 1% none At 0.65 false accepts are 2.4% (too many) and at 0.70 false rejects are 11.2% (too many). No threshold meets both; the detector needs to be better, not retuned. 4 A shared class device with a patient user False rejects at most 25% and false accepts at most 1% 0.70 0.70 gives 11.2% and 0.8%. 0.75 has false rejects of 26.2%, which is over the limit.

Provenance: The scores are synthetic: 1,000 "Hey Pico" scores drawn near mean 0.80 with standard deviation 0.08 (capped at 1.0) and 1,000 other scores near mean 0.35 with standard deviation 0.15, from the fixed-seed generator (seed 77) in src/chapters/12-wake-word-detection/01-detector-math-test.py. The percentages in the table are that script's output.

Rules: False reject = wake score < threshold. False accept = other score >= threshold. The threshold control has the range 0.50 to 0.90, step 0.05, default 0.70, unit score. Percentages are shown to 1 decimal. The scenario answer is chosen as stated in Content.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the threshold and watches the two histograms' tails and the two percentages. The learner should notice that the two numbers move in opposite directions.
  2. The learner starts the 4 scenarios. Scenario 1 is shown with its limits.
  3. The learner chooses a threshold or "none" and submits.
  4. The sim marks the threshold on the histograms, shows both percentages at the chosen value and at the answer, and shows the Why text.
  5. After scenario 4, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that scenario 3 cannot be solved by moving the threshold.

Feedback: 4 scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 4" is shown.

Starting State: The threshold is at 0.70 with both histograms visible and the question "How many of each error would you accept?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's trade-off table has the same 9 rows. It states that 0.70 gives 11.2% false rejects and 0.8% false accepts.

docs.title: The Honest Limits of Template Matching
docs.text:
A template matcher on a 12.8 kHz microphone is a modest detector, and this section says so plainly. It is a good way to learn how wake-word detection works, and with careful enrollment and a tuned threshold it can work for one person in one room. It should not be sold as a replacement for the products you know.

To see the shape of the limits, tools/pipeline-synthetic-test.py runs the real feature and detector code, on a computer, on synthetic speech-like audio from a vowel-formant synthesizer: a clean pattern of vowels and bursts, with fixed seeds. It enrolls five synthetic utterances and scores 80 more of the enrolled voice, 160 other clips (random phrases, near-misses of "Hey Pico", and noise), and clips at different paces and voices. The audio is synthetic and much cleaner than real speech, so these results are not accuracy claims. At a threshold of 0.70 the test rejected 7.5 percent of the enrolled voice's "Hey Pico" clips (6 of 80; 5 of those 6 were never scored at all, because too few of their frames opened the level gate) and accepted 18.1 percent of the other clips, because the made-up near-misses and random phrases share vowel shapes with the template. The real rates are what 08 measures.

docs.title: Speaking Pace Sensitivity
docs.text:
Speaking pace sensitivity is that the template matches only when the phrase is said at about the speed it was enrolled at. The window compares frame \( i \) of the live sound with frame \( i \) of the template, so if the student speaks 20 percent faster, the "p" burst that was in frame 13 arrives in frame 11, and every later part is early. Nothing stretches or squeezes the time axis to compensate. The synthetic pace sweep of the pipeline test shows the shape (enrolled voice, 40 clips per pace):

Pace (time compared with enrollment) Mean best score Rejected at 0.70 0.7 (faster) 0.518 100% 0.8 0.656 78% 0.9 0.739 5% 1.0 (as enrolled) 0.787 5% 1.1 0.689 22% 1.2 (slower) 0.559 100% 1.3 0.429 100%

The score falls off quickly on both sides, so a student who says it more slowly when tired or more quickly when rushed will be missed. A method that does stretch time is dynamic time warping, which aligns two sequences by finding the cheapest path through a table of frame-to-frame distances; it costs far more computation and is a good pointer for further reading, not something this book builds. A cheaper remedy is to enroll at more than one pace and keep more than one template.

docs.title: Trained Keyword Spotting
docs.text:
Trained keyword spotting is what commercial wake-word systems use instead. A small neural network is trained, on a computer, on thousands of recordings of many speakers saying the word and many hours of other sound, and then the trained weights are loaded onto the device. Such models learn what is common across speakers and paces and learn to reject confusable phrases, which is what a single enrolled template cannot do. They also take features like the MFCCs above as input. Building and training them is outside this book (the course description lists it as a topic not covered), but you now know what they are replacing: a template made from five of your own utterances.

The limits, summarized, are these.

  • The template fits one speaker, microphone, and room; a new voice or a changed room may need re-enrolling.
  • The window needs the phrase at about the enrolled pace.
  • The detector knows no phonetics, so similar-sounding phrases can score high.
  • The plain-Python transform cannot keep up with 40 ms frames; the live detector needs Chapter 10's work.
  • Accuracy numbers are not claims until you have measured them.

Do Not Read Synthetic Numbers as Accuracy

The tables marked synthetic show how the math behaves and what shapes to expect, not how well your kit will hear "Hey Pico". Measure with 08-threshold-sweep.py, at several thresholds, with several speakers and paces, before you claim a false-accept or false-reject rate.

docs.title: What Has and Has Not Been Measured
docs.text:
The code in this chapter ran, off the device, on a computer against a stand-in for the Pico's pins, microphone, and timer. The math is tested by 01-detector-math-test.py, and the end-to-end pipeline by the synthetic test. Nothing here has run on the Pico yet. This table lists what you will have to measure.

Question Script Status Milliseconds per frame for each feature step and the total 03-feature-timing.py and 06-self-test.py Not yet measured; the plain-Python FFT is expected to be over the 40 ms budget How repeatable your "Hey Pico" is 05-enroll.py consistency Not yet measured (the synthetic values are 0.686 to 0.879) How fussy the alignment is for a real template 06-self-test.py shifted scores Not yet measured Scores for "Hey Pico" and for other phrases 07-score-trace.py Not yet measured False rejects and false accepts at several thresholds 08-threshold-sweep.py Not yet measured; the chapter's tables are synthetic Other speakers and other paces 08-threshold-sweep.py with SPEAKER and PACE set Not yet measured; the tables above are synthetic False accepts per hour in ordinary use 09-live-detector.py, with approval Not yet measured; needs a fast transform and Chapter 17's approval Detection latency 09-live-detector.py Not yet measured

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
A frame of 512 samples becomes 16 log band energies. The last 25 frames form a rolling window, which is not scored until its fill reaches 100 percent. Mean subtraction removes each band's steady part, normalization removes the strength, and a dot product with the enrolled template gives a score from -1 to 1. If at least 8 frames of the window had speech, the score reaches the threshold, and no cooldown is running, the detector fires: the microphone closes, the confirmation beep plays, the window resets, and a 2-second cooldown starts. Enrollment builds the template from five of your own utterances. Push-to-talk stays the default listening mode, and always-on listening is an advanced option that needs approval.

Key takeaways:

  • A wake word is a phrase the device listens for; "Hey Pico" is long enough and varied enough for a template detector.
  • Feature extraction reduces a frame to 16 log band energies (MFCC-like, without the DCT); the plain-Python FFT is a reference that Chapter 10 replaces with a fast one.
  • The rolling window holds 25 frames (1 second, 1,600 bytes); never score it before the fill percentage is 100.
  • Mean subtraction removes steady colouring, unit normalization removes strength, and the dot product is the cosine of the angle between window and template.
  • Enrollment averages five of your own utterances into wake_template.bin; the template fits one speaker, microphone, and room.
  • The threshold, the speech-present rule, the cooldown, and the confirmation beep (microphone closed) turn scores into decisions.
  • Raising the threshold trades false accepts for false rejects, and some requirements cannot be met by any threshold.
  • Template matching is a modest detector: it is pace and speaker sensitive, and every accuracy number must be measured.
  • Always-on listening needs approval (Chapter 17); push-to-talk (Chapter 11) is the default.

Test yourself with these two questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

The window is 60 percent full and the room is noisy. Why must the detector not score it, and what does the code return? Click to expand

A 60 percent full window has 15 real frames and 10 frames of zeros (or old data), so its band means and length do not describe a second of sound, and normalizing it can make a meaningless pattern look like a strong match. Window.score() returns None until the fill percentage is 100, and the detector also requires at least 8 frames with the level gate open before it scores.

You moved the kit to a room with a different hum and a cheaper microphone. Why can the score still work, and what might not? Click to expand

The hum and the microphone's frequency response add steady amounts to the band energies, and mean subtraction removes anything steady in a band, so the score is largely unchanged. What it cannot remove is noise that changes during the second, a much lower speech-to-noise ratio (the level gate may stay shut), or a different speaker. Recalibrate (Chapter 11) and measure again with 08-threshold-sweep.py.

A Detector You Can Explain

You just built and tested a wake-word detector from log band features, a rolling window, mean subtraction, unit normalization, and a dot-product score, and you know exactly where it is weak. Few people can say why their assistant wakes up; you can.

In Chapter 13 we connect the device to the agent that answers the questions you ask it.

docs.title: Wi-Fi, HTTP, and Connecting to the Agent
Summary
docs.text: This chapter connects the Pico to the school network. Students join Wi-Fi, understand IP addresses and the local network, and exchange JSON with the buddy server using HTTP POST and the requests library. They also learn why plain HTTP is acceptable only on a trusted classroom network.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score JSON 18 Wi-Fi Connection 132 Network Station Mode 1 IP Address 128 HTTP Protocol 74 Local Network 7 HTTP POST 53 REST Endpoint 1 Plain HTTP LAN Use 1 mDNS Discovery 1 requests Library 8

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems
  • Chapter 4: The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring

docs.title: The Device Leaves Its Island
docs.text:
Until now everything ran on the Pico itself: the microphone, the display, the speaker. But the part that knows about tests and due dates, the buddy server, lives on another computer. This chapter builds the road between them: joining the school's Wi-Fi, finding the server, and sending it a question in a form it understands.

Let's Make the Call

By the end of this chapter your Pico will join the school Wi-Fi, ask the buddy server "when is my next test?", and print the answer on the round display. Let's listen closely! A network is just two programs agreeing on what to say.

Here is the whole trip in seven steps, with the part that does each one. Every step is a section of this chapter.

Step What happens Who does it Section 1 The Pico joins the Wi-Fi network and is given an address Pico and the access point Joining the Network 2 The Pico works out where the server is Pico IP Addresses 3 The question is written as JSON text Pico JSON: A Shape Both Sides Agree On 4 The Pico opens a connection and sends an HTTP POST Pico HTTP: The Language of the Question 5 The server reads the request and decides on a reply Buddy server The Buddy Server's Endpoint 6 The server sends the reply back Buddy server The Buddy Server's Endpoint 7 The Pico reads the reply, closes the connection, and shows the answer Pico Reading the Reply Safely

docs.title: Joining the Network
docs.text: A Wi-Fi connection is the link between the Pico's radio and an access point, the box (or ceiling unit) that the school's network hangs from. The Pico 2 W's radio is the separate wireless chip from Chapter 4. It speaks 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only, so a network that offers only 5 GHz will never appear in a scan.

docs.title: Network Station Mode
docs.text:
Network station mode means the Pico joins somebody else's network, the way a phone or laptop does. MicroPython gives it a name, network.STA_IF ("station interface"). The other choice, network.AP_IF, makes the Pico an access point that other devices join. This book always uses station mode, because the buddy server is on the school's network, not on the Pico's.

import network

wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)    # station mode
wlan.active(True)                      # switch the radio on
wlan.connect(ssid, password)           # start joining; this returns at once

connect() does not wait. It starts the join and returns, and the join takes anywhere from a fraction of a second to several seconds. A program that assumes it is finished on the next line sends its first request into nothing. Instead, poll wlan.status() and give up after a time limit. The helper module wifi_link.py in src/chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/ does exactly this, and every other file in the chapter uses it.

start = time.ticks_ms()
while True:
    code = wlan.status()
    if code == 3:                      # connected, with an IP address
        return wlan
    if code < 0:                       # a definite failure
        raise WifiError(code)
    if time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), start) > timeout_ms:
        raise WifiError(code, "gave up")
    time.sleep_ms(200)

The loop has three ways out: success, a definite failure, and the clock running out. The code is a number from the CYW43 wireless driver, and each value means something you can show on the display.

status() network.STAT_ name Meaning What the device should do 0 STAT_IDLE Not trying Call connect() 1 STAT_CONNECTING Joining Wait, with the time limit running 2 (none) Joined, no IP address yet Wait; the address is on its way 3 STAT_GOT_IP Connected Carry on -1 STAT_CONNECT_FAIL Failed, reason unknown Show an error; retry later -2 STAT_NO_AP_FOUND Network name not found Check the name, the distance, and the 2.4 GHz rule -3 STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD Wrong password Stop and show it; retrying cannot help

Worked example. A student mistypes the password in secrets.py. The loop starts at status 1, and after the access point rejects the password the driver reports -3. wifi_link.connect() raises WifiError with the text "wrong password", and the display's status region says so, instead of spinning for ever. A student whose school network is 5 GHz only gets -2, "network not found", even though the name is correct. The two fixes are very different, which is why the code keeps the numbers apart. 01-wifi-connect.py prints each state with the milliseconds since the join began, so you can see how long your network takes. That is a measurement for you to make; the book does not know your access point.

Check the Signal First

When a connection is flaky, print wlan.status("rssi") before suspecting your code. It returns the signal strength in dBm, a negative number that gets more negative as the signal weakens. As a rule of thumb, a reading much weaker than -80 dBm is a poor link.

The Wi-Fi name and password come from secrets.py on the Pico (wifi_ssid and wifi_pass), the same file the kit's other programs use. It is listed in the repository's .gitignore so it is never committed.

Never Print the Password

A print(secrets.wifi_pass) left in a program ends up in screenshots, forum posts, and shared logs. Print the network name only, as 01-wifi-connect.py does, and keep secrets.py out of every commit.

docs.title: IP Addresses
docs.text:
Once the Pico is connected it has an IP address, the number that identifies it on the network, in the way a house number identifies a house on a street. An IPv4 address is four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, such as 192.168.1.23. That is 32 bits, packed as four bytes. The Pico does not choose its address. A DHCP server, usually built into the school's router, hands one out for a limited time (a lease) when the Pico joins.

wlan.ifconfig() returns four values, always in this order.

Position Name Example What it is 0 IP address 192.168.1.23 This Pico's address 1 Netmask 255.255.255.0 Says which part of an address names the network 2 Gateway 192.168.1.1 The router: the way out of this network 3 DNS server 192.168.1.1 Turns names like example.com into numbers

docs.title: The Netmask
docs.text:
Part of every address names the network and part names the device on it. The netmask says where the line falls. Write the address and the mask in binary, and keep only the bits where the mask has a 1. The result, the network address, is the same for every device on the same network.

Worked example. The Pico is 192.168.1.23 and the server is 192.168.1.50, both with mask 255.255.255.0. The mask keeps the first three numbers and throws away the last one.

Device Address Mask Kept (network address) Pico 192.168.1.23 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.0 Server 192.168.1.50 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.0 Another room's device 192.168.2.50 255.255.255.0 192.168.2.0

The Pico and the server have the same network address, so they are on the same network and can talk directly. The third device keeps 192.168.2.0, a different network, so a message to it must go through the gateway.

Masks do not always fall between whole numbers. Take 255.255.240.0, where the third number of the mask is 240, which is 11110000 in binary. It keeps the top 4 bits of the third number and drops the bottom 4. Then 172.16.5.5 and 172.16.15.1 both keep 172.16.0.0, because 5 and 15 are both below 16, while 172.16.16.1 keeps 172.16.16.0 and is on a different network. The number of host bits left over sets the size of the network: with \( h \) host bits, there are \( 2^h - 2 \) usable device addresses, because the all-zeros address names the network and the all-ones address is for broadcasting.

Netmask Host bits \( h \) Usable addresses \( 2^h - 2 \) Typical use 255.255.255.0 8 254 One classroom or lab 255.255.255.128 7 126 Half a classroom subnet 255.255.240.0 12 4,094 A school wing 255.255.0.0 16 65,534 A whole campus

02-ip-and-subnet.py does the arithmetic with shifts and masks, runs on your computer or the Pico, and on the Pico also checks whether your BUDDY_HOST is on the Pico's own network. If it is not, the first thing to suspect is a wrong address in buddy_config.py, or a server on a separate guest network.

docs.title: The Local Network
docs.text:
A local network (LAN, local area network) is a group of devices that can reach each other directly, without going through the internet. A classroom's Wi-Fi network is one. Local networks use private address ranges that internet routers refuse to forward, defined by a standard called RFC 1918.

Range Netmask length Where you meet it 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255 10.0.0.0/8 Schools, campuses 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 172.16.0.0/12 Some school districts 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 192.168.0.0/16 Homes, small labs

Notice that 172.32.0.9 is not private even though it starts with 172; the range stops at 172.31. If ifconfig() shows an address outside these ranges, the Pico is probably not on a classroom network at all.

Because the Pico gets its address from DHCP, the server's address can change when the router restarts, which would silently break BUDDY_HOST. The fix is a DHCP reservation on the router (the router always hands the server the same address), or a fixed address outside the router's DHCP range. Ask the school's network administrator, who will want to know the server's MAC address.

docs.title: Diagram: Same-Subnet Checker
docs.text:
Same-Subnet Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: same-subnet-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate whether two IPv4 addresses are on the same network, given a netmask, in 8 cases, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: IP address, netmask, network address, same network, binary form of a number from 0 to 255 (all defined in this chapter above this block; binary numbers are in Chapter 3).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 cases the learner chooses "same network" or "different networks", then types the network address of the first device. A case is correct when both answers match the Answer columns in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Using the explorer (typing any addresses and watching the binary AND) is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Addresses that start with the same number are always on the same network. (2) A mask can only fall between whole numbers. (3) The all-zeros and all-ones device addresses can be given to a device.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation requires the learner to carry out the mask-and-compare procedure on new numbers. Showing the two addresses and the mask in binary, with the mask's 1 bits highlighted, ties the procedure to what the mask keeps, and asking for the network address as well as the yes/no answer shows the work.

Content:

The explorer shows an address, a second address, and a netmask. Each is shown as four numbers and as four groups of 8 bits. The sim computes the network address of each as the bitwise AND of the address and the mask. The two addresses are on the same network when the two network addresses are equal.

# First address Netmask Second address Same network? Network address of the first Why (shown as feedback) 1 192.168.1.23 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.50 same 192.168.1.0 The mask keeps the first three numbers, and both start 192.168.1. 2 192.168.1.23 255.255.255.0 192.168.2.50 different 192.168.1.0 The third numbers, 1 and 2, differ and the mask keeps them. 3 10.4.7.88 255.255.0.0 10.4.200.9 same 10.4.0.0 The mask keeps only 10.4, and both start 10.4. 4 10.4.7.88 255.255.255.0 10.4.200.9 different 10.4.7.0 The same two addresses, but this mask also keeps the third number, 7 and 200. 5 172.16.5.5 255.255.240.0 172.16.15.1 same 172.16.0.0 240 is 11110000, so only the top 4 bits of the third number are kept; 5 and 15 are both 0000. 6 172.16.5.5 255.255.240.0 172.16.16.1 different 172.16.0.0 16 is 00010000, so its kept bits are 0001, not 0000. 7 192.168.1.200 255.255.255.128 192.168.1.20 different 192.168.1.128 128 is 10000000: 200 keeps the top bit (1) and 20 keeps 0. 8 192.168.1.130 255.255.255.128 192.168.1.200 same 192.168.1.128 130 and 200 are both 128 or more, so both keep the top bit 1.

For exploration the learner can type any two addresses (each number 0 to 255) and choose a netmask from 255.255.255.0, 255.255.255.128, 255.255.240.0 or 255.255.0.0. The default is 192.168.1.23, 255.255.255.0 and 192.168.1.50.

Provenance: The arithmetic is the chapter sections "The Netmask" and "The Local Network", and the same cases (1 to 6) are in the table printed by 02-ip-and-subnet.py. The addresses are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative."

Rules: The network address is the bitwise AND of each of the four numbers of the address with the matching number of the mask. Two addresses are on the same network when their network addresses are equal. If the learner types a number outside 0 to 255, the sim ignores the change and keeps the previous value.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner opens the explorer and changes the second address's last number, watching its bits and the kept bits change.
  2. The learner changes the netmask from 255.255.255.0 to 255.255.0.0 and notices which cases flip from different to same.
  3. The learner starts the 8 cases. Case 1 is shown.
  4. The learner chooses same or different, types the first address's network address, and submits.
  5. The sim highlights the kept bits of both addresses and shows the Why text.
  6. After case 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that cases 3 and 4 use the same two addresses and have opposite answers.

Feedback: 8 cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. They are , and the network address is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: The explorer shows 192.168.1.23 and 192.168.1.50 with 255.255.255.0, with the question "Are these two on the same network?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the netmask keeps the network part of an address, that 255.255.240.0 keeps the top 4 bits of the third number, that 172.16.5.5 and 172.16.15.1 are on the same network under that mask while 172.16.16.1 is not, and that a network with \( h \) host bits has \( 2^h - 2 \) usable addresses.

Binary Makes Masks Click

Netmasks that fall inside a number, like 240, feel strange the first time. If the AND is slippery, write the two numbers out in eight bits, as you did for sample values in Chapter 3, and cross out the bits the mask throws away.

docs.title: JSON: A Shape Both Sides Agree On
docs.text:
The Pico and the server are different programs in different places, so they need a shared way to write down a question. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text format for labeled values. It has objects in curly braces { } holding name and value pairs, lists in square brackets [ ], strings in double quotes, numbers, true, false, and null. MicroPython reads and writes it with the same json module as a computer.

import json

request = {"device": "desk-07", "kind": "question", "text": "when is my next test"}
text = json.dumps(request)      # dict -> text, ready to send
back = json.loads(text)         # text -> dict again

This is the Chapter 1 request-reply contract, now defined for real. A request has exactly three fields, and a reply has exactly three.

Direction Field Type Meaning Request device string Which desk device is asking (DEVICE_ID) Request kind string "question" in this chapter Request text string What the student said, already as text Reply speak string The sentence to say aloud Reply show string A short line for the display, 30 characters or fewer Reply next_mode string One of clock, listening, thinking, speaking, settings (Chapter 7's modes)

Three habits keep JSON from causing trouble. First, count bytes, not characters: the text {"device": "desk-07", "kind": "question", "text": "when is my next test"} is 73 bytes, and HTTP will need that number. An accented letter such as the é in "café" takes two bytes in UTF-8, so call .encode() before you count. Second, expect bad input: single quotes, a trailing comma, or a missing brace all make json.loads raise ValueError, and a Pico must catch it instead of crashing on a bad reply. Third, do not rely on formatting: MicroPython's json.dumps has no indent option, so the output is always one line.

03-json-contract.py runs these checks on your computer or the Pico: the request is 73 bytes, the reply {"speak": "Your next test is Biology on Friday.", "show": "Biology test: Friday", "next_mode": "clock"} is 103, and four malformed texts are all rejected.

docs.title: HTTP: The Language of the Question
docs.text:
An address finds the server's computer, but a computer may run many programs. A port is a number that picks one: the buddy server listens on port 8080. The pair (address, port) is where the conversation happens.

The HTTP protocol (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules for what is said on that connection. It is a request and a reply, and the client always speaks first. The Pico is the client: it opens a TCP connection to the server, sends a request, and waits. The buddy server is the server: it answers one request and (in our version) closes the connection. HTTP is stateless: the server remembers nothing between requests, which is why every request carries device.

An HTTP request is plain text with four parts, always in this order.

Part Example Job Request line POST /v1/ask HTTP/1.0 Method (what to do), path (where), HTTP version Header lines Content-Length: 73 Facts about the request, one Name: value per line Blank line (just \r\n) Marks the end of the headers Body {"device": ...} The data itself (empty for some methods)

Each line ends with two characters, carriage return and line feed, written \r\n. Here is exactly what 04-raw-http-post.py builds for the default settings. The <CRLF> marks are not sent as text; they show where \r\n goes.

POST /v1/ask HTTP/1.0<CRLF>
Host: 192.168.1.50:8080<CRLF>
Content-Type: application/json<CRLF>
Content-Length: 73<CRLF>
Connection: close<CRLF>
<CRLF>
{"device": "desk-07", "kind": "question", "text": "when is my next test"}

That is 121 bytes of head (119 for the five lines and 2 for the blank line) plus the 73-byte body, 194 bytes in all. The reply has the same shape, with a status line in place of the request line.

HTTP/1.0 200 OK<CRLF>
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8<CRLF>
Content-Length: 103<CRLF>
<CRLF>
{"speak": "Your next test is Biology on Friday.", "show": "Biology test: Friday", "next_mode": "clock"}

The three-digit status code tells the client how things went, by its first digit: 2 means success, 4 means the client made a mistake, and 5 means the server failed.

Code Name When the buddy server sends it 200 OK The request fit the contract and here is the reply 400 Bad Request The body is not valid JSON, or fields are missing or wrong 404 Not Found No such path 405 Method Not Allowed GET sent to a path that wants POST 411 Length Required No Content-Length header 413 Content Too Large The body is bigger than the server allows (2,048 bytes) 500, 503 Server error, busy The server failed; trying again later may work

A Request Is Just Text

Notice how little magic there is: a web request is a few lines of text that you could type by hand. Once you can read one, a failed request stops being mysterious, because the status code and the headers tell you which side made the mistake.

docs.title: HTTP POST
docs.text:
HTTP has several methods. HTTP GET asks for something and sends no body. HTTP POST sends data for the server to act on, with the data in the body. The buddy server needs the student's words, so the Pico uses POST. (A GET could carry the words in the URL, but URLs end up in logs and are limited in length, so the question belongs in the body.)

The one number a POST must get right is Content-Length: the count of bytes in the body. The server reads that many and stops. Get it wrong and one of two things happens.

Header says Body really has What the buddy server does 73 73 Reads all of it and answers 200 60 73 Reads 60 bytes, finds the JSON cut off, and answers 400 90 73 Waits for the 17 missing bytes while the Pico waits for an answer. Nothing happens until a timeout

The third row is why every socket on the Pico needs a time limit, which Chapter 14 builds in properly.

rawhttp.py builds the request. It encodes the body first, so the number it writes is a byte count.

def build_post(host, port, path, payload, extra_headers=None):
    body = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    lines = [
        "POST {} HTTP/1.0".format(path),
        "Host: {}:{}".format(host, port),
        "Content-Type: application/json",
        "Content-Length: {}".format(len(body)),
        "Connection: close",
    ]
    head = "\r\n".join(lines) + "\r\n\r\n"
    return head.encode("utf-8") + body

"\r\n".join(lines) puts the line break between lines, and the extra "\r\n\r\n" ends the last header and adds the blank line. We say HTTP/1.0 and Connection: close on purpose: the server closes the connection after its reply, so the Pico never has to work out where one reply ends and the next begins.

Worked example. Sending it with only a socket takes eight steps, and 05-socket-post.py does all of them.

addr = socket.getaddrinfo(host, port)[0][-1]   # ask for the (address, port) pair
sock = socket.socket()
sock.settimeout(8)                              # every wait gives up after 8 seconds
try:
    sock.connect(addr)
    sock.send(raw)                              # the 194 bytes above
    status, headers, body = rawhttp.read_response(sock, 2048)
finally:
    sock.close()                                # always, even after an error

read_response reads until it sees the blank line, splits the head into a status code and headers, then reads exactly Content-Length more bytes. It refuses a reply whose Content-Length is above 2,048, so a wrong server cannot fill the Pico's memory.

docs.title: Diagram: HTTP Request Reader
docs.text:
HTTP Request Reader

Type: microsim sim-id: http-request-reader Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret the parts of an HTTP POST request and its reply by answering 8 questions about the request text, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: HTTP protocol, request line, header, blank line, body, Content-Length, status code, HTTP POST (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 questions the learner chooses one of three answers. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over a line of the request to read its label is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The blank line is optional decoration. (2) A wrong Content-Length is harmless. (3) A 4xx status means the server is broken. (4) The body can be longer than Content-Length says.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level interpretation requires the learner to explain what a part of the message means in a concrete example, not to name it. Choosing the effect of a changed or wrong value makes the learner use the meaning of each part.

Content:

The request shown on screen, with its lines numbered:

Line Text L1 POST /v1/ask HTTP/1.0 L2 Host: 192.168.1.50:8080 L3 Content-Type: application/json L4 Content-Length: 73 L5 Connection: close L6 (blank line) L7 {"device": "desk-07", "kind": "question", "text": "when is my next test"}

The 8 questions, each with three choices:

# Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which line says what the client wants done, and where? L1, L2, L7 L1 The request line holds the method (POST), the path (/v1/ask) and the HTTP version. 2 Which line tells the server how many bytes of body to read? L3, L4, L5 L4 Content-Length counts the body's bytes. 3 What does the blank line L6 do? It ends the headers, so the body starts after it; it is optional; it separates two requests It ends the headers, so the body starts after it Without it the server would keep reading header lines. 4 Content-Length says 60 but the body is 73 bytes. What does the buddy server do? Reads 60 bytes and answers 400 because the JSON is cut off; reads all 73 and answers 200; waits for 13 more bytes Reads 60 bytes and answers 400 because the JSON is cut off The server trusts the header, so it stops at 60 and the JSON is incomplete. 5 Content-Length says 90 but the body is 73 bytes. What happens? The server answers 200; the server answers 400; the server waits for 17 more bytes, and the Pico's timeout ends it The server waits for 17 more bytes, and the Pico's timeout ends it The server is still reading and the Pico is waiting for the reply, so neither moves. 6 Which line tells the server the body is JSON? L2, L3, L5 L3 Content-Type names the format of the body. 7 The reply starts with HTTP/1.0 400 Bad Request. Whose mistake is it? The client's request was wrong; the server is broken; the Wi-Fi dropped The client's request was wrong A first digit of 4 means the client made the mistake; 5 means the server did. 8 The reply has Content-Length: 103. How many body bytes should the Pico read? 73, 103, as many as arrive until a timeout 103 The reply's Content-Length counts the reply's body, and the Pico stops there.

Provenance: The request is the one printed by src/chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/04-raw-http-post.py with the default buddy_config.py. The reply length 103 is the length of the Chapter 1 reply as JSON. The server behaviors in questions 4 and 5 are those of server/buddy_server.py.

Rules: Question order is fixed and the choices of each question are shown in the order in the table. Each question has one attempt. The score is the number of correct answers.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner hovers over each of the lines L1 to L7 to read what it is called.
  2. The learner starts the 8 questions. Question 1 is shown.
  3. The learner picks an answer and submits.
  4. The sim shows the correct answer and the Why text, and highlights the lines involved in the request.
  5. After question 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that questions 4 and 5 differ only in whether the header number is smaller or larger than the real body.

Feedback: 8 questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: The request is shown with numbered lines and nothing selected, with the question "Which line says what the client wants done, and where?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the request is 194 bytes in all, 121 of head and 73 of body; that the reply is 103 bytes of body; that a Content-Length smaller than the body gives a 400 and a larger one makes the server wait; and that a first status digit of 4 means the client's mistake.

docs.title: The Buddy Server's Endpoint
docs.text:
A REST endpoint is a path on a server that does one named job when it receives a request, such as POST /v1/ask. The /v1/ is a version number: if the contract ever changes, /v2/ask can exist beside it and old devices keep working. The buddy server has two endpoints in this chapter.

Method and path Job Success POST /v1/ask Run the brain on a question 200 and the three-field reply GET /v1/health Say that the server is up 200 and {"ok": true, ...}

The server is server/buddy_server.py, about 190 lines of Python's standard library, so there is nothing to install. It runs on your computer, not on the Pico.

cd src/chapters/13-wifi-http-agent-link/server
python3 buddy_server.py

It prints the address that other devices on the network should use, and that address goes into BUDDY_HOST in buddy_config.py. The brain is Chapter 1's decide() function. The server asks it for an answer, and puts the answer into the three-field reply. That one function is the only place where "the brain" lives, so Chapter 16 can replace it with a school calendar and Chapter 14 can feed it transcribed speech without the Pico noticing.

def make_reply(text, events):
    speak, show = decide(text, events)
    return {"speak": speak, "show": show[:30], "next_mode": "clock"}

Before it calls the brain the server checks the request against the contract, and answers with a status code and a JSON body {"error": "..."} when something is wrong. python3 server/test_server.py runs 13 checks with no Pico, including a body that is not JSON (400), a missing field (400), an oversize body (413), and a GET where a POST belongs (405).

docs.title: Reading the Reply Safely
docs.text:
A request is not finished when the bytes leave the Pico. Two rules apply to the reply, and both protect the Pico's small memory (Chapter 2).

Read a bounded amount. The reply says how big its body is in Content-Length. The code compares that number with MAX_REPLY_BYTES (2,048) before reading anything, and never reads more. The whole exchange here is 194 bytes out and a little over 100 bytes of body back, tiny next to the Pico's heap. The danger is not these messages. It is the day a wrong server sends a megabyte.

Always close the socket. An open connection holds memory and one of the network stack's small, fixed number of sockets. If a program forgets to close one on every path, including the paths where an error was raised, it works for a while and then fails with an error that looks unrelated. That is why socket.close() is in a finally block, the same rule as mic.deinit() in Chapter 2.

docs.title: The requests Library
docs.text:
Writing build_post and read_response once teaches you what HTTP is, but you should not hand-write it in every program. The requests library wraps the same steps, and its call looks like this.

import requests

response = requests.post(
    "http://192.168.1.50:8080/v1/ask",
    json={"device": "desk-07", "kind": "question", "text": "when is my next test"},
    timeout=8)
try:
    reply = response.json()
    print(response.status_code, reply["show"])
finally:
    response.close()

json= turns the dictionary into JSON, sets Content-Type, and works out Content-Length. timeout= sets the socket time limit. response.json() reads the whole body and parses it. response.close() closes the socket, and is the line people forget.

Whether the library is on your Pico depends on the firmware. The Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W builds of MicroPython do not include it as a built-in module, as far as the port's file list shows. Install it once, while connected to Wi-Fi.

import mip
mip.install("requests")

mip downloads the package from the micropython-lib collection into the lib folder on the Pico, and 06-requests-post.py runs this for you if the import fails. At the time of writing, micropython-lib lists the package as requests version 1.1.1. Older firmware called it urequests, which has no timeout argument, so 06-requests-post.py says so if it hits that. Which version mip gave your Pico is a fact to write down.

There is one more thing to know about this library, and it matters in Chapter 14. When a web address begins with https://, the library as we read it turns off certificate checking. For http:// on a classroom network that does not matter. For https:// it means the connection is encrypted but would also connect to an impostor, and Chapter 14 shows how to do better.

By hand (05-socket-post.py) requests (06-requests-post.py) Lines of your code About 12 About 5 You see the raw text Yes No Content-Length You count it Done for you Timeout sock.settimeout() timeout= (newer versions) Needs installing No Yes, with mip Closes for you No: use finally No: call response.close()

docs.title: Showing the Link on the Display
docs.text:
A device that fails silently feels broken. The status region from Chapter 6 (the top bar, 15 characters wide) is the right place to say what the link is doing, and the agent message region (30 characters) shows the answer. 07-ask-buddy-display.py ties it together: the status bar walks through "joining", "online", "asking...", and "ok" with the elapsed milliseconds, and an error word if anything goes wrong.

def put(region, text, color):
    x, y, width = region
    display.text(SMALL, text[:width].ljust(width), x, y, color, config.BLACK)

The function cuts the text to the region's width and pads it with spaces to exactly that width, so the new text covers the old without redrawing the screen. A full-screen fill takes at least 86 ms (Chapter 5), while a 15-character status redraw is \( 15 \times 8 \times 16 \times 2 = 3{,}840 \) bytes. Each press of MODE sends the next question and shows the server's show field. Because the code catches OSError, ValueError and KeyError, stopping the server makes the status say "error" and the device carries on.

docs.title: Finding the Server by Name: mDNS
docs.text:
Typing 192.168.1.50 into a file is awkward if it changes. mDNS discovery (multicast DNS) lets a device find another by a name ending in .local instead, such as buddy.local. The device asks the whole local network "who is buddy.local?" and the owner answers with its address. No DNS server is needed. A Raspberry Pi running school software is usually reachable this way, and most laptops answer to their own .local names.

Two different things hide behind "mDNS support", and the Pico's support for them differs.

Job Meaning Status for the Pico 2 W Announcing The Pico answers to study-buddy-07.local MicroPython's network.hostname() is documented as sent to DHCP and, if the port supports it, to mDNS. Reports from the project's issue tracker suggest the RP2 port gained this in 2025, and that it does not work in every mode. Unconfirmed on the kit. Resolving The Pico looks up buddy.local and gets a number We found no documentation that socket.getaddrinfo() on the Pico sends mDNS queries; it uses the DNS server from ifconfig(). Unconfirmed, and probably not available.

Because it is uncertain, the book's default does not depend on it. 08-mdns-check.py tries to resolve each name in a list and prints the answer or the failure, with sys.version, and then states the fallback: the fixed address in buddy_config.py, protected by a DHCP reservation. If buddy.local does work on your firmware, you can set BUDDY_HOST = "buddy.local", but keep the IP address in a comment beside it.

docs.title: Why Plain HTTP Is Acceptable Here, and Only Here
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter uses http://, and every byte of it travels unencrypted. Plain HTTP LAN use means using unencrypted HTTP only on a network the school controls. Anyone who can capture traffic on that network can read the questions in the 194-byte request. On a classroom network that is a small group of people the school manages, the questions are not secrets, and there are no passwords in the exchange, so the risk is low and the simplicity is worth it. The device also never sends anything the student did not just say.

Plain HTTP is not acceptable when the data crosses the internet, or any network the school does not control, such as a public hotspot or a student's home network where a stranger's laptop could be connected. It is also not acceptable the moment the exchange carries a password or a login token, because someone watching the network would learn it and could use it. Chapter 14 adds a token and HTTPS, Chapter 17 asks which data should leave the room at all, and the buddy server's startup message reminds you every time: "plain HTTP, no login: trusted classroom network only."

Do Not Port-Forward This

It is tempting to make the server reachable from home by opening a port on the router. Do not do this with the Chapter 13 server: it has no login and no encryption, so anyone on the internet could ask it questions. Keep it on the classroom network, and use Chapter 14 before anything else.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
You can now describe a request from end to end. The Pico joins Wi-Fi in station mode with a time limit, and gets an IP address, a netmask, a gateway and a DNS server from DHCP. It checks that the server's address is on its own local network. It writes the question as JSON, wraps it in an HTTP POST with the right Content-Length, and sends it to /v1/ask. The server's brain returns a three-field JSON reply, the Pico reads a bounded amount of it, closes the connection in a finally block, and draws the answer in the message region.

Key takeaways:

  • Station mode joins someone else's network; connect() returns at once, so poll status() with a time limit and treat -3 and -2 differently.
  • An IP address is four bytes given by DHCP; the netmask picks out the network part, and two devices are on the same network when their network addresses match.
  • The local network uses RFC 1918 private ranges; keep the server's address stable with a DHCP reservation.
  • JSON is the shared shape: three fields in, three fields out, and count the bytes.
  • An HTTP request is plain text: request line, headers, a blank line, then the body; the status code's first digit says whose mistake it was.
  • A POST must say the right Content-Length; too small gives a 400 and too large makes the server wait.
  • A REST endpoint is a path that does one job; POST /v1/ask carries the Chapter 1 contract.
  • Read a bounded reply and close the socket in finally; requests helps, but you still call close().
  • .local names are uncertain on the Pico, so keep a fixed address as the fallback.
  • Plain HTTP is for a trusted classroom network only, never the internet and never with a password.

Test yourself with these two questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

The Pico's address is 10.4.7.88 with netmask 255.255.255.0 and the server is at 10.4.200.9. Why does the request fail, and what is the fix? Click to expand

The mask keeps the first three numbers, so the Pico is on 10.4.7.0 and the server is on 10.4.200.0: different networks, and the request must go through the gateway, which may not forward it. Check that BUDDY_HOST is right and that both devices are on the same network, or ask the network administrator to allow the traffic.

Your program prints the status code 200 but then fails with a memory error after about a dozen requests. What did you forget? Click to expand

Most likely the program never closed the response or the socket, so each request left a connection open. Put response.close() (or sock.close()) in a finally block so it runs on every path, and read at most MAX_REPLY_BYTES of the body.

Your Pico Is on the Network

You just joined a Wi-Fi network in station mode, read an IP address and netmask, wrote the Chapter 1 contract as JSON, and sent it as an HTTP POST to a REST endpoint. Your Pico can now ask the buddy server a question and show the answer.

In Chapter 14 we make the link carry real speech, lock it with a token, and survive a network that drops.

docs.title: Streaming Speech, Security, and Network Resilience
Summary
docs.text: This chapter makes the agent link work for real speech. Students upload recorded audio in memory-safe chunks, use speech-to-text and text-to-speech services, and stream audio over a WebSocket. They also add authentication tokens and HTTPS, and handle timeouts, retries, and offline fallback when the network fails.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score WebSocket 3 Authentication Token 6 TLS Encryption 5 Text-to-Speech Service 7 HTTPS 4 Chunked Audio Upload 4 Streaming Audio 2 Certificate Handling 1 Network Failure Handling 7 Audio Chunk Size 1 Speech-to-Text Service 2 Barge-In Interruption 1 Retry and Backoff 1 Timeouts 1 Offline Fallback 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture
  • Chapter 2: MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems
  • Chapter 7: Buttons, State Machines, and Device Modes
  • Chapter 8: I2S Audio: Recording and Playing Sound
  • Chapter 11: Microphone Calibration and Push-to-Talk
  • Chapter 13: Wi-Fi, HTTP, and Connecting to the Agent

docs.title: From One Question to Real Speech
docs.text:
Chapter 13 sent a typed question and got a typed answer. A real device has to send a recording of someone talking, get back speech, keep working when the Wi-Fi hiccups, and keep strangers out. Each of those has a catch on a board with 520 KB of RAM, and this chapter is about the catches.

Let's Make It Talk

In this chapter you will hold a button, say a sentence, and hear the buddy server's answer come back through your own speaker, with a login, a plan for bad networks, and a way to interrupt. Let's listen closely! The trick is sending sound in pieces small enough for a tiny memory.

Chapter 1's data flow had eight steps, and Chapter 13 handled them with typed text. Step 1 is still the student speaking. Here is what steps 2 to 8 become.

Step What happens Where Section 2 The microphone's samples are made smaller (16-bit) and kept Pico Recording an Utterance for the Network 3 The recording travels to the server in chunks, with a token Network Chunked Audio Upload; Authentication Tokens 4 The server turns speech into words Server Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech 5 The brain decides on a reply (Chapter 13's decide()) Server (unchanged) 6 The server turns the reply into speech Server Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech 7 The speech comes back in pieces Network Playing the Answer 8 The Pico plays it, and the listener may interrupt Pico Interrupting: Barge-In

docs.title: Recording an Utterance for the Network
docs.text:
Chapter 11 builds the full push-to-talk recorder with a noise floor and voice-activity detection. This chapter needs only a small one, utterance.py, so that it stands on its own: hold MODE, record, release.

The microphone delivers 32-bit words, 4 bytes per sample (Chapter 8). A speech service does not need 24 bits of precision, and the Pico cannot afford them. Converting each sample to 16 bits as it arrives halves the memory.

Length 32-bit words 16-bit samples Share of the chip's 520 KB (532,480 bytes), 16-bit 3 s \( 3 \times 12{,}800 \times 4 = 153{,}600 \) bytes 76,800 bytes 14.4 % 5 s 256,000 bytes 128,000 bytes 24.0 % 10 s 512,000 bytes 256,000 bytes 48.1 %

The 3 s row in 32-bit is Chapter 2's 29 percent figure. Five seconds in 32-bit words (256,000 bytes) is almost half the chip and almost certainly fails, as Chapter 2 warned. So utterance.record() converts each 20 ms read (1,024 bytes, 256 samples) into 512 bytes of 16-bit audio as it goes.

def convert(raw, out, pos):
    shifted = [v >> SHIFT for v in struct.unpack(_UNPACK, raw)]   # 32-bit word -> 24-bit sample
    mean = sum(shifted) // READ_SAMPLES                           # this chunk's DC offset
    struct.pack_into(_PACK, out, pos,
                     *[max(-32768, min(32767, ((x - mean) * GAIN) >> 8)) for x in shifted])

Each step has a reason from earlier chapters. The right shift by MIC_SAMPLE_SHIFT recovers the 24-bit value, subtracting the chunk's mean removes the microphone's wandering DC offset (Chapter 8 measured it moving between frames), and the multiply by GAIN of 8 followed by >> 8 is the same 18 dB boost the kit's test 07 uses to bring speech up to a playable level. The max/min clips instead of wrapping around, which would sound like a crack (Chapter 3).

The conversion has to finish inside the 20 ms between reads, or the microphone's ring buffer starts to fill (Chapter 8's frame budget). Chapter 8 measured about 10 ms for a similar loop over 512 samples, so there is reason to expect this one to fit, but no one has measured this code on the kit. 03-record-utterance.py prints the worst conversion time against the 20,000 microsecond budget, and if it is over, the fix is the kit's test 07 method: record 32-bit words, convert after you let go, and limit the utterance to 3 s. Allocate the recording buffer first, before the heap fragments, with utterance.make_buffer().

docs.title: Chunked Audio Upload
docs.text:
Chunked audio upload means sending the recording to the server in pieces instead of in one write. Here is the reason. The obvious way to send a POST is to join the header and the body into one bytes object and call send once.

request = head + body          # NEVER with a recording: this copies it
sock.send(request)

Joining makes a new object as big as both. A 5 s recording is 128,000 bytes, so the join needs another 128,000 contiguous bytes while the recording still exists: 256,000 bytes in two blocks. Chapter 2's fragmentation rule says a block that size is hard to find. The fix costs nothing. Send the header first, then send the recording itself in slices of a memoryview, which points into the existing buffer without copying it.

sock.write(head)
view = memoryview(pcm)[:nbytes]
sent = 0
while sent < len(view):
    piece = view[sent:sent + chunk]
    sock.write(piece)
    sent += len(piece)

buddy_http.request() does this, with a deadline check before every piece. Slicing a memoryview is free, so the only memory the upload needs beyond the recording is a few small objects. The server still sees one ordinary POST whose Content-Length was known up front.

There is a second way to send a body of unknown length, called Transfer-Encoding: chunked, in which each piece is preceded by its size in hexadecimal. The requests library will do it for you when data= is a generator. The book does not use it, for three reasons. The Pico knows the total as soon as the button is released. Many simple servers do not accept chunked request bodies (ours answers 411, Length Required). And a request that fails halfway is simpler to reason about when the length is fixed.

Worked example. A 5 s utterance is 128,000 bytes. With 2,048-byte chunks that is \( \lceil 128{,}000 / 2{,}048 \rceil = 63 \) calls to write. Each chunk is \( 2{,}048 / 25{,}600 = 0.08 \) s, 80 ms, of audio. No more than 2,048 bytes is ever in flight beyond the recording itself.

docs.title: Audio Chunk Size
docs.text:
The audio chunk size is how many bytes go in each write. It is a trade-off among four things, and 01-chunk-arithmetic.py prints all of them.

Chunk (bytes) Chunks for 5 s Audio per chunk Typical TCP segments WebSocket extra bytes Extra as % 512 250 20 ms 1 8 1.56 % 1,024 125 40 ms 1 8 0.78 % 2,048 63 80 ms 2 8 0.39 % 4,096 32 160 ms 3 8 0.20 % 8,192 16 320 ms 6 8 0.10 %

The "segments" column assumes a TCP segment carries up to 1,460 bytes, the usual size on an Ethernet-style network; the real value on your network may differ. The "extra bytes" column is a WebSocket client frame's 8-byte header (2 for the opcode and length, 2 more when the length is 126 or over, and 4 for the mask), which the WebSocket section explains. Small chunks cost more calls and a little more overhead, and large chunks cost latency (the first sound cannot leave until the chunk is full) and cost more to lose when one fails.

The book's defaults come from two numbers already in this book. For the HTTP upload, UPLOAD_CHUNK_BYTES = 2048 (80 ms, two audio reads): large enough that the overhead is a rounding error, small enough that a stalled network is noticed within one deadline check. For streaming over a WebSocket, STREAM_CHUNK_BYTES = 1024, which is 512 samples, exactly Chapter 8's 40 ms frame, so each frame the loop produces is one message. Neither value was tuned on the kit.

docs.title: Diagram: Chunk-Size and Heap Explorer
docs.text:
Chunk-Size and Heap Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: chunk-heap-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine 8 upload designs to decide whether each fits in a given free heap and, for those that fit, how many sends it needs, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: 16-bit and 32-bit recording sizes, memoryview slice, chunk, free heap, contiguous block (all defined in this chapter above this block and in Chapter 2).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 cases the learner chooses "fits" or "does not fit", and for a case that fits, types the number of sends. A case is correct when the choice matches the Fits column and, for fitting cases, the number matches the Sends column exactly. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Moving the explorer's sliders is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Sending in chunks makes the recording itself smaller. (2) Joining the header and body is harmless because the recording is already in memory. (3) A bigger free heap total always means a big block is available. (4) Streaming needs the whole recording in memory.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level examination requires the learner to break a design into the blocks it needs and compare them with what is available. Using the same rule on eight designs lets the learner see which designs move the memory problem, rather than remove it.

Content:

Four designs are described. In each, S is the length in seconds, R16 is the 16-bit recording size \( S \times 25{,}600 \) bytes, and R32 is the 32-bit size \( S \times 51{,}200 \) bytes.

Design Description Largest memory it needs A Record 16-bit. Join the header and the body into one bytes object, then send it once. Two blocks of R16 at the same time: \( 2 \times R16 \) in all, the largest single block R16 B Record 16-bit. Send the header, then send the recording in slices of a chunk size K bytes. R16 for the recording, plus a small K-byte staging area: \( R16 + K \) in all, the largest single block R16 C Record 32-bit, convert in place after release, send the first half in slices of K bytes. R32 for the buffer, plus K: \( R32 + K \) in all, the largest single block R32 D Stream each 1,024-byte frame as it is converted and keep nothing. One 1,024-byte staging frame, at any length of speech

The rule: a case fits when the total memory the design needs is no more than the free heap F minus a reserve of 40,000 bytes, which stands for the code, display, and network buffers. The number of sends is the length divided by the chunk size, rounded up (for design D, the frames of 1,024 bytes).

# Design S (s) K (bytes) F (bytes) Fits Sends Why (shown as feedback) 1 B 3 2,048 180,000 fits 38 R16 is 76,800; plus 2,048 is 78,848, under 140,000. 76,800 / 2,048 is 37.5, rounded up to 38. 2 B 5 2,048 180,000 fits 63 R16 is 128,000; plus 2,048 is 130,048, under 140,000. 128,000 / 2,048 is 62.5, rounded up to 63. 3 A 5 not used 180,000 does not fit none The join needs 128,000 + 128,000 = 256,000, over 140,000. 4 C 5 2,048 180,000 does not fit none R32 is 256,000, over 140,000 by itself. 5 C 3 2,048 260,000 fits 38 R32 is 153,600; plus 2,048 is 155,648, under 220,000. The first half to send is 76,800 bytes: 38 sends. 6 B 10 2,048 260,000 does not fit none R16 is 256,000, over 220,000. 7 D 10 1,024 100,000 fits 250 One 1,024-byte frame needs no recording. 10 s is 256,000 bytes: 256,000 / 1,024 is 250 frames. 8 B 5 8,192 180,000 fits 16 R16 is 128,000; plus 8,192 is 136,192, under 140,000. 128,000 / 8,192 is 15.6, rounded up to 16.

For exploration the learner sets S from 1 to 10 s in steps of 1 s (default 5), K from 512 to 8,192 bytes in the five sizes of the chapter's table (default 2,048), and F from 100,000 to 260,000 bytes in steps of 10,000 (default 180,000), and sees each design's memory need drawn against the free heap with the reserve.

Provenance: The recording sizes follow from the kit's 12,800 samples per second, with 4 bytes per sample for 32-bit words and 2 for 16-bit samples (config.MIC_SAMPLE_RATE). The reserve of 40,000 bytes and the free heap values are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative." The learner's own free heap comes from Chapter 2's memory report.

Rules: Total need and largest block follow the Largest memory column. A case fits when the total need is at most \( F - 40{,}000 \). Sends are \( \lceil \text{bytes to send} / K \rceil \), where the bytes to send are R16 for designs A and B, R16 (the converted half) for design C, and \( S \times 25{,}600 \) split into 1,024-byte frames for design D. A design that does not fit has no send count.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the three sliders and watches each design's bar against the free heap line.
  2. The learner starts the 8 cases. Case 1 is shown.
  3. The learner chooses fits or does not fit and, if it fits, types the number of sends.
  4. The sim draws the case's memory need against the free heap and shows the Why text.
  5. After case 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that designs A and C fail at 5 s where design B fits, and that design D fits at any length.

Feedback: 8 cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. It <, with N sends if it fits>: ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Design B at 5 s, 2,048 bytes, and 180,000 free is drawn, with the question "Does this fit in the free heap, and how many sends does it need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a 5 s recording is 128,000 bytes in 16-bit and 256,000 in 32-bit, that joining the head and body needs a second block as large as the recording, that 2,048-byte chunks make 63 sends for 5 s, and that a WebSocket frame header is 8 bytes.

Chunks Move the Problem, Not the Data

Sending in pieces does not make the recording smaller. It stops you from making a second copy, and only streaming (never keeping the whole recording) removes the big block entirely. Ask "how many copies of the data exist at once?" of every design.

docs.title: Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech
docs.text:
The Pico does not understand speech and cannot make it. Both jobs belong to the buddy server, which has the memory and the processing power. In server/buddy_server.py the whole voice path is three function calls, and each one is a swappable piece.

heard = stt.transcribe(pcm, rate)                      # speech-to-text
reply = brain.make_reply(heard, EVENTS)                # the brain: Chapter 13's decide()
speech = tts.synthesize(reply["speak"], DEVICE_RATE)   # text-to-speech

docs.title: The Speech-to-Text Service
docs.text:
A speech-to-text service turns a recording into written words. Servers get it in one of two ways: a program running on the server's own computer, or a company's web service. The server's stt.py has two backends, chosen with the BUDDY_STT environment variable.

Backend What it does Needs stub (default) Checks that the recording is not silent (an RMS loudness test), then returns a fixed phrase. It does not recognize speech. Nothing service The place, clearly marked in the file, where you write the call to a real service A provider your school approved, and an API key in the server's STT_API_KEY environment variable

The stub exists so every other part of the pipeline can be tested with no account and no internet. With the stub, whatever you say, the answer is about "when is my next test", and a silent recording gives "Sorry, I did not catch that." Most services want a WAV file rather than raw samples, so stt.pcm_to_wav() adds the 44-byte header from Chapter 3. Keys live only in the server's environment. They are never in a file you share and never on the Pico.

A cloud service means the student's voice leaves the classroom. Chapter 17 asks the questions to answer before you do that, and the stub keeps this chapter from needing an answer.

docs.title: The Text-to-Speech Service
docs.text:
A text-to-speech service does the opposite: it turns the reply's speak sentence into audio. The same pattern applies: tts.py has a stub backend (one beep per word, rising in pitch, so you can hear that audio arrived and how long a sentence is) and a marked place for a service backend with its key in TTS_API_KEY.

The catch is the format. The Pico's speaker is set up for 16-bit mono at 12,800 samples per second, the same settings as the kit's test 07. A real service usually returns something else, so the server must convert before it sends.

A service may return The Pico can play it? What the server must do 16-bit mono PCM at 12,800 Hz Yes Nothing 16-bit mono PCM at another rate (22,050, 24,000) Only at the wrong speed Resample to 12,800 Hz with tts.to_device_pcm() Stereo PCM No Mix to mono first WAV After the 44-byte header is removed Strip the header, then as above MP3 or Opus No: the Pico cannot decode them Decode on the server

Resampling by linear interpolation is enough for speech, and going down to 12,800 Hz discards everything above 6,400 Hz (Chapter 3's Nyquist limit), which the speaker could not reproduce anyway. A common surprise is a sentence that plays too fast and too high: that is the wrong rate, the same chipmunk effect as Chapter 8. The server also applies the device's volume (GET /v1/speech/<id>?volume=40 scales the samples), so the Pico does no per-sample work. At volume 40 the peak is \( 0.4 \times 32{,}767 \approx 13{,}107 \), the same figure as Chapter 8's tone.

Worked example. A sentence that takes 2.5 s to say is \( 2.5 \times 12{,}800 \times 2 = 64{,}000 \) bytes of speech. The Pico never holds all of it. The next section shows why.

docs.title: Playing the Answer
docs.text:
Streaming audio means playing sound while it is still arriving, instead of waiting for all of it. The server sends the speech with a Content-Length and X-Audio-Rate: 12800, and buddy_http.request() reads the body into one reusable 2,048-byte buffer and hands each filled buffer to a function, which writes it to the speaker.

def sink(view):
    speaker.write(view)         # blocks until the chunk is in the speaker's buffer

buddy_client.speech(path, config.VOLUME, sink, chunk_buf)

The speaker's write blocks until its 8,192-byte buffer has room (Chapter 8), and the socket read blocks until the next chunk arrives, so the two pace each other. The network is the producer, the I2S buffer is the consumer, and one 2,048-byte buffer sits in the middle. This is the ring-buffer idea of Chapter 8 again, with the Wi-Fi link in place of the microphone. At the natural end of the sound the code lets the speaker's buffer drain before deinit(), and it closes the microphone for the whole time the speaker is open, which is Chapter 8's rule against the self-hearing problem. The speech request is deliberately not retried: a retry would start the sentence again after part of it had played.

docs.title: Interrupting: Barge-In
docs.text:
Barge-in interruption is the listener cutting off the device while it is speaking. People do it all the time: the answer starts, they know what it will say, and they say "stop" or ask something else. A good device lets them.

Voice barge-in would need the microphone open while the speaker plays, and Chapter 8 explained why that fails: the microphone hears the speaker, about 15 times louder than a quiet room in the kit's test. Telling the device's voice from the listener's would need echo cancellation, which Chapter 8 called out of scope for a Pico. So in this book barge-in is a button press: the device checks MODE between chunks, and if it is down, it stops.

What interrupts Works on the kit? Why Pressing MODE Yes A button is not affected by sound Saying "stop" No The microphone is closed while speaking, and hearing over the speaker needs echo cancellation A new wake word Not in this book Same problem as saying "stop"

Stopping takes three steps in 04-upload-voice.py: raise an exception from the playback function (which also closes the socket, so the rest of the speech is not downloaded), call speaker.finish(drain=False) so deinit() discards what is queued, and wait out the quiet tail (120 ms, from Chapter 8's measurement) before the microphone is opened again. Skipping the drain matters. The speaker's buffer holds up to \( 8{,}192 / (12{,}800 \times 2) = 0.32 \) s of sound, and left to drain it would keep talking for a third of a second after the press. Because the loop checks the button once per 2,048-byte chunk (80 ms of audio), the expected stop time is one chunk plus the discarded buffer, about 80 ms. That is an estimate from arithmetic; no one has measured it on the kit.

On a WebSocket the same press also sends {"event": "cancel"}, so the server stops sending speech too.

docs.title: Authentication Tokens
docs.text:
Chapter 13's server answers anyone who can reach it. An authentication token is a secret string that the device presents with every request, so the server can tell the school's devices from everyone else. In this book it travels in an HTTP header, X-Buddy-Token, and it lives in secrets.py on the Pico next to the Wi-Fi password.

# secrets.py on the Pico  (never committed)
buddy_token = "a-long-random-string"

headers = {"X-Buddy-Token": TOKEN, "X-Buddy-Device": cfg.DEVICE_ID}

On the server, BUDDY_TOKENS holds one or more accepted tokens, and every endpoint except /v1/health refuses a request with a missing or wrong one by answering 401 and doing nothing else. The check compares in constant time (hmac.compare_digest), so the time it takes does not reveal how many leading characters were right. The Pico treats 401 as not worth retrying: the same token will fail the same way, so the status region says "bad token" and stops.
