docs.title: From Parts to a Working Device
docs.text:
You now have every piece of the Study Buddy: wired parts, a display that redraws only what changed, a button state machine, and a microphone and speaker on I2S, plus sound analysis, a wake word, and a link to the school agent. This chapter is about the skill that makes all of that survive real life, which is finding out what is wrong when something is. Then you put the pieces together and build something of your own.

From Working Parts to a Working Device

In this chapter you will build the tools that find a bad wire in minutes, put every subsystem into one loop that keeps up with the microphone, and finish with a project that is yours. Let's listen closely! Every real device spends more time being debugged than being written.

docs.title: Seeing What the Device Is Doing
Serial Debugging
docs.text:
Serial debugging means finding a problem by reading the text a program sends over the USB serial port. Everything print() writes travels to your computer, where Thonny's shell or mpremote shows it. It is the oldest and still the most useful debugging tool on a microcontroller, because it works even when the display does not.

Four rules keep it useful. First, only one program can use the Pico's serial port at a time, so quit Thonny before you run mpremote (Chapter 2). Second, print what you need to decide something: the value, its unit, and a label. Third, do not print on every 40 ms frame. Twenty-five lines a second floods the shell and slows the loop; print about once a second, as Chapter 8's 02-mic-frame-reader.py does. Fourth, use the REPL to try one line at a time before you write it into a file.

Task Command Notes List the connected boards mpremote connect list If your Pico is missing, check the cable (some are charge-only) Open the REPL mpremote repl Ctrl-C stops the program; Ctrl-D soft-reboots; the exit key is printed when it starts Run a file without saving it mpremote run selftest.py The file stays on your computer Run one line mpremote exec "import selftest; selftest.run()" For a file already on the Pico Read a file from the Pico mpremote fs cat :log.txt Or copy it: mpremote fs cp :log.txt . Restart the program mpremote soft-reset The upload script uses this too

machine.reset() Ends Your Conversation

machine.reset() restarts the whole chip, so the USB connection drops, the last lines you printed may never arrive, and every pin and bus goes back to its start state. A program that resets itself on every error can trap you in a reset loop that never reaches the REPL. While developing, print the problem and stop; to get out of a loop, send Ctrl-C right after connecting, then run mpremote fs rm main.py.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Logging is print() with discipline: each line has a time, a level, and a message, and the program decides where each line goes. log.py keeps three places, because each costs something different.

Place What goes there Cost Lost when Serial (the shell) Lines at or above level Time to print The shell is closed RAM ring Every line, in a ring of the last ring lines A few hundred bytes Power goes off Flash file WARN and ERROR only, with a size cap Slow writes; flash wears (Chapter 2) Never, until you delete it

The four levels are DEBUG (details for a bug hunt), INFO (normal events), WARN (odd but recovered), and ERROR (something failed). The ring is the trick that matters most: after something strange, log.dump() shows what happened just before, even though you were not printing it. The flash file is capped. When a write would pass max_bytes, the file is renamed to log.txt.1, replacing the older copy, so the worst case is twice the cap.

from log import Log, INFO, WARN

log = Log(level=INFO, ring=40, path="log.txt", max_bytes=8192)
log.info("mic opened at %d Hz", 12800)
log.warn("frame overrun: %d us", 52000)
log.dump()

The first line makes a logger that prints INFO and above, keeps the last 40 lines in RAM, and writes WARN and above to log.txt, never letting it pass 8,192 bytes. Each %d is filled in by the argument that follows it, in the old % formatting style. The last line prints the ring, oldest line first. 01-log-demo.py writes 200 lines through a deliberately tiny 400-byte cap and checks that the ring holds exactly the last 10, that the file stays under the cap, and that only WARN and ERROR reached flash. It runs on a computer too, and it prints PASS.

One rule from Chapter 17 applies to every log: never log audio or the words people said. Log levels, counts, and codes.

docs.title: What a Probe Is
docs.text:
A probe program is a small program that tests one subsystem and prints evidence about it. A good probe does four things: it touches only the part it tests, it changes nothing that matters, it prints the measured numbers before the verdict, and it ends with one line that says PASS, FAIL, ASK, or SKIP. The kit's 02-probe.py is a probe for the whole board. This chapter adds one per part, so you can ask a narrow question: not "is my kit broken?" but "does the microphone send changing numbers?"

The four verdicts say what the program actually knows. PASS means it measured the right thing. FAIL means it measured the wrong thing. ASK means it cannot tell and a person must look or listen. SKIP means the part is not wired. This matters because the display and the amplifier cannot report back to the Pico (the kit README says so), so a probe can draw a pattern but cannot know if you can see it.

Probe Part What it measures Honest limit 02-display-probe.py Display SPI rate you really got, three timed fills, rings at the glass edge and SAFE_RADIUS A person must say what they saw (ASK) 03-mic-probe.py Microphone Spread, DC offset, loudness in bits, samples at full scale, for 5 s It cannot tell a swapped wire from no power 04-speaker-probe.py Speaker (+ mic) Plays a 1 kHz tone and listens with the microphone A quiet room and a far microphone look the same as a dead speaker (ASK) 05-button-probe.py Buttons Idle reads, then each press with its bounce edges A button that reads 1 may be unwired 06-wifi-probe.py Wi-Fi radio Networks seen, channel, signal; joins if secrets.py exists A 5 GHz-only network never appears 07-wiring-check.py All wires The wire list from config.py and the pin-plan rules It cannot see a wire

Worked example. You run 03-mic-probe.py and the verdict says FAIL - flat line: every sample is 12345. A flat line means the microphone started with no error but sent the same number every time. The probe lists what to check, in the kit README's order: SCK on GP10, WS on GP11, SD on GP12; VDD on 3V3; GND and L/R on GND; and the Chapter 17 mute switch. You find SD and SCK swapped, fix them, and the next run prints a PASS line. (The numbers in this example are made up to show the format.)

Every probe calls the same functions in checks.py, which is also what the self-test uses. One implementation means a bug is fixed once.

A Probe Asks One Question

Notice what makes a probe powerful: it removes everything but the part under suspicion. When the whole device fails, nothing is learned. When the microphone probe fails with every other part unplugged, you know where to look.

docs.title: Wiring Verification
docs.text:
Wiring verification is checking every wire against one reference, the pin assignment table from Chapter 4. Most "broken" kits are wiring mistakes, and most wiring mistakes are found by comparing, not by reasoning. The reference must be the same as what the program uses, or the table and the code can drift apart. So the wire list here is computed from config.py.

tools/wiring_table.py reads config.py as text, with no Pico modules, and prints the table below. The same function runs on the Pico as 07-wiring-check.py. A change to a pin in config.py changes the printout.

Part Part pin Pico pin Header pin Display SCL GP2 4 Display SDA GP3 5 Display RST GP4 6 Display DC GP5 7 Display CS GP6 9 Display BL GP7 10 Microphone SCK GP10 14 Microphone WS GP11 15 Microphone SD GP12 16 Button MODE one leg GP13 17 Button UP one leg GP14 19 Button DOWN one leg GP15 20 Amplifier DIN GP19 25 Amplifier BCLK GP20 26 Amplifier LRC GP21 27 Amplifier GAIN GP18 24

The power wires follow: display VCC and microphone VDD to 3V3 (header pin 36), amplifier VIN to VBUS or 3V3 (pin 40 or 36), and every GND, including the microphone's L/R and the buttons' other legs, to any GND pin. The tool prints these too. Sixteen signal wires are checked by the program; the power wires it cannot see, so you check those by eye.

The method is a ritual. Print the list, put a finger on one wire at a time, say its part and Pico pin out loud, and tick it. Do power and ground last, and check that the microphone's VDD goes to 3V3, not 5 V (Chapter 4). Then run check_pin_plan, which tests three rules the table cannot show by itself: each I2S word-select pin is the clock pin plus one, no GP number is used twice, and none of GP23, GP24, GP25, or GP29 (the wireless chip's) is used.

Worked example. The kit's config.py is edited so the microphone's WS is GP13, to match a wire placed there. The pin-plan check prints FAIL - microphone word select GP13 must be GP11 (clock + 1); GP13 used by 'Microphone WS' and 'Button MODE one leg'. It names the rule and the second victim, because GP13 is also the MODE button. The fix is the one the kit README gives: move the wire, and do not edit config.py to match the wrong wire.

docs.title: The Self-Test Program
docs.text:
A self-test program runs every check, prints a verdict per subsystem, and shows a summary on the display. selftest.py is built from the same checks.py functions as the probes. You run it after assembling, after every change, and, if you like, at power-up.

Check What it measures What it cannot know Files config.py, the driver, both fonts are on the board Whether they are the right versions Memory Free heap, and that a 3 s recording (153,600 bytes) fits How fragmented the heap will be later Flash At least 64 KB of flash free Wear Pin plan The three pin rules above A wire in the wrong hole Buttons All three read 1 when untouched; optionally each press and its bounce An unwired button reads 1 Display Draws a ring and text, then asks UP or DOWN It cannot see the screen: ASK, then a person decides Microphone Not a flat line, no full-scale samples, loudness and DC offset Whether the L/R wire is on the channel the program reads Speaker Plays a 1 kHz tone and checks the microphone hears it at least 2.0 bits above the room Whether it sounds good Wi-Fi The radio sees networks; joins if secrets.py exists Whether the school server is up

The speaker check borrows Chapter 8's finding that the device hears itself. On the test board a 1 kHz tone at volume 40 read 3.9 bits above the quiet room (about 15 times louder), so the check asks for half of that, 2.0 bits. This is a number from one board. If your speaker is quieter, or the microphone is farther away, the check says ASK instead of FAIL, because "the microphone did not hear it" is not proof that nobody could.

Worked example. This is what the self-test prints when the microphone's WS wire is on GP13 (produced by running the real program against a fake Pico layer where the fault was simulated, so the timings are left out).

Files       PASS config.py, driver and both fonts are present
Memory      PASS heap 180,000 bytes free; a 3 s recording fits
Pin plan    FAIL microphone word select GP13 must be GP11 (clock + 1); GP13 used by 'Microphone WS' and 'Button MODE one leg'
Buttons     PASS all three read 1 (not pressed); an unconnected wire also reads 1
Display     PASS a person saw the ring and the text
Microphone  FAIL microphone failed to start: invalid ws (must be sck+1) (word select must be the pin after the clock: SCK GP10, WS GP11)
Speaker     PASS a person heard the beep
Wi-Fi       PASS radio sees 2 network(s); no secrets.py, so no connection tried

7 PASS  2 FAIL  0 ASK  0 SKIP

Two lines point at the same wire from two angles: the pin-plan rule, and the error that I2S() raised. When two checks agree, trust the diagnosis. The summary also appears on the round display, one row per check, with the word as well as a color, so a person who cannot tell red from green reads the same result. A row is "{:<11}{:>5}", 16 characters at 8 pixels each, 128 pixels wide. The first row sits at y = 62, where the visible circle of radius 168 is \( 2\sqrt{168^2 - 118^2} \approx 239 \) pixels wide, so it fits with room to spare.

docs.title: Diagnosing the Three Classic Failures
docs.text: A diagnosis goes from a symptom to a cause, asking the cheapest question first. Three failures account for most "it doesn't work" reports on this kit: a silent microphone, distorted audio, and a blank display. Each table below is a decision tree written flat. Start at the first row and ask its question. If the answer is yes, that row's cause is your likely cause: run its quick test, then apply the fix. If the answer is no, go to the next row. Every cause comes from the kit README, a test file's header, or an earlier chapter, and tools/diagnose.py asks the same questions at the terminal. A tree names the likely cause, so run the quick test before you change anything.

docs.title: Diagnosing a Silent Microphone
docs.text:
The symptom is a level meter that never moves, or a probe that reports a flat line.

Row Ask Likely cause Quick test Fix M1 An error at start, and it says must be sck+1? WS is not on the pin after SCK Compare with the table: SCK GP10, WS GP11 Move the wire back. Do not edit config.py: SCK on GP12 would need WS on GP13, the MODE button M2 An error at start, with another message? A previous run left the I2S block open, or memory is short (likely) Ctrl-D, run again, print gc.mem_free() Close the microphone in a finally block M3 No error, but the spread is 0 (a flat line)? Swapped SCK, WS, or SD wires; no power; or the mute switch is on In order: SCK, WS, SD; VDD on 3V3, not 5 V; GND and L/R on GND; the mute switch Re-seat the wires. A swapped microphone starts with no error and sends zeros M4 The loudness barely changes when you talk next to it? L/R is on 3V3, so the microphone answers in the right slot while the program reads the left Look at where L/R goes Move L/R to GND M5 The meter is pinned at the top? The 32-bit samples were not shifted right by 8, so values are 256 times too big; or the room or SD wire is noisy Print a few samples before and after >> config.MIC_SAMPLE_SHIFT Shift by MIC_SAMPLE_SHIFT and subtract the frame's DC offset M6 None of the above The microphone works; the level you chose is the problem Probe 03: does a clap jump several bits? Calibrate the noise floor first; for quiet playback raise PLAYBACK_GAIN

docs.title: Diagnosing Distorted Audio
docs.text:
The symptom is a sound that is wrong: silent, crackling, the wrong pitch, stuttering, clicking, or hissing.

Row Ask Likely cause Quick test Fix A1 Is the speaker silent, not distorted? No power or ground at the amplifier, or a signal wire is wrong Probe 04; VIN and GND, then BCLK GP20, LRC GP21, DIN GP19 Fix the wire. If I2S() raises an error, LRC must be right after BCLK A2 Does it crackle only when loud? The samples clip: peaks are cut flat Lower VOLUME; the crackle should go Reduce VOLUME (test 05) or PLAYBACK_GAIN (test 07) A3 Is the pitch wrong, too high and fast or too low and slow? The playback sample rate is not the recording rate Print both rates Use MIC_SAMPLE_RATE for both A4 Does it stutter or have gaps? The loop takes longer than one 40 ms frame: a frame overrun Wrap the microphone in OverrunCounter; read the summary Redraw only changed regions, or slice big jobs A5 Is the start clicky, or the end cut off? deinit() ran before the buffer drained; or a WAV header was played as sound Listen with and without f.seek(44); lengthen the tail Write silence and wait the buffer's length; skip the 44-byte header; fade 10 ms A6 Is there hiss or buzz even when nothing plays? Power or ground noise: loose grounds, long wires Re-seat every GND; keep microphone and amplifier wires apart Shorter wires and one solid ground rail A7 None of the above No cause matched Play the 05 tone and a 07 recording separately Fix the path that distorts

docs.title: Diagnosing a Blank Display
docs.text:
The symptom is a screen that shows nothing, or nothing right.

Row Ask Likely cause Quick test Fix D1 Is the screen completely dark, with no light? The backlight is off: BL not wired, VCC or GND missing, or set_backlight(True) never ran Check BL to GP7, VCC to 3V3, GND Wire BL to GP7 and call config.set_backlight(True) D2 Did the program stop with an error before drawing? A kit file is missing: config.py, lib/gc9b72.py, or a font Self-test "Files", or 02-probe.py section 4 Run upload-chapter.sh D3 Is it lit but only black or random noise? A control wire is wrong: SCL GP2, SDA GP3, RST GP4, DC GP5, or CS GP6 07-wiring-check.py; touch each wire Fix the wire; the colors are in config.py D4 Is the picture speckled or torn? The SPI speed is too fast for the wiring Print the SPI object to see the rate you got BAUDRATE = 12_000_000 (nothing exists between 12 and 24 MHz) D5 Is part of what you drew missing? It was drawn outside the visible circle: corners and edge are hidden Chapter 4's 04-display-visible-area.py Stay inside SAFE_RADIUS, 168 pixels from the center D6 Is the picture rotated or mirrored? The driver's rotation argument Try 0, 1, 2, 3 in config.init_display() Choose the one that matches D7 Are old letters left over, or is the picture sheared or striped? Text was not padded to a fixed width, or a buffer is not width x height x 2 bytes Print len(buffer) and compare Pad with .center(width); size buffers exactly D8 None of the above A program from an earlier kit may be running as main.py mpremote fs ls mpremote fs rm main.py

Cheapest Question First

Order your own checks by cost, not by how interesting the cause is. "Is it completely dark?" takes one second and splits the display problem in two. Reading a datasheet to explain a speckle can wait until you have tried the 12 MHz setting.

The next activity checks that you can follow a symptom to a cause.

docs.title: Diagram: Diagnosis Decision Tree Trainer
docs.text:
Diagnosis Decision Tree Trainer

Type: microsim sim-id: diagnosis-decision-tree-trainer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate the likely cause of each of 6 reported kit failures from three other causes in the same decision tree, choosing the correct cause for at least 5 of 6 cases.

Prerequisites: flat line, backlight, sample rate, frame overrun, wire swap (all defined in the sections of this chapter above this block and in Chapters 4 and 8); the three diagnosis tables in this chapter, whose rows are named M1 to M6, A1 to A7, and D1 to D8.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 cases the learner reads the reported symptoms and chooses one of 4 candidate causes before the decision tree is shown. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct row in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Walking the tree by answering its questions in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any failure of the microphone means the microphone is broken. (2) A program that runs without an error has no wiring fault. (3) A dark screen is always a software bug. (4) The answer to a distorted sound is always to lower the volume.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating at the Analyze level means telling apart causes that produce similar symptoms. Asking the learner to commit to a cause from four candidates, and only then showing the tree that leads to it, makes the learner use the symptom details that separate the candidates.

Content:

The sim has three trees, one per symptom: silent microphone (rows M1 to M6), distorted audio (rows A1 to A7), and blank display (rows D1 to D8). A tree is a list of rows. Each row asks a yes-or-no question; yes ends the walk at that row's cause, and no goes to the next row of the same tree. The last row of each tree (M6, A7, D8) has no question and is reached when every earlier answer is no. The rows, with their questions, causes, quick tests, and fixes, are the rows of the three tables in the chapter section "Diagnosing the Three Classic Failures". The questions, in order:

Row Question M1 An error at start, and it says "must be sck+1"? M2 An error at start, with another message? M3 No error, but the spread is 0, a flat line? M4 The loudness barely changes when you talk next to it? M5 The meter is pinned at the top? A1 Is the speaker silent, not distorted? A2 Does it crackle only when loud? A3 Is the pitch wrong? A4 Does it stutter or have gaps? A5 Is the start clicky, or the end cut off? A6 Is there hiss or buzz even when nothing plays? D1 Is the screen completely dark, with no light? D2 Did the program stop with an error before drawing? D3 Is it lit but only black or random noise? D4 Is the picture speckled or torn? D5 Is part of what you drew missing? D6 Is the picture rotated or mirrored? D7 Are old letters left over, or is the picture sheared or striped?

The 6 cases, in this order. Each case lists the 3 other candidate causes, which are rows of the same tree.

# Reported symptoms Correct row Three other candidates (rows) 1 "The microphone test stops at once with: invalid ws (must be sck+1)." M1 M3, M4, M5 2 "No error. The probe says every sample is 12345 and the spread is 0." M3 M1, M4, M6 3 "The screen is completely dark. The program runs and prints no errors." D1 D2, D3, D4 4 "The screen is lit and shows the right picture, but it is speckled, on long wires." D4 D3, D5, D7 5 "A recording I made plays back higher and faster than I spoke." A3 A2, A4, A6 6 "The sound stutters. The overrun counter reports many passes longer than 40 ms." A4 A1, A3, A5

Provenance: The causes and tests come from the kit README, the headers of kit tests 05 and 07, config.py, and Chapters 2 to 8, as cited in the source field of src/chapters/18-testing-integration-capstones/tools/diagnose.py. The six cases are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: Each case has exactly one correct row. A tree question is answered only yes or no. The candidate order is shuffled for each learner, with a fixed seed per case.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores one tree: picks a symptom, answers its questions, and reads the cause, test, and fix at the end.
  2. The learner starts the 6 cases. Case 1 shows its symptoms and the four candidate causes.
  3. The learner chooses a cause and submits.
  4. The sim shows the correct cause, then walks the tree for that case, highlighting the questions answered and the cause reached, with the quick test and the fix.
  5. After case 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that the cheap early questions rule out whole branches.

Feedback: 6 cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The likely cause is : look at ". The correct cause is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The three symptom names are shown with the question "Which one are you diagnosing?" and no tree open.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names three failures (silent microphone, distorted audio, blank display); states that the microphone tree has rows M1 to M6, the audio tree A1 to A7, and the display tree D1 to D8; that a swapped microphone starts with no error and sends zeros; that the sck+1 rule applies to the microphone and the amplifier; and that BAUDRATE 12,000,000 is the fix for speckle.

docs.title: Putting the Subsystems in One Loop
docs.text:
System integration is making the parts you built separately work together without breaking each other. Each earlier chapter was tested alone, with the whole 40 ms frame to itself. In the finished device they share it. The integration question is never "does each part work?" but "does the sum of the parts fit in the time, memory, and attention available?"

Start with a map. The device has six subsystems, and a state machine (Chapter 7) decides which are active.

Subsystem Owns Talks to Built in Input Three buttons, microphone read The state machine, audio Chapters 7, 8 Audio I2S in and out, tones, playback Input, DSP, the speaker Chapters 3, 8 DSP Loudness, FFT, band energies, wake word Audio, display Chapters 9, 10, 12 Display Regions: status, time, mascot, spectrum, message State machine, DSP Chapters 5, 6 Network Wi-Fi, HTTP, MQTT check_msg Agent, state machine Chapters 13, 14, 15 Agent The buddy server and its calendar Network only Chapters 1, 16

The main loop of the finished device has one structure: wait for a frame, then run what is due.

sched = Scheduler(frame_us=40000)
sched.add("audio", do_audio, 0, 12)          # period 0 = every pass; budget in ms
sched.add("buttons", do_buttons, 0, 1)
sched.add("spectrum", draw_spectrum, 0, 9)
sched.add("status", draw_status, 200, 4)     # every 200 ms
sched.add("network", poll_network, 200, 3)
while True:
    mic.readinto(buf)      # blocks until a frame is ready: this starts a pass
    sched.run_pass()       # run every task that is due and fits in what is left

scheduler.py is a cooperative scheduler: a task runs until it returns, and nothing can interrupt it. A task's budget is therefore a promise, not a limit. What the scheduler can do is run tasks in the order added (earlier means more important); skip a due task whose budget does not fit into the time left in this frame, for at most three passes so it cannot starve; time every run and count the ones that exceed their budget; and count passes that take longer than the frame. The period 0 means "every pass," for the work tied to each audio frame.

A note on buttons: if the loop blocks 40 ms in readinto, polled buttons are checked 25 times a second, and a tap shorter than 40 ms can be missed. Either read the microphone in 20 ms chunks as test 07 does, or use the button interrupt from Chapter 7.

docs.title: The Frame Overrun Counter
docs.text:
A frame overrun is a pass of the main loop that takes longer than one 40 ms frame (Chapter 8 introduced the budget, and Chapter 10 measures it closely). A frame overrun counter counts them. It works because readinto() blocks until the next frame is ready: the time between two returns of readinto() is the length of one pass. overrun.py wraps the microphone in an object with the same readinto() and deinit(), so you can drop it in without changing the loop.

mic = OverrunCounter(config.init_microphone())
# ... use mic.readinto(buf) exactly as before ...
print(mic.summary())

def _note(self, pass_us):
    if pass_us > self.frame_us + self.jitter_us:
        self.overruns += 1
    self.backlog = max(0.0, self.backlog + pass_us / self.frame_us - 1.0)
    if self.backlog > self.ring_frames:
        self.lost_est += self.backlog - self.ring_frames
        self.backlog = self.ring_frames

_note is called once per pass. A pass longer than the frame plus jitter_us (2 ms, the same timing noise allowance Chapter 8's test used) is an overrun. The backlog is Chapter 8's model: it grows by pass / frame - 1 frames on a slow pass, shrinks on a fast one, and never goes below zero. When it passes the ring's depth, ring_frames (9.77, the depth Chapter 8 measured on one board), the excess is counted as estimated lost frames. Run the model on the passes from Chapter 8: at 50 ms per pass the first loss comes on pass 40, which is \( 40 \times 50 = 2.0 \) seconds, and at 130 ms it comes on pass 5, which is 0.65 seconds. Both match the chapter. The backlog and lost numbers are a model, so treat overruns and worst_us as measurements and the rest as an estimate. Chapter 10's 06-frame-loop-budget.py measures the same thing in more detail (a 95th percentile and a display reserve); OverrunCounter is the small version you can leave in the finished device.

docs.title: The Time Budget in Numbers
docs.text:
The budget table uses numbers measured in earlier chapters wherever they exist. The others are assumptions, marked, which you replace with your own timings.

Task Cost per run Runs Source Read a frame and compute its loudness 10.0 ms every pass Chapter 8, plain-Python loudness on the test board Poll the three buttons 0.5 ms every pass Assumed Redraw the spectrum region 8.5 ms every pass Chapter 6, measured Redraw the status bar 3.0 ms every 200 ms Chapter 6, measured Redraw the time region 3.8 ms every 1,000 ms Chapter 6, measured Check for an MQTT message 2.0 ms every 200 ms Assumed One full-screen redraw 129.4 ms when it happens Chapter 5, measured

A typical pass costs \( 10.0 + 0.5 + 8.5 = 19.0 \) ms, which leaves \( 40 - 19.0 = 21.0 \) ms for the FFT, the wake word, and everything else (Chapter 10's results table is where the FFT's cost is filled in). The worst scheduled pass adds the three periodic tasks: \( 19.0 + 3.0 + 2.0 + 3.8 = 27.8 \) ms, leaving 12.2 ms. Compare two bad plans. Redrawing all five regions every frame costs 28.1 ms measured (Chapter 6), so with the loudness work the pass is \( 10.0 + 28.1 = 38.1 \) ms, only 1.9 ms from the edge. One full-screen redraw makes the pass \( 19.0 + 129.4 = 148.4 \) ms.

08-scheduler-demo.py runs these costs through the scheduler in four scenarios. The costs are inputs to a model, not measurements of the program, so the results show how the design behaves, not how fast your Pico is. On a computer with a fake clock the output below is what the demo printed for 250 frames (10 seconds).

Scenario What it does Passes over 40 ms Worst pass Max backlog Model-estimated lost normal Only the tasks in the table 0 27.8 ms 0.00 frames 0.00 frames stall One full redraw (129.4 ms) every 2 s 5 148.4 ms 2.71 frames 0.00 frames bug A full redraw on every pass 62 157.2 ms 9.77 frames 71.53 frames sliced The same redraw in 8 strips of 16.2 ms 0 35.2 ms 0.00 frames 0.00 frames

Read the table in order. The stall scenario overruns five times but loses nothing in the model: the pass is \( 148.4/40 - 1 = 2.71 \) frames behind, which is about 108 ms, and the ring holds about 9.8 frames (Chapter 8), so the following light passes catch up. A one-off stall costs latency, the delay before the device reacts, not audio. The bug scenario never catches up: the backlog sits at the ring's depth of 9.77 frames, and the model says 71.5 frames were lost. The sliced scenario does the same job without an overrun by doing \( 129.4/8 \approx 16.2 \) ms of it per pass: \( 10.0 + 0.5 + 8.5 + 16.2 = 35.2 \) ms. When status, network, and the slice would all land in one pass, they total 40.2 ms, so the scheduler defers the slice (its 17 ms budget does not fit in the 16 ms left) and the pass stays at 24.0 ms.

A Stall Costs Time, a Treadmill Costs Sound

Notice the difference between a slow pass and a slow loop. One slow pass makes the device late and then it recovers. A loop that is slow on average never recovers, and that is when audio is lost. Budget for the average, then check the worst case.

The activity below lets you build a pass and see whether it fits.

docs.title: Diagram: Frame Budget Scheduler Timeline
docs.text:
Frame Budget Scheduler Timeline

Type: microsim sim-id: frame-budget-scheduler-timeline Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine 6 loop passes against the 40 ms frame budget by calculating each pass's total time to within 0.1 ms and deciding whether it overruns, with at least 5 of 6 fully correct.

Prerequisites: frame, frame budget, task, task budget, cooperative scheduler, deferral, overrun (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 passes the learner types the total milliseconds the pass takes and chooses "overruns" or "fits" before the answer is revealed. A pass is fully correct when the number is within 0.1 ms of the Total column in Content and the choice matches the Overrun column. Mastery is 5 of 6 fully correct. Switching tasks on and off in the free-build timeline in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A task with a big budget only costs its budget. (2) The scheduler can interrupt a task that runs too long. (3) A pass that fits in 40 ms on average cannot overrun. (4) Turning the scheduler on always makes every task run.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a pass at the Analyze level means relating its parts to the whole. Summing task costs to a total and comparing it with the frame makes the learner relate each task to the shared budget, and the case where the scheduler defers a task shows how the parts interact.

Content:

The tasks, with their cost per run and budget in milliseconds, in the order the scheduler considers them (earlier is more important):

Order Task Cost (ms) Budget (ms) 1 audio 10.0 12 2 buttons 0.5 1 3 spectrum 8.5 9 4 status 3.0 4 5 network 2.0 3 6 time 3.8 4 7 redraw (full screen) 129.4 140 8 slice (one eighth of the redraw) 16.2 17

The frame budget is 40 ms. The 6 passes, in this order:

# Scheduler Tasks due in the pass Total (ms) Overrun Why (shown as feedback) 1 off audio, buttons, spectrum 19.0 fits 10.0 + 0.5 + 8.5 = 19.0, which leaves 21.0 ms. 2 off audio, buttons, spectrum, status, network, time 27.8 fits 19.0 + 3.0 + 2.0 + 3.8 = 27.8, which leaves 12.2 ms. 3 off audio, buttons, spectrum, redraw 148.4 overruns 19.0 + 129.4 = 148.4, which is 108.4 ms over the frame. 4 off audio, buttons, spectrum, status, network, slice 40.2 overruns 19.0 + 3.0 + 2.0 + 16.2 = 40.2, which is 0.2 ms over. 5 on audio, buttons, spectrum, status, network, slice 24.0 fits After network the pass has used 24.0 ms, which leaves 16.0 ms. The slice's budget is 17 ms, which does not fit, so it is deferred. 6 off audio, buttons, spectrum, slice 35.2 fits 19.0 + 16.2 = 35.2, which leaves 4.8 ms.

Provenance: The costs for audio, spectrum, status, and time are the measurements in Chapters 8 and 6, the redraw cost is the Chapter 5 measurement, and the slice cost is 129.4 divided by 8, rounded to 16.2. The buttons and network costs, and all the budgets, are assumed values from 08-scheduler-demo.py. The sim labels the costs "model inputs, not a measurement of your program."

Rules: Total = sum of the costs of the tasks that run in the pass. A pass overruns when Total > 40.0. With the scheduler on, tasks are considered in the Order column; a task is deferred (not run) when its budget is greater than 40.0 minus the total so far. With the scheduler off, every due task runs. Answers are in milliseconds with one decimal place.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner switches the 8 tasks on and off in a free-build timeline and flips the scheduler on and off. The timeline shows each task as a block along the 40 ms frame, and a block past 40 ms is marked as an overrun.
  2. The learner starts the 6 passes. Pass 1 shows the scheduler setting and the due tasks.
  3. The learner types the total and chooses overruns or fits, then submits.
  4. The sim reveals the total, draws the pass on the timeline, marks any deferred task, and shows the Why text.
  5. After pass 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that passes 4 and 5 hold the same tasks and differ only in the scheduler.

Feedback: 6 passes, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The total is ms and it : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The timeline shows the three always-due tasks (audio, buttons, spectrum) with the scheduler off, and the question "How much of the 40 ms is left?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the task costs in the table "The Time Budget in Numbers"; that a typical pass is 19.0 ms and the worst scheduled pass is 27.8 ms; that a full-screen redraw makes a pass 148.4 ms; that the slice is about 16.2 ms and a pass with status, network, and the slice would be 40.2 ms; and that the scheduler defers the slice, leaving 24.0 ms.

docs.title: Build Order and the Regression Checklist
docs.text:
The order you assemble the device in is part of the design, because each step gives the next a working base.

  1. Pico alone: kit test 01 (the LED blinks) and test 02 (the board probe).
  2. Buttons: test 03. Display: test 04. Speaker: test 05. Microphone with the display: test 06. Everything: test 07.
  3. Add logging and the self-test (this chapter). From now on, run selftest.py after every change.
  4. Add the audio loop with the OverrunCounter, then the display regions inside the scheduler.
  5. Add DSP (Chapters 9 and 10), calibration and push-to-talk (Chapter 11), and the wake word (Chapter 12).
  6. Add the network link (Chapters 13 and 14), MQTT alerts (Chapter 15), and the school agent (Chapter 16).
  7. Add the privacy features of Chapter 17: the hardware mute, the listening indicator, and the plan.

A regression is something that used to work and no longer does, and it is the most common bug in a growing device: you add a feature and break an old one. The defense is to run the same short checklist after every change.

After every change, check How Passes when The kit still checks out selftest.py No FAIL The display still updates quickly Watch a changing region; run 02-display-probe.py if unsure Fills time like before The loop keeps up Read the OverrunCounter summary after 60 s 0 overruns, or only the ones you expect Push-to-talk still works end to end Hold MODE, ask a question, hear the reply Reply plays, then the clock returns The listening indicator is still true 03-indicator-test.py from Chapter 17 PASS Nothing new is stored mpremote fs ls No audio or transcript files Secrets stay out of git check_secrets.py PASS

docs.title: Choosing and Scoping a Capstone
docs.text:
A capstone project is a device feature you design, build, test, and defend yourself, using what the book taught. It is the difference between following a recipe and cooking. Every capstone needs the same six things before you start, and a rubric (below) grades the same six.

  1. A one-sentence purpose in plain words, and the one person it is for.
  2. A list of requirements you can test, each a sentence that ends in "so that ..." or a number you measure.
  3. Thresholds that come from a calibration step the program runs (Chapter 11's idea: measure the quiet room first), never from a number you guessed or copied.
  4. A passing selftest.py, and an OverrunCounter summary you can show.
  5. A privacy statement: what the device hears, what leaves it, what is kept, and who knows (Chapter 17).
  6. A user test with at least three classmates (below).

The four starters in this chapter each work on the base kit, use only what the book has taught, and are small enough to finish in a few sessions. They are starting points: change the purpose and they become your own. The logic of each lives in detectors.py, which 09-detectors-test.py exercises on synthetic sound and scripted buttons. Synthetic means made up by the test: it shows how the logic behaves, not how a real clap, voice, or fan looks to your microphone.

docs.title: Clap Detector
docs.text:
A clap detector notices a short, sharp sound. Speech and steady noise stay loud for many frames; a clap is loud for one or two frames and falls straight back. ClapDetector therefore watches the frame loudness in bits (the log scale from Chapter 3) and reports a clap when a run of one or two frames at least jump bits above the calibrated floor ends. The jump is max(2.0, 4 x the spread of the quiet frames), so a noisier room needs a bigger jump. The 2.0 is the "heard" margin of kit test 06: 2 bits is 4 times the quiet room's average level.

Here is what 09 printed for the synthetic room, whose noise floor was built to be 12.5 bits like the test board's.

Burst peak compared with the room's noise amplitude Claps found out of 40 10 times 0 20 times 0 40 times 1 80 times 40 160 times 40

Read the table as a sensitivity curve. The sharp edge between 40 and 80 times exists because an 8 ms burst is only a small part of a 40 ms frame's average, so it must be loud to move the frame by 2 bits. Your real threshold depends on your microphone and room, which is why the program calibrates. Two more results from the same test: 180 seconds of syllable-like sound made 0 false claps, and 180 seconds after a fan-like step to 4 times the noise made 0 false claps (the floor drifted up to it). But a single loud frame, such as a sharp "p" or "k", counted as a clap 40 times out of 40. That is a limit of the design, not a bug: it cannot separate a one-frame spike from a clap. Try This in the program suggests adding a crest-factor check.

Requirement Test Learns the quiet room before listening The shell prints the floor and jump after 2 s Counts a clap near the microphone 5 claps at 0.5 m count 5 Ignores talking and steady noise 30 s of talking and a fan count 0 Two claps within 1 s toggle a light The on-screen light switches Reports what it cannot do The README lists the one-frame-spike limit

Extensions: record the distance at which claps stop counting at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 m; add the crest-factor check; make a triple clap do something different.

docs.title: Classroom Noise Monitor
docs.text:
A classroom noise monitor shows how loud a room is as one of three words, QUIET, TALKING, or LOUD. NoiseMonitor smooths the loudness with a moving average (time constant 1 second by default, like the slow setting of a sound level meter), compares it with limits that are bits above the room's own floor, and changes the word only after the new band has held for 12 frames (0.5 s) so it does not flicker. The limits are 2.0 and 4.0 bits above the floor, which is 4 and 16 times the quiet level, or about 12 and 24 dB. These are relative to your microphone and room, not sound-pressure decibels, because the microphone is uncalibrated. The starting limits are values to tune with your class.

On the synthetic 60 seconds (20 s quiet, 20 s at 6 times the noise, 10 s at 25 times, 10 s quiet), the band was TALKING at the end of the second stretch (smoothed level +2.6 bits above the floor), LOUD at the end of the third (+4.7 bits), and QUIET again at the end. The monitor counted 30.6 s QUIET, 20.4 s TALKING, and 9.0 s LOUD, which add to 60: the smoothing and the 0.5 s dwell shift a little time between bands. A sound that flickered across the limit every 3 frames changed the band 0 times in 20 seconds.

Level Only: Say So, and Mean It

A noise monitor is still a microphone in a classroom, so build it so it cannot keep sound: it is handed one number per frame, keeps three counters, and writes no file. Put "Level only. No audio saved." on the screen and tell the room first (Chapter 17).

Requirement Test Level only The code never stores samples or writes a file; mpremote fs ls shows none Says so The screen shows "Level only. No audio saved." Calibrates The floor is measured at start and shown Stable The word does not flicker when someone speaks at the limit Summarizes Seconds per band are printed each minute

Extensions: let UP and DOWN change the limits and save them; show the last 10 minutes as a strip chart in one region; ask three classmates what "too loud" means for silent reading and for group work, and set two modes.

docs.title: Study Timer Buddy
docs.text:
A study timer buddy runs focus and break periods so a student can work in short blocks. StudyTimer is a state machine (Chapter 7) with three states, IDLE, FOCUS, and BREAK, plus a paused flag. MODE starts, pauses, or resumes; a long MODE press skips to the other phase; UP and DOWN change the focus length from 5 to 60 minutes while idle. The defaults of 25 minutes of focus and 5 of break, with a 15 minute break after every 4th focus, are common study-technique values, and they are settings you can change.

Time comes from a deadline, not from counting seconds in a loop (Chapter 7's non-blocking rule). The timer stores when the phase ends, and remaining = end - now is computed each pass with time.ticks_diff, so a slow pass cannot make the clock drift and the millisecond counter's wrap-around is handled. Pausing stores the remaining time; resuming sets a new end. A 25 minute focus is \( 25 \times 60 \times 1000 = 1{,}500{,}000 \) ms.

The scripted test in 09 checks that 15:00 remain after 10 minutes of a 25 minute focus, that 30 minutes spent paused change nothing, that the 4th focus is followed by the 15 minute break, and that a focus still ends on time when the millisecond counter wraps in the middle of it. The program redraws a region only when its text changes, so the screen sends bytes once a second.

Requirement Test Starts, pauses, resumes with MODE A scripted press sequence gives the right states Stays accurate 25:00 ends within one pass of 25 minutes by a stopwatch Never blocks The OverrunCounter shows 0 overruns Beeps at the end of each phase You hear it, then the next phase begins Redraws only what changed Only the seconds change on screen each second

Extensions: hold UP to ask "how long is left?" through the push-to-talk path (Chapters 11 and 14); let the mascot sleep during focus and wake for breaks; count completed focus periods across the day.

docs.title: Homework Reminder Buddy
docs.text:
A homework reminder buddy shows the next TEST: and DUE: items and how soon each is. It uses the same title convention as the school agent (Chapter 16): a title that starts with TEST: or DUE: is a reminder, and anything else is ignored. The program must work with or without the agent. It reads events.json from the Pico if you copied one (tools/trim_events.py cuts the 92-event Cedar Ridge file of 27,187 bytes down to the 50 test and due events, 4,197 bytes), and otherwise uses a three-item list built into the file. The agent link is an upgrade, not a requirement: replace load_events() with a request to your server when it is ready.

Dates use plain arithmetic: day_number(y, m, d) turns a date into a day count, and the difference of two counts is the days between them, with no datetime module. The test checks month ends, a leap day, and that date_text undoes day_number for 576 dates. A Pico has no calendar until you give it one, so "today" starts at the Cedar Ridge demo date of 2026-10-19 and UP and DOWN move it a day at a time.

On that date the reminders are, soonest first: TOMORROW, the Algebra II test; IN 2 DAYS, the English draft; IN 3 DAYS, the Biology report. An alert and a beep happen once, the first time an item is tomorrow or today, and Reminders remembers what it has announced so it does not repeat.

Requirement Test Works with no agent and no network Start with no events.json: the built-in list appears Reads only TEST and DUE The picture day and the football game are not shown Sorts soonest first The three items appear in 1, 2, 3 day order Announces once Moving the date back and forth does not repeat an alert Respects privacy Only school events are used; no student data is stored

Extensions: read the same file from the school server (Chapter 16); add a second alert "3 days before" a test; show the course name from the event.

docs.title: Grading a Capstone
docs.text:
Use one rubric for all four projects, so the grade measures the same skills whatever you built. Each criterion has three levels: Meets (full points), Approaching (about half), and Not yet (none).

Criterion Points Meets Function 5 Every requirement in your list passes its test, and you show the tests Calibration 3 Thresholds come from a measurement the program makes, shown on screen or in the log Reliability 3 selftest.py passes, and the OverrunCounter shows no unexpected overruns Privacy 3 The device says what it hears and keeps; a plan exists; nothing stores audio User testing 3 Three or more testers, notes kept, at least one change made because of what they did Code and notes 3 Pins come from config.py, regions redraw only on change, and a README gives wiring and test results

That is 20 points. A capstone that passes every requirement but skips the user test cannot score above 17.

docs.title: User Testing
docs.text:
User testing is watching people other than you try to use your device, and writing down what happens. You already know how it works, so you cannot see what a new person sees. The protocol is short and uses user-test-sheet.md.

  1. Choose the tasks. Write 3 or 4 jobs a user would do, in their words: "Start a 25 minute timer." Do not mention buttons.
  2. Choose testers. Three to five classmates who did not build it. A small group like this typically finds most of the common problems, which is why designers test early and often. Tell each one what you will record and that they may stop at any time; record notes, never their voice or a picture.
  3. Read the script and stay quiet. Say "I am testing the device, not you." Ask them to think aloud. Do not help unless they are stuck for a full minute.
  4. Record what you see: done on their own (yes or no), seconds taken, wrong presses or hesitations, and their exact words. Afterward ask what was hardest, what they expected, whether they could tell what the device does with sound, and an ease score from 1 to 5.
  5. Decide what to change. Merge duplicate problems across sheets and count how many testers hit each. Fix a problem that stopped someone, then any problem two or more testers hit. Change one thing, then test it again with a new person.

Worked example (invented, to show the method). Three testers try the study timer. Two press MODE once to start, then hold it expecting it to stop, and instead skip to the break. Both problems come from one cause: nothing on the screen says a long press skips. The change is a one-line hint, "Hold MODE: skip", in the idle screen. The retest with a fourth tester shows no skips. This is the evidence for a design choice, which is what the course outcome "justify the design choices based on user testing with classmates" asks for.

Watching Someone Struggle Is Hard

It can sting to watch a classmate fumble with something you built, and that is normal. You have already debugged wiring and timing, which are harder. Each fumble is a free lesson you did not have to guess.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
You can now find a fault with a probe instead of a guess, check every wire against a list computed from config.py, and run a self-test after every change. You can walk a symptom to a cause, keep the whole device inside a 40 ms frame, and build, test, and defend a project that is yours.

Key takeaways:

  • Serial output, the REPL, and mpremote share one port, so quit Thonny first. Log with levels, a RAM ring, and a capped flash file, and never log audio or words.
  • A probe tests one part and prints evidence before a verdict of PASS, FAIL, ASK, or SKIP. The display and amplifier cannot report back, so they stay ASK until a person answers.
  • Verify wiring against a table computed from config.py; the pin-plan rules catch swapped I2S pairs, reused pins, and wireless-chip pins.
  • Diagnose with the cheapest question first, then confirm with the quick test before changing anything.
  • A frame overrun counter times the gap between readinto() calls. A one-off stall costs latency; a loop that is slow on average loses audio.
  • Integrate with a budget (a 19.0 ms typical pass leaves 21.0 ms), slice big jobs, and rerun the regression checklist after every change.
  • A capstone has a purpose, testable requirements, calibrated thresholds, a self-test, a privacy statement, and a user test with classmates.

Test yourself with these questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

Your clap detector counts every sharp 'p' as a clap. Is the threshold wrong? Click to expand

Probably not. The detector watches loudness over 40 ms frames, so a one-frame spike looks the same as a clap. The test shows this limit: single-frame spikes counted 40 times out of 40. To separate them you need another feature, such as a crest-factor check, and you should test it on both kinds of sound.

A pass takes 148.4 ms once every 2 seconds. Does the microphone lose audio? Click to expand

By the model, no. The pass runs \( 148.4/40 - 1 = 2.71 \) frames behind, about 108 ms, which is less than the ring's depth of about 9.8 frames, and the next light passes catch up. It costs latency. If the same pass happened every frame, the model says audio would be lost.

Why does the self-test report the display as ASK and not PASS? Click to expand

The display controller cannot report back to the Pico, so the program can only draw a pattern. A person has to say what they saw. The program turns ASK into PASS or FAIL only when someone answers with UP or DOWN.

A Device You Can Trust and Fix

You just learned to probe a part, verify wiring from config.py, write a self-test, diagnose the three classic failures, budget a 40 ms frame across every subsystem, and build and test a capstone with classmates. You can now fix your own Study Buddy and make it yours.

docs.title: Cover Image Prompt
docs.text:
Please generate a professional-quality cover image for this textbook. This image will be used in social media previews and must follow the formatting guidelines for an Open Graph image preview.

Required specifications: - Format: PNG - Wide-landscape format - Size: 1200x630 pixels (1.91:1 aspect ratio) - This is the Open Graph standard for social media previews

The image has four layers, back to front: background montage, color treatment, mascot, and title text.

docs.title: Subject & Tone
docs.text: Open Study Buddy is a hands-on textbook about building a low-cost, fully open, personal AI study-buddy device from a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, a round 360 x 360 color display, a digital microphone, a small speaker, and three push buttons. The device listens, shows what it heard, speaks answers aloud, and announces school tests and project due dates. The intended audience is high school students (grades 9-12), coding clubs, and the teachers who run school maker programs. The visual tone should be friendly, modern, and technical: the excitement of a student maker project that actually works, not the cold look of corporate AI.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Place Open Study Buddy in the center of the image, in a clean, highly legible, bold sans-serif font. Use a white font color with a subtle drop shadow or a dark navy scrim behind it so it stays readable against the busy montage background. Add a small subtitle line beneath it in a lighter weight: "Build your own open AI agent with MicroPython". Do not shrink the title to fit; instead simplify the background directly behind the text.

docs.title: Background Montage
docs.text:
Arrange a montage of the following 8 concepts around the title, each rendered in a consistent flat-vector illustration style (see Style below) so the composition reads as one image rather than a collage of unrelated styles:

  1. The Open Study Buddy device (hero element, right of the title) - a small desk device whose face is a large round color display showing a friendly glowing "listening" ring and a short text bubble, with a tiny circuit board and three small round push buttons (Mode, Up, Down) at its base.
  2. Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W - a small green microcontroller board with a silver Wi-Fi module, drawn top-down with gold pads along both edges.
  3. FFT audio spectrum - a row of glowing vertical bars of varying height in teal-to-amber gradient, like a live equalizer, sitting on a dark baseline.
  4. Sound waveform - a smooth blue sine wave with evenly spaced sample dots along it, showing sampling.
  5. INMP441 microphone and speaker - a tiny round microphone breakout board next to a small speaker cone, with curved sound-wave arcs between them.
  6. MQTT school alert - a school-building icon sending dotted lines to three small devices, with a speech-bubble badge reading "TEST TOMORROW".
  7. School calendar - a monthly calendar page with two dates circled in orange, one marked with a small test-paper icon, one with a flag.
  8. Privacy shield with microphone - a shield containing a microphone with a small mute slash and a green "listening" indicator dot, signaling consent-first design.

Optionally add a few faint circuit-trace lines and Wi-Fi arcs connecting the elements, kept very low contrast so they do not add clutter.

docs.title: Mascot
docs.text: Place the book's mascot, Sage the Owl, in the lower-left corner, sized so it does not overlap the title text. Sage is a small, compact, flat-vector cartoon owl with a slate-blue body (#2E6DA4), a cream chest, small round orange-framed glasses, orange beak and feet (#F5871F), bright curious eyes, and a warm closed-mouth smile. Sage is roughly two heads tall and has a transparent background. Pose: welcoming, with one wing slightly raised in greeting. Use the existing reference image docs/img/mascot/welcome.png for consistency.

docs.title: Style & Composition
docs.text:
• Illustration style: flat vector with clean lines and bold simple shapes, matching Sage's art style. Apply it to every montage element.
  • Color palette: deep navy and slate blue (matching Sage) for the background, with teal accents and warm orange (#F5871F) highlights; small touches of Pico green on the circuit board.
  • Lighting/mood: bright and optimistic, with a soft glow around the device display and the spectrum bars, as if the device is switched on.
  • Composition: title centered, montage elements arranged in a loose ring around it with the device as the largest element, Sage in the lower-left, generous negative space immediately behind the title so it stays readable. Keep all important content inside a safe margin of about 5% from each edge, since social platforms crop the edges.

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text:
• Do not render dense paragraphs of illegible text anywhere in the image. The only readable text should be the title, the subtitle, and the short "TEST TOMORROW" badge.
  • Avoid generic stock-photo cliches (handshakes, isolated lightbulbs, people pointing at whiteboards, glowing human-shaped robots or brains).
  • Avoid photorealistic human faces; show no students' faces.
  • Do not use any commercial AI product logos or trademarks.
  • Do not let montage elements visually compete with or overlap the title.
  • Do not draw the round display as a rectangle; it must be a circle.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Open Study Buddy
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement

View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 3 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with 15 categories
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (4% - 10% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file

View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.text: The 326 concepts in the learning graph are grouped into 15 categories. Each concept belongs to exactly one category. The TaxonomyID is the 3-5 letter code used in learning-graph.csv. Categories are ordered from foundational material to the capstone projects.

docs.title: Personal Agents and Architecture (FND)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: FND Concepts: 22

What a personal agent is, open versus cloud agents, the Open Study Buddy architecture, and the swappable-brain progression from a rule-based buddy server to open-source agent frameworks.

TaxonomyID: MPY Concepts: 20

Sound, sampling, the Nyquist limit, the I2S bus, machine.I2S, audio buffers and frames, tone and stored-audio playback, and the self-hearing problem.

docs.title: Signal Processing and FFT (DSP)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: DSP Concepts: 26

Time and frequency domains, the DFT and FFT, bins, windowing, magnitude spectra, band energies, loudness and spectrum displays.

docs.title: High-Performance MicroPython (PERF)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: PERF Concepts: 20

Making MicroPython fast enough for real time: viper, inline assembly, the assembly FFT, typed arrays, allocation-free code, cycle counting and benchmarking.

docs.title: Mic Calibration and Push-to-Talk (CAL)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: CAL Concepts: 14

Measuring the noise floor and speech level, signal-to-noise ratio, level gates, push-to-talk recording and utterance boundaries.

docs.title: Wake-Word Detection (WAKE)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: WAKE Concepts: 24

Detecting 'Hey Pico': enrollment, feature extraction, template correlation, thresholds, false accepts and rejects, limits, and comparison with trained models.

docs.title: Networking and Agent Link (NET)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: NET Concepts: 26

Wi-Fi, HTTP and JSON on the school LAN, chunked audio upload, speech services, WebSocket streaming, HTTPS, and handling network failure.

docs.title: MQTT and Push Alerts (MQTT)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: MQTT Concepts: 22

Publish/subscribe messaging: brokers, topics, QoS, retained messages, last-will, umqtt, non-blocking check_msg, and connecting to Home Assistant.

docs.title: School Agent and Calendar (SCH)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: SCH Concepts: 24

Connecting the agent to a school calendar via JSON then iCalendar feeds, test and due-date events, briefings, reminders and per-school customization.

docs.title: Privacy and Responsible Listening (PRIV)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: PRIV Concepts: 18

Consent, parent and school approval, data minimization and retention, local versus cloud processing, threat models, mute and indicators.

docs.title: Testing, Integration and Capstones (TEST)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: TEST Concepts: 16

Probe and self-test programs, wiring checks, logging, diagnosing silent microphones and blank displays, system integration and capstone projects.

docs.title: Pedagogical Flow
docs.text: The order above is the suggested teaching order. Personal-agent ideas, the MicroPython review and the hardware come first. Display, buttons and audio follow, then signal processing and performance. Calibration and wake-word detection build on audio and the FFT. Networking comes next, and MQTT builds on it. The school-agent, privacy and integration categories bring the pieces together.

docs.title: Teacher's Guide
docs.text: This page holds the Purchasing Guide section of the Teacher's Guide for Open Study Buddy.

docs.title: Purchasing Guide
docs.text:
The whole book runs on one kit, the Study Buddy base kit: a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 WH, a 2.1-inch 360×360 round color display (GC9B72), an INMP441 I²S microphone, a MAX98357A I²S amplifier with a small speaker, three push buttons, a breadboard and wiring. One kit costs about $28 at single-unit prices and about $21 per student for a class of 20. Every part except the Pico ships from China in 8–12 days (median 9) in our 2026 AliExpress orders, so order at least three weeks before the hardware chapters start, and four to five weeks ahead for a full classroom set.

Prices checked October 2026

Component prices move, and marketplace listings turn over constantly. Treat every figure here as a planning estimate, not a quote. Each part shows the low and high AliExpress prices we found in web searches on October 20, 2026, with eBay and Amazon prices for comparison. Figures marked estimate could not be confirmed from a current listing, and each one says why.

Don't order the wrong one: a 360×360 SPI display with the GC9B72 controller

The kit's driver (lib/gc9b72.py) only works with the 2.1-inch, 360×360, 4-wire SPI round display built on the GC9B72 controller. Marketplaces list 2.1-inch round 480×480 panels (ST7701, RGB or MIPI interface) and 1.28-inch GC9A01 round displays right beside it, with nearly identical photos. Neither will work. Look for "GC9B72" and "360x360" in the listing title.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi Pico 2 WH
docs.text:
Photo pending. See the image brief.

Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 4: The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring and every chapter after it, including Wi-Fi in Chapter 13: Wi-Fi, HTTP, and Connecting to the Agent. It runs the student's MicroPython and talks to every other part.

The Pico 2 W is Raspberry Pi's RP2350 microcontroller board with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Buy the WH version, which has its header pins already soldered so it drops straight into the breadboard. The plain "Pico 2 W" has bare pads.

Requirements: It must be a Pico 2 W (RP2350). The older Pico W (RP2040) and the plain Pico 2 (no Wi-Fi) look almost the same in listing photos. The book's audio, FFT and Wi-Fi chapters assume the RP2350's 520 KB of RAM and the wireless chip. The radio is 2.4 GHz only, so confirm with your school's IT team that a 2.4 GHz network is available.

Prep work: None for the WH. A plain Pico 2 W needs its headers soldered on (about 15 minutes).

Cost: ~$6.99 each in quantity 1 (Micro Center "Pico 2W with Header", SC1634) · ~$6.99 each in a classroom order of 20+ · ~$6.99 at district scale (estimate: we assume the fixed retail price holds). Price range: AliExpress $3.53–$31.09 (the low end is a promotional listing of uncertain origin; listings titled "100% New Original" were $20.75); eBay about US$15–$23 (eBay Australia listings at AU$23.75–AU$34.98; we could not load US eBay results); Amazon $13.99 for the Pico 2 W without headers and $18.95 for a pre-soldered version.

AliExpress lead time: Not recommended. Marketplace Picos cost two to four times the Micro Center price and are the boards most likely to be relabeled. Micro Center stores have it the same day, and its online store lists "usually ships in 5–7 business days".

Trusted sellers: Micro Center, Adafruit, SparkFun, Digi-Key and PiShop.us. Genuine boards say "Pico 2 W" on the silkscreen and carry an RP2350 chip.

docs.title: 2.1-inch Round Display (GC9B72, 360x360)
docs.text:
Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 5: Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size and Chapter 6: Drawing Directly to Display Regions, then the face, text and level meter in every later chapter.

A 2.1-inch round IPS color screen with 360×360 pixels and a GC9B72 controller, driven over 4-wire SPI at 3.3 V. The module has a 10-pin header (GND, VCC, SCL, SDA, RST, DC, CS, BL, SDO, TE). The kit uses the first eight. GalaxyCore has never published a GC9B72 datasheet, so the book's driver was ported from the one known-good public init sequence. That makes the exact controller matter more than usual.

Requirements: It must say GC9B72, 360x360 and SPI. The 480×480 2.1-inch round panels need an RGB or MIPI interface that the Pico does not have.

Prep work: None. The header comes soldered. Peel off an 8-wire strip of the ribbon cable for it (see below).

Cost: ~$6.12 in quantity 1 (the AliExpress listing we bought from, US$6.12) · ~$5.39 each in a classroom order of 20+ (the lowest current AliExpress search price) · no district tier found. Price range: AliExpress $5.39–$6.12 (TZT's own store lists it at $3.45); eBay ~$8–$15 (estimate: we could not load current US eBay results); Amazon: no matching 360×360 GC9B72 listing found, only the 480×480 panels that will not work. A European marketplace lists it at €14.64 plus shipping.

AliExpress lead time: 8–12 days (median 9), the same as our other AliExpress packages. The glass panel ships in a bigger padded box, and a cracked screen means reordering and another 9 days, so buy one or two spares.

Spotting a bad batch: A blank screen with the backlight on usually means a wiring mistake, so run test 04 first. A panel with a dead line or a dark sector after a correct test is a defect. Set it aside and use a spare.

Search keywords: GC9B72 2.1 inch round display 360x360, 2.1 inch round TFT SPI GC9B72

docs.title: INMP441 I2S Microphone
docs.text:
Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 8: I2S Audio: Recording and Playing Sound, Chapter 11: Microphone Calibration and Push-to-Talk and Chapter 12: Wake-Word Detection. It turns the student's voice into 24-bit samples.

A digital MEMS microphone with its own ADC, sending samples straight to the Pico over I²S. Buy the INMP441 by name. The "INMP441-compatible" MS3625 and MS4030 boards are cheaper, but the kit's calibration numbers were measured on the INMP441. It is a 3.3 V part: VDD goes to 3V3, never to VBUS.

Prep work: Some minor soldering required. Most listings ship with the six-pin header loose, as in the photo, and soldering it takes about 5 minutes per board. Listings sold as "solderless" have the header fitted and are worth the extra few cents for a no-solder kit. Tie the L/R pin to GND.

Cost: ~$3.00 in quantity 1 (AliExpress singles at $2.19–$4.39) · ~$1.00 each in a classroom order of 20+ (AliExpress listings around $0.99) · ~$0.89 each at district scale (an Alibaba tiered listing at $0.89 for 10–999 pieces). Price range: AliExpress $0.99–$4.39 (coin-deal listings as low as $0.33 are for new shoppers only); eBay ~$3–$8 (UK listings at £5.82–£5.99, Germany €2.28 plus €1.60 shipping); Amazon $8.54–$9.99 per 3-pack.

AliExpress lead time: 8–12 days (median 9).

Spotting a bad batch: A dead or badly soldered microphone reads as all zeros, which looks exactly like the swapped-wire fault in the kit README. Check the wiring, then the solder joints, then swap in a spare.

docs.title: MAX98357A I2S Amplifier
docs.text:
Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 7: Buttons, State Machines, and Device Modes (the volume beep) and Chapter 8: I2S Audio: Recording and Playing Sound, then every chapter where the buddy speaks. It turns I²S audio from the Pico into power for the speaker.

A digital-to-analog converter and a 3 W class-D amplifier on one small board, with seven pins (LRC, BCLK, DIN, GAIN, SD, GND, VIN) and a two-screw output terminal. The kit drives its GAIN pin from GP18 so software can pick 6, 9 or 12 dB. Buy the mono MAX98357A breakout, not the analog PAM8403 boards or the larger stereo TDM boards that show up in the same searches.

Prep work: Some minor soldering required on most listings. The seven-pin header and the screw terminal usually ship loose, which takes about 10 minutes per board. Some listings are sold as "pre-soldered" for about the same price, and we recommend those for a no-solder kit.

Cost: ~$1.53 in quantity 1 · ~$0.99 each in a classroom order of 20+ (most AliExpress listings) · no district tier found. Price range: AliExpress $0.93–$1.53 (pre-soldered listings about $0.99); eBay ~$2–$6 (estimate: we could not load current US eBay results; Adafruit's genuine breakout is $5.95); Amazon $6.88 for a 2-pack, $7.59 for 3, $8.54 for 4 and $11.99 for 6 ($2.00–$3.44 each).

AliExpress lead time: 8–12 days (median 9).

Spotting a bad batch: No sound with test 05 is almost always the I²S pin rule (LRC must be the pin right after BCLK) or a loose screw terminal. If test 02 reports no warnings and the speaker is known good, swap the board.

docs.title: Speaker (3525, 8 ohm, 2 W)
docs.text:
Photo pending. See the image brief.

Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 8: I2S Audio: Recording and Playing Sound and every chapter where the buddy beeps, plays back a recording or speaks.

A small sealed "3525" cavity speaker, 35 × 25 mm, with a red and black lead ending in a 2-pin JST PH 2.0 plug. The kit's speaker is the 8 Ω, 2 W version: it was measured at 7.4 Ω DC resistance. The same listings also sell a 4 Ω, 3 W version. Either works with the MAX98357A, but the 8 Ω one is quieter and draws less current from the Pico's USB supply, so stay with it.

Prep work: About 2 minutes. Cut off the JST plug, strip 5 mm from each wire, and clamp the wires in the amplifier's screw terminal (red to +).

docs.title: Momentary Push Buttons (6x6 mm)
docs.text:
Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×3: Mode, Up and Down)

Used for: Chapter 7: Buttons, State Machines, and Device Modes and push-to-talk in Chapter 11.

Standard 6×6 mm, four-leg, through-hole tactile switches. Each one connects GP13, GP14 or GP15 to GND and uses the Pico's internal pull-up, so no resistor is needed. Colored caps are optional but help students tell Mode from Up and Down.

Prep work: None. They are breadboard-ready as shipped. Show students that the four legs are two connected pairs, so a button wired with both wires on the same side reads "pressed" all the time.

Cost: ~$0.15 for three in quantity 1 (a 100-pack is $4.99 on Amazon) · ~$0.05 each in a classroom order of 20+ (one 100-pack covers 20 kits with 40 spares) · ~$0.04 each at district scale (Alibaba switches at a 1,000-piece minimum order). Price range: AliExpress ~$0.01–$0.03 each in 100-packs (estimate: not re-checked this month); eBay ~$3–$6 per 100 (estimate); Amazon $4.99 per 100.

AliExpress lead time: 8–12 days (median 9).

Spotting a bad batch: Legs bent too short to seat, or switches that never click. Discard the odd bad one; the 100-pack has plenty of spares.

docs.title: Solderless Breadboard (830 Point)
docs.text:
Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 4: The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring and every wired test after it.

A full-size 830 tie-point breadboard ("MB-102"). Buy the full size: the Pico, microphone, amplifier and three buttons do not fit on a 400-point half-size board, and the chapter's advice to keep the microphone's wires away from the amplifier's needs the room.

docs.title: Dupont Ribbon Cable (Male-to-Female, 20 cm)
docs.text:
Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×8 wires, one-fifth of a 40-wire ribbon)

Used for: The display cable in Chapter 5: Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size.

A 40-wire ribbon of Dupont jumpers with a female socket on one end and a male pin on the other. Peel off an 8-wire strip for the display: the female ends push onto the display's header and the male ends go into the breadboard. config.py records a color for each display wire (SCL orange, SDA yellow, RST green, DC blue, CS purple, BL gray, VCC red), so peel the strip where those colors line up. One ribbon makes cables for five kits.

Prep work: Peel the ribbon into 8-wire strips, about 1 minute per kit. Keep the strip intact: it stays in pin order and is far harder to miswire than loose jumpers.

Cost: ~$2.95 per ribbon in quantity 1 (PiShop US) · ~$1.00 per ribbon in a classroom order of 20+ (AliExpress from about $0.99), about $0.20 per kit · ~$0.65 per ribbon at district scale (an Alibaba listing). Price range: AliExpress from ~$0.99; eBay ~$2–$4 (estimate); PiShop $2.95.

AliExpress lead time: 8–12 days (median 9).

Spotting a bad batch: Female sockets too loose to grip a header pin. Test-fit one strip on the display when the order arrives.

docs.title: Micro-USB Data Cable
docs.text:
Photo: Electronicgrup, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Used in: Study Buddy base kit (×1)

Used for: Chapter 4 and every chapter after it. It powers the kit and carries the Thonny connection.

The Pico 2 WH has a Micro-USB port, not USB-C. The cable must carry data: charge-only cables look identical and are the most common reason a Pico "isn't detected" on day one. If your laptops have only USB-C ports, buy USB-C to Micro-USB cables. A computer USB port supplies about 500 mA, which is enough for this kit at the volumes the tests use.

Confirm it says data or sync

Look for "data", "sync" or "480 Mbps" in the listing. A cable sold only as a "charging cord" may have no data wires at all.

Prep work: None. Test each cable with a Pico in Thonny on arrival and discard any that only charge.

Cost: ~$2.50 in quantity 1 (Cable Matters 3-pack, $7.49 on Amazon) · ~$2.50 each in a classroom order of 20+ (seven 3-packs) · ~$1.00 each at district scale (estimate). Price range: AliExpress ~$0.80–$2.00 (estimate: not checked this month); eBay ~$2–$4 (estimate); Amazon $7.49–$9.44 per 3-pack.

AliExpress lead time: 8–12 days (median 9). Cables are the easiest part to buy domestically the week of the lab if a few are missing.
