docs.title: Ordering lead time
docs.text:
These figures are based on our 2026 AliExpress orders to Minnesota: 8 packages, measured from order date to delivery.

Source Orders measured Typical delivery Notes AliExpress 8 packages 8–12 days (median 9) Every 2026 package arrived within two weeks Micro Center — same day in store; online "ships in 5–7 business days" The place to buy the Pico 2 WH Amazon — 1–3 days with Prime (estimate, not measured) The fallback for cables, buttons and breadboards

The per-part notes above flag the parts that ship differently: the display (fragile glass in a larger padded box) and the breadboards (bulky, sometimes split into several packages). The kit has no batteries, so no part is held up by lithium shipping rules. If a later version adds a battery pack, expect it to ship separately and take longer.

Our recommendation: place AliExpress orders at least three weeks before you need the parts, and four to five weeks ahead for a full classroom set. Eight packages is a small sample, and the extra weeks mean a lost package or a cracked display can be reordered and still arrive in time. Use Micro Center or Amazon for last-minute gaps. Expect longer delays around Lunar New Year, when Chinese factories and shipping largely stop for two weeks or more.

Buy one, then buy twenty. Order a single display, microphone and amplifier from a seller first, confirm they are the GC9B72 360×360 display, a genuine INMP441 and a mono MAX98357A, then place the classroom order with the same sellers.

Order spares. Add 10–15% over the class count for the display, microphone, amplifier and Pico. Two spares of each add about $30 to a class order.

Watch the pack sizes. Buttons come in hundreds, breadboards in tens and cables in threes. Round the order up to the pack, not to the roster.

Buy boards from authorized resellers. Micro Center sells the genuine Pico 2 WH for less than any marketplace listing we found.

Expect the odd bad unit, not a bad order. Test every part on arrival with the kit's numbered tests (01–07) and discard the occasional dud.

Check your district's purchasing rules first. Many districts cannot reimburse AliExpress orders and require a domestic vendor with a W-9. If so, the Amazon and Micro Center prices are your real prices. The round display has no Amazon listing we could find, so a district with that rule will need an exception for it or a different domestic seller.

docs.text: Written for a text-to-image model because no suitably licensed photograph of this part was found in the workspace. (The pico-w.png in learning-micropython shows the older RP2040 Pico W, which is the wrong board.) Wikimedia Commons is worth one more check before generating. Delete this note once the image exists.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: A single Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W microcontroller board, a long narrow green printed circuit board about 51 mm × 21 mm, with a silver rectangular metal RF shield can near one end covering the wireless chip, a small black square RP2350 processor chip in the middle, a white BOOTSEL push button, a silver Micro-USB connector at the opposite short end from the shield, and a row of 20 gold castellated pin holes along each long edge, with "Pico 2 W" printed in white silkscreen. Resting flat on a plain white seamless background. Soft, even product-photography lighting with no harsh shadows. Shot directly overhead. The board fills roughly 60% of the frame. Sharp focus throughout, high detail, no text overlay, no watermark, no hands, no packaging, no other objects.

docs.title: Physical details that must be right
docs.text:
• Size: 51 mm × 21 mm, about 1 mm thick
  • Package / form factor: Pico form factor, 2 × 20 castellated pins at 2.54 mm pitch
  • Color: green solder mask, gold pads, silver shield can
  • Leads/pins: 40 edge pins plus 3 debug pins at the end opposite the USB port
  • Distinguishing marks: the metal RF shield can (absent on the plain Pico 2), the "Pico 2 W" silkscreen, the RP2350 chip

docs.title: What it must not look like
docs.text:
• The plain Pico 2 has no metal shield can. The shield is the visual tell for the W.
  • The older Pico W (RP2040) looks very similar but says "Pico W" and has an RP2040 chip. Do not render an RP2040 or the text "Pico W".
  • Not the larger Raspberry Pi single-board computers.

docs.title: Demo Script
docs.text:
Set the server's "today" to Monday, October 19, 2026 (see the calendar), then try:

Say The agent should find "When is my next test?" TEST: Algebra II Unit 3 - Quadratics, tomorrow at 8:00 AM "What is due this week?" English 10 personal narrative draft (Wed), Biology osmosis lab report (Thu) "Is there school on Friday?" Yes, and the Griffins play Eastbrook at 7:00 PM on Griffin Field "When does the quarter end?" Friday, October 30, which is also Spirit Day (green and gold) "What's happening tonight?" Nothing on Monday evening; the next event is the Friday football game "When is Thanksgiving break?" No school Nov 25–27

To change the data, edit scripts/build-school-calendar.py and rerun it from the repo root. It regenerates events.json, calendar.ics, and calendar.md together so they never disagree.

Instructor note

Cedar Ridge is fictional. Any resemblance to a real school, teacher, or event is coincidental. When you build a real school edition, replace the name, slogan, mascot, and calendar, and keep the TEST: and DUE: title prefixes.

docs.title: Gale the Griffin
docs.text: Gale is the mascot of the Cedar Ridge Griffins. A griffin is half eagle and half lion, so Gale stands for sharp eyes (aim high) and a keen listener (listen closely). Gale has no gender; write "Gale" or they/them.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Agent Data Flow Step-Through
docs.text: Run the Agent Data Flow Step-Through MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: Embed This MicroSim
docs.text:
Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/agent-data-flow-step-through/main.html" width="100%" height="582px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When you ask your Study Buddy "When is my next test?", the answer takes eight steps to reach you, and three different parts do the work: the terminal on your desk, the network (Wi-Fi) between the computers, and the buddy server on a school computer. This MicroSim walks through those eight steps one at a time.

Before each of steps 2 to 8 is revealed, you predict which part performs it. The sim then shows the owner, a one-line description of the step, and the concrete data at that step, such as the sample sound values (illustrative), the request fields device = desk-07 and kind = question, the text "when is my next test", and the reply "Your next test is Biology on Friday." Each revealed step becomes a numbered chip under the part that performed it, so by the end the steps are grouped by owner. There is no animation: each step waits for you.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the previous step and the next job on the card.
  2. Predict the part that performs it: press Terminal, Network, or Server. Each step gets one prediction.
  3. Read the owner, the description, the data, and the feedback. Then press Next. Next stays disabled until you make a prediction.
  4. After step 8, press See summary to see your score and the steps grouped by owner.
  5. Press Restart to start again from step 1.

Mastery is 6 of 7 predictions correct. The running score is shown at the top right.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will explain which of three parts (terminal, network, server) performs each of the eight steps that carry a spoken question to a spoken answer, by predicting the owner of steps 2 to 8 with at least 6 of 7 correct (Bloom's Taxonomy: Understand, verb explain).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Students should have read the chapter section How the Terminal and Server Talk, which defines the agent terminal, the buddy server, the request-reply contract, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict before you look (8 minutes). Students step through all eight steps individually, committing to a prediction each time.
  2. Explain the pattern (5 minutes). Using the summary screen, students write one sentence explaining why the server owns steps 4, 5, and 6. The word "memory" should appear in a good answer.
  3. Trace a new question (5 minutes). Students write the data at each of the eight steps for a different question, such as "When is my lab report due?"

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. The network carries the request in step 3 but never reads it. Why is it useful that the Wi-Fi link does not need to understand the question?
  2. Which steps would change if the school replaced the brain in step 5 with a smarter one? Which steps would stay exactly the same?
  3. If your buddy stays silent, which step would you test first, and why?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The Pico decides the answer. Step 5 is owned by the server.
  • The microphone sends sound straight to the speaker. Six steps separate them.
  • The Wi-Fi link understands the question. Steps 3 and 7 only carry data.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: A student who predicts 6 or more of the 7 owners correctly has met the objective. Ask students below 6 to explain, for each missed step, which part has the needed memory or hardware.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture
  • Speech recognition on Wikipedia
  • Speech synthesis on Wikipedia
  • Client-server model on Wikipedia

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture.

Show the full specification 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** agent-data-flow-step-through<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/conversational-ai/tree/main/docs/sims/response-generation-architecture<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** explain<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will explain which of three parts (terminal, network, server) performs each of the eight steps that carry a spoken question to a spoken answer, by predicting the owner of steps 2 to 8 with at least 6 of 7 correct.

**Prerequisites:** agent terminal, buddy server, request-reply contract, speech-to-text, text-to-speech (all defined in the section "How the Terminal and Server Talk" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** Before each of steps 2 to 8 is revealed, the learner commits to the part that performs it: Terminal, Network, or Server. A prediction is correct when it matches the Owner column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct. Pressing Next without predicting is not allowed.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The Pico decides the answer. (2) The microphone sends sound straight to the speaker. (3) The Wi-Fi link understands the question.

**Instructional Rationale:** Understand-level explanation needs the learner to trace the process with concrete data. Step-through with prediction before reveal makes the learner reason about which part has the memory and the job, and the concrete values shown at each step prevent a vague answer. There is no animation, because animation would hide the data at each step.

**Content:**

The scenario is the question "When is my next test?" The learner sees these eight steps in order, with the data shown at each step:

| Step | What happens | Data shown | Owner | Why the owner (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The student speaks | The spoken words "When is my next test?" | Student | Shown to start the scenario, and not predicted. |
| 2 | The microphone captures sound as digital numbers | Illustrative sample values: 12, -40, 85, 130, 60, -25 | Terminal | The microphone is wired to the Pico, so the terminal captures the sound. |
| 3 | The request travels to the server | The request fields: device = desk-07, kind = question, plus the sound numbers | Network | The Wi-Fi link only carries the request. It does not read or change it. |
| 4 | The server converts speech to text | The text "when is my next test" | Server | Speech-to-text needs more memory than the Pico has, so the server does it. |
| 5 | The brain decides the reply | Event found: "TEST: Biology, Friday". Reply text: "Your next test is Biology on Friday." | Server | The calendar and the decision logic live on the server. |
| 6 | The server converts the reply to speech and packages it | The reply fields: speak = the sentence as audio, show = "Biology test: Friday" | Server | Text-to-speech also needs more memory than the Pico has. |
| 7 | The reply travels back to the terminal | The same reply fields moving from the server to desk-07 | Network | The Wi-Fi link only carries the reply. |
| 8 | The terminal shows and plays the reply | The display shows "Biology test: Friday". The speaker says "Your next test is Biology on Friday." | Terminal | The display and speaker are wired to the Pico, so the terminal outputs the reply. |

**Provenance:** An illustrative scenario written for this sim from the chapter section "How the Terminal and Server Talk". The sample values are illustrative and the sim labels them "illustrative".

**Rules:** There are eight steps and three owners. The prediction applies to steps 2 to 8, which is 7 predictions. A prediction is correct when it equals the Owner of that step. The score is the number of correct predictions, from 0 to 7. The correct owner is always revealed after the prediction, and the data for that step is then shown.

**Learner Activity:**

1. Step 1 is shown. The learner sees the spoken question.
2. For step 2 the learner chooses Terminal, Network, or Server.
3. The sim reveals the correct owner, the step description, and the data shown for that step, with the reason if the prediction was wrong.
4. The learner presses Next and repeats for steps 3 to 8.
5. After step 8, the sim shows a summary that groups the eight steps by owner and shows the score.

**Feedback:** Seven predictions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Owner>. <Why the owner>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The <Owner> does this step. <Why the owner>". The owner is revealed immediately after each prediction. A running score "n of 7" is shown.

**Starting State:** Step 1 is shown with the spoken question, the terminal and the server shown as separate parts, and the question "Which part performs step 2?"

**Chapter Anchors:** There are eight steps. Step 1 is the student's, two steps happen on the terminal (2 and 8), three happen on the server (4, 5, 6), and two happen on the network (3 and 7). The example question is "When is my next test?" and the example reply is "Your next test is Biology on Friday."

docs.title: Agent Hosting Trade-Off Explorer
docs.text: Run the Agent Hosting Trade-Off Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: Embed This MicroSim
docs.text:
Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/agent-hosting-tradeoff-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="667px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An agent has to run on a computer somewhere, and where it runs decides who controls it, what it costs, and who can see your data. The chapter compares three options, a cloud agent, a self-hosted agent, and a school-hosted agent, using four questions. This MicroSim asks you to use that comparison to make recommendations.

You read four illustrative scenarios, such as a coding club that wants to read and change its agent's code, or a family that wants audio to stay on the home network. For each one you first recommend a hosting option and then name the deciding factor, A to D:

  • A. Who runs the computer?
  • B. Who decides what data it can touch?
  • C. What is the typical cost pattern?
  • D. Who keeps it running?

The comparison table stays on screen but is not highlighted until you have made both choices. Then the decisive cell is highlighted in gold and the reason is shown. At the end, the table shows a numbered badge in the decisive cell for each scenario.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario on the card.
  2. In the first row of buttons, press Cloud agent, Self-hosted agent, or School-hosted agent.
  3. In the second row, press A, B, C, or D for the deciding factor. The factor buttons unlock after you choose an option. Each choice gets one attempt.
  4. Read the highlighted table cell and the feedback, then press Next scenario.
  5. After scenario 4, press See results to see your score and the decisive cells. Press Restart to try again.

A scenario counts as fully correct only when both the option and the factor are correct. Mastery is 3 of 4 scenarios fully correct.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will recommend one of three hosting options (cloud agent, self-hosted agent, school-hosted agent) for each of four scenarios and identify the deciding factor, with at least 3 of 4 scenarios fully correct (Bloom's Taxonomy: Evaluate, verb recommend).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Students should have read the chapter section Where an Agent Lives, including the table "Comparing the Three Hosting Options".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recommend and justify (8 minutes). Students complete the four scenarios individually.
  2. Defend a choice (7 minutes). In pairs, students pick the scenario they found hardest and argue for a different option. Their partner names the factor that rules it out.
  3. Write a scenario (5 minutes). Each student writes a fifth scenario where cost (factor C) is the deciding factor, then swaps with a partner.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Scenarios 3 and 4 have the same deciding factor but different options. What changes between them?
  2. Is a cloud agent ever the right choice? What would have to be true about the questions you ask it?
  3. A school-hosted agent is a self-hosted agent run by a school. What does a student gain and give up when the school runs it?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A cloud agent is always the best choice because it is easiest. Scenarios 2 to 4 favor other options.
  • Self-hosting is only for experts. Scenario 4 is a family.
  • Hosting only affects cost, not who sees the data. Factor B decides two of the four scenarios.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: A student with 3 or 4 scenarios fully correct has met the objective. For students who chose the right option but the wrong factor, ask them to point to the table cell that makes the difference.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture
  • Cloud computing on Wikipedia
  • Self-hosting (network) on Wikipedia

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture.

Show the full specification 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** agent-hosting-tradeoff-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** recommend<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will recommend one of three hosting options (cloud agent, self-hosted agent, school-hosted agent) for each of four scenarios and identify the deciding factor, with at least 3 of 4 scenarios fully correct.

**Prerequisites:** cloud agent, self-hosted agent, school-hosted agent, and the four comparison questions (all defined in the section "Where an Agent Lives" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each scenario, the learner first commits to a hosting option and then commits to the deciding factor from four choices. A scenario is fully correct when both choices match the Correct columns in Content. Mastery is 3 of 4 scenarios fully correct. Reading the comparison table is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A cloud agent is always the best choice because it is easiest. (2) Self-hosting is only for experts. (3) Hosting only affects cost, not who sees the data.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluate-level recommending requires the learner to weigh criteria against a situation. Choosing the option and then naming the one factor that decides it makes the learner justify the choice, and committing before the table is highlighted prevents simply reading the answer off.

**Content:**

The learner sees the four comparison questions as the factors, labeled A to D:

| Factor | Question |
|---|---|
| A | Who runs the computer? |
| B | Who decides what data it can touch? |
| C | What is the typical cost pattern? |
| D | Who keeps it running? |

The three options and their answers to the four factors are exactly the values in the chapter table "Comparing the Three Hosting Options". The learner sees four scenarios in this fixed order:

| # | Scenario shown to the learner | Correct option | Correct factor | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A student wants an agent today, with no setup, and the questions contain nothing private. | Cloud agent | D | The vendor keeps it running, so the student has nothing to maintain. |
| 2 | A coding club wants to learn how agents work by reading and changing the agent's code. | Self-hosted agent | A | The club runs the computer, so it can open and change the software. |
| 3 | A school wants every classroom device to announce the school calendar, with the school deciding what is kept. | School-hosted agent | B | One school server serves every device, and the school decides what data it touches. |
| 4 | A family wants an assistant whose audio never leaves their home network. | Self-hosted agent | B | The family decides what data the agent touches, and nothing goes to a vendor. |

**Provenance:** The options and factors come from the chapter section "Where an Agent Lives". The four scenarios are illustrative, written for this sim, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

**Rules:** An option answer is correct when it equals the Correct option for that scenario. A factor answer is correct when it equals the Correct factor. A scenario is fully correct only when both are correct. The score is the number of fully correct scenarios, from 0 to 4.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads scenario 1 and chooses one of the three options.
2. The learner chooses the deciding factor, A to D.
3. The sim then highlights the matching cells of the comparison table and shows the Why text.
4. The learner continues through scenarios 2 to 4 in the same way.
5. After scenario 4 the sim shows the score and the cells of the comparison table that were decisive in each scenario.

**Feedback:** Four scenarios, fixed order, one attempt for the option and one for the factor. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect option: "Not quite: <Why>". Incorrect factor with a correct option: "Right option. The deciding factor is <factor letter and question>: <Why>". The correct answers are revealed after both choices are made. A running count "Scenarios fully correct: n of 4" is shown.

**Starting State:** The comparison table is visible without highlights, scenario 1 is shown, and the question on screen is "Which option would you recommend?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter table "Comparing the Three Hosting Options" has four questions and three options with the exact values used in the Content. The chapter states that a cloud agent is run by a vendor, and that a school-hosted agent is a self-hosted agent run by a school.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The buddy server can grow through three agent progression levels while the desk terminal stays exactly the same:

  • Level 1 is a rule-based buddy server of about 100 lines with no LLM. It adds fixed rules and tools that read the school calendar.
  • Level 2 is the same server plus speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and one LLM call. It adds spoken input and output and free-form questions.
  • Level 3 is an optional open-source agent framework behind the same contract. It adds a ready-made planning loop, memory, and approval rules.

This MicroSim has two parts. In Part 1 you place eight abilities, one at a time, at the lowest level where each first appears. Each placement drops a numbered chip onto the correct rung of the ladder: green when you were right, orange when you missed it. In Part 2 you compare the replies the three levels give to the same question, "Do I have anything big coming up this week?", and see that the request and the reply fields never change. Only the reply text does.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the ability on the card.
  2. Press Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3. Each ability gets one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback, then press Next. Next stays disabled until you answer.
  4. After ability 8, press Compare replies to see your score.
  5. In Part 2, press each level button to see that level's reply. Compare the request box and the reply box across all three levels.
  6. Press Restart to start Part 1 again.

Mastery is 7 of 8 placements correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will differentiate the three agent progression levels by placing 8 abilities at the lowest level where each first appears, with at least 7 of 8 correct (Bloom's Taxonomy: Analyze, verb differentiate).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Students should have read the chapter section The Swappable Brain, which defines rule-based agents, LLM-backed agents, agent tools, agent memory, agent approval rules, open-source agent frameworks, and the three levels.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Place the abilities (8 minutes). Students complete Part 1 individually.
  2. Compare the replies (4 minutes). Students view all three replies in Part 2 and list what changed and what stayed the same.
  3. Explain the ladder (5 minutes). Students write one sentence for each level naming the single most important thing it adds.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Ability 2 uses a tool at Level 1. Why is it a mistake to think only Level 3 can use tools?
  2. The terminal code is identical at all three levels. What makes that possible?
  3. The Level 2 reply is more helpful than Level 1, but an LLM can produce a confident answer that is wrong. How does reading dates through a tool help?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Only Level 3 can use tools. Ability 2 appears at Level 1.
  • A higher level needs a different terminal. The request and reply fields in Part 2 are identical at every level.
  • An LLM always gives a correct answer. The chapter warns that confident is not correct; dates should come through a tool.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: A student with 7 or 8 correct placements has met the objective. Students below 7 should reread "Agent Progression Levels" and explain each missed ability using the "What it adds" column.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture.

Show the full specification 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** agent-progression-level-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-agent-anatomy<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** differentiate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will differentiate the three agent progression levels by placing 8 abilities at the lowest level where each first appears, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

**Prerequisites:** rule-based agent, LLM-backed agent, agent tools, agent memory, agent approval rules, open-source agent framework, and the three levels (all defined in the section "The Swappable Brain" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 abilities, the learner commits to Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct level column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. Comparing the three replies in the second part is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Only Level 3 can use tools. (2) A higher level needs a different terminal. (3) An LLM always gives a correct answer.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level differentiation requires the learner to tell which capability comes from which kind of brain. Placing each ability on the ladder after predicting, and then comparing the replies of all three levels to the same question, shows that the abilities differ while the request-reply contract stays the same.

**Content:**

The three levels are the values in the chapter table "Agent Progression Levels". The learner sees the abilities one at a time in this fixed order:

| # | Ability shown to the learner | Correct level | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Matches the question text against fixed rules a person wrote. | Level 1 | A rule-based server is made of exactly these rules. |
| 2 | Reads events from the school calendar using a tool. | Level 1 | Even the rule-based server calls tools when a rule says to. |
| 3 | Answers a question worded in a way no rule anticipated. | Level 2 | Interpreting free-form wording is what the LLM call adds. |
| 4 | Converts the student's speech to text and the reply back to speech. | Level 2 | Level 2 adds speech-to-text and text-to-speech. |
| 5 | Chooses for itself which tool to call for a new kind of request. | Level 2 | An LLM-backed agent can choose tools instead of following a rule. |
| 6 | Remembers a preferred reminder time between conversations using a ready-made memory feature. | Level 3 | A framework supplies memory so you do not build it yourself. |
| 7 | Asks for approval before a risky action using ready-made approval rules. | Level 3 | A framework supplies approval rules that apply before an action. |
| 8 | Runs a planning loop with tools, memory, and approvals supplied by a published toolkit. | Level 3 | That combination is what an open-source agent framework provides. |

After the eight placements, the learner compares replies. The question is "Do I have anything big coming up this week?" and the learner chooses a level to see its reply:

| Level | Reply shown |
|---|---|
| 1 | "Sorry, I only know about tests and due dates." |
| 2 | "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday." |
| 3 | "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday. I can set a reminder for Thursday at 7 pm. Should I?" |

For every level the sim also shows the same request and the same reply shape, with the fields `device`, `kind`, and `text` in the request and `speak`, `show`, and `next_mode` in the reply.

**Provenance:** The levels and the replies come from the chapter sections "Agent Progression Levels" and "The Swappable Brain". The calendar events are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

**Rules:** A placement is correct when it equals the Correct level for that ability. The score is the number of correct placements, from 0 to 8. The request and reply fields are identical for all three levels. Only the reply text differs.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads ability 1 and chooses Level 1, 2, or 3.
2. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, then the learner continues through ability 8.
3. After ability 8, the sim shows the score.
4. The learner chooses a level and reads its reply to the sample question, and does the same for the other two levels.
5. The learner should notice that the request and reply fields never change between levels.

**Feedback:** Eight abilities, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. This first appears at <correct level>: <Why>". The correct level is revealed immediately after each answer, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

**Starting State:** Ability 1 is shown with the three levels, and the question "At which level does this ability first appear?"

**Chapter Anchors:** There are three levels. Level 1 is about 100 lines and uses no LLM. Level 2 adds speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and one LLM call. Level 3 is an optional open-source agent framework. The terminal and the request-reply contract do not change between levels.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
In MicroPython, a statement allocates heap memory when it creates a new object that is not a small integer. Small integers (from -230 to 230 - 1 on the Pico's 32-bit port) live inside the value itself, and storing into an existing buffer never allocates. Everything else (floats, slices, lists, tuples, strings, big integers) creates garbage that the collector must clean up later.

This MicroSim shows twelve statements, one at a time. You choose Allocates or Does not allocate; the sim then shows either the new object appearing on the heap or the existing value or buffer that was written, with the reason. After statement 12 it lists the statements you got wrong. The answers are predictions from the MicroPython object model for the Pico's 32-bit port, labeled "expected" until 03-allocation-and-floats.py has been run on the kit.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
The MicroSim opens in its starting state and nothing moves until you act.

  • Allocates / Does not allocate: Choose your answer. One attempt per statement.
  • Next statement / See results: Move on after the feedback.
  • Start over: Return to statement 1 with a fresh score.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will distinguish 12 MicroPython statements that allocate heap memory from those that do not, with at least 10 of 12 correct.

Bloom's Taxonomy level: Analyze (distinguish)

docs.title: Audience and Duration
docs.text: High school students (grades 9-12) building the Open Study Buddy; about 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: heap, garbage collection, small integer, float object, typed array, pre-allocated buffer, memoryview (defined in Chapter 2 and in this chapter above the block).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Read the rule at the top of this page, then predict statements 1 and 2 aloud before choosing.
  2. Guided practice (5 min): After each wrong answer, name the object that was created (or the buffer that was written) before moving on.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Complete all twelve statements. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text: (1) Any arithmetic is free. (2) A slice never copies. (3) Floats are stored inside the value, like small integers. (4) Writing into an array allocates.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. What do all the statements that do not allocate have in common?
  2. A memoryview slice copies no data. Why does it still allocate?
  3. Why would statement 11 give a different answer on a 64-bit computer?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The quiz inside the MicroSim is the evidence of mastery: each item is scored on the first attempt only, the correct answer and its reason are shown after every submission, and the final screen reports the score against the mastery threshold.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
Full specification from Chapter 10 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** allocation-classifier<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish 12 MicroPython statements that allocate heap memory from those that do not, with at least 10 of 12 correct.

**Prerequisites:** heap, garbage collection, small integer, float object, typed array, pre-allocated buffer, memoryview (defined in Chapter 2 and in this chapter above the block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 12 statements the learner chooses "Allocates" or "Does not allocate" and submits before the answer is shown. A choice is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading the Why text after an answer is feedback, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Any arithmetic is free. (2) A slice never copies. (3) Floats are stored inside the value, like small integers. (4) Writing into an array allocates.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level distinction asks the learner to separate cases by a hidden property, whether a new object is created, using the object model rather than memorized examples. Committing before the answer is shown makes the learner apply the model, and the Why text names the object that is created, which is what the learner needs for the next unfamiliar statement.

**Content:**

The 12 statements are shown one at a time in this order, each with its answer. The answers are what MicroPython's object model predicts for the Pico's 32-bit chip; `03-allocation-and-floats.py` measures them on the board.

| # | Statement | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `x = x + 1` (x is a small whole number) | Does not allocate | A small integer lives inside the value itself. |
| 2 | `y = y * 1.0001` (y is a float) | Allocates | The float result is a new heap object. |
| 3 | `arr_f[3] = arr_f[3] * 1.0001` (arr_f is array('f')) | Allocates | Reading an element makes a float object, and so does the product. |
| 4 | `arr_h[3] = (arr_h[3] * 3) >> 1` (arr_h is array('h')) | Does not allocate | Every value is a small integer. |
| 5 | `part = buf[0:8]` (buf is a bytearray) | Allocates | A slice of a bytearray is a new bytearray. |
| 6 | `part = view[0:8]` (view is a memoryview) | Allocates | A memoryview slice is a new, small memoryview object, though it copies no data. |
| 7 | `t = [0] * 16` | Allocates | A new list is created. |
| 8 | `t = struct.unpack("<4i", words)` | Allocates | A new tuple holds the four results. |
| 9 | `struct.pack_into("<i", words, 0, 7)` | Does not allocate | It writes into memory the program already owns. |
| 10 | `s = "%d" % 12345` | Allocates | A new string is built. |
| 11 | `z = big + 1` (big is 2**30) | Allocates | 2**30 does not fit a 31-bit small integer on a 32-bit chip, so the value is a big-integer object. |
| 12 | `buf[5] = 77` | Does not allocate | It stores into a byte of an existing bytearray. |

**Provenance:** The answers are predictions from the MicroPython object model on a 32-bit port with the default object layout (source: `ports/rp2/mpconfigport.h`, which sets single-precision floats and does not override the object representation). They are labelled "expected" in the sim until `03-allocation-and-floats.py` has been run on the kit. Statement 11 depends on a 31-bit small integer and is not true on a 64-bit computer; the sim says so.

**Rules:** A statement allocates when it creates a new object that is not a small integer. A small integer is a whole number from -2**30 to 2**30 - 1. Storing into an existing buffer never allocates.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads statement 1 and chooses Allocates or Does not allocate.
2. The sim shows the answer and the Why text, and a running score.
3. The learner continues through statement 12.
4. After statement 12, the sim lists the statements the learner got wrong. The learner should notice that the safe statements either work on small integers or write into an existing buffer.

**Feedback:** 12 statements, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. <Answer>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 12" is shown.

**Starting State:** Statement 1 is shown with the question "Does this line create a new object?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that floats allocate, small integers do not, a bytearray slice copies, a memoryview slice makes a small object, `struct.pack_into` writes in place, and that the predictions are confirmed on the kit by `03-allocation-and-floats.py`.

docs.text:
1. Maximising MicroPython speed - MicroPython documentation - Avoiding allocation in fast code.
  2. MicroPython on microcontrollers - MicroPython documentation - The heap, garbage collection and pre-allocated buffers.
  3. Garbage collection (computer science) - Wikipedia - Why freeing objects costs time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The microphone delivers one 2,048-byte frame every 40 ms into a ring buffer that holds about 9.77 frames (0.39 s). The main loop does P milliseconds of work and then reads one frame. If P is 40 ms or less the loop keeps up; if it is longer, a backlog grows by (P / 40 - 1) frames every pass until the ring overflows and audio is lost.

The graph shows the backlog after each pass against the ring capacity, and marks the pass and time of the first lost audio. In explore mode you move P from 10 to 100 ms. In the quiz you calculate, for six loop timings, how many seconds pass before audio is lost, or type "never". This is a model based on one board's measurement of the ring depth; the 130 ms timing is the measured full-screen update time from Chapter 5.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
The MicroSim opens in its starting state and nothing moves until you act.

  • Start the 6 timings / Back to explore: Switch between the slider and the quiz.
  • Answer box and Submit: Type seconds (within 0.1 s) or never. One attempt per timing.
  • Next timing / See score: Move on after the feedback.
  • Time per pass P slider: Explore only: 10 to 100 ms in steps of 0.1 ms, default 40.0 ms.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will examine 6 loop timings against the 40 ms frame budget to decide whether each keeps up with the microphone and, for those that do not, calculate the time until the first audio is lost, to within 0.1 s.

Bloom's Taxonomy level: Analyze (examine)

docs.title: Audience and Duration
docs.text: High school students (grades 9-12) building the Open Study Buddy; about 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: audio frame, ring buffer, frame time budget, backlog (all defined in the sections above this block). The model is stated in the Rules field and shown on screen.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Move P from 40.0 to 41.0 ms and then to 60 ms. Record how long each runs before audio is lost.
  2. Guided practice (5 min): For timing 3, write the growth per pass, divide the ring capacity by it, and multiply the pass count by 45 ms before submitting.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Complete all six timings. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text: (1) A loop that takes slightly longer than the frame is fine because the buffer is big. (2) A loop that is faster than the frame wastes audio. (3) The ring holds all the audio forever.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. A loop only 5 ms too slow still loses audio within 3.6 s. Why does a big ring not save it?
  2. Why does a loop faster than 40 ms not waste audio?
  3. What changes in the graph if the ring were twice as deep?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The quiz inside the MicroSim is the evidence of mastery: each item is scored on the first attempt only, the correct answer and its reason are shown after every submission, and the final screen reports the score against the mastery threshold.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
Full specification from Chapter 8 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** audio-frame-budget-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** examine<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will examine 6 loop timings against the 40 ms frame budget to decide whether each keeps up with the microphone and, for those that do not, calculate the time until the first audio is lost, to within 0.1 s.

**Prerequisites:** audio frame, ring buffer, frame time budget, backlog (all defined in the sections above this block). The model is stated in the Rules field and shown on screen.

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 6 timings the learner types the seconds until the first sample is lost, or "never". An answer is correct when it equals "never" where the Answer column says never, or is within 0.1 s of the number in the Answer column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Changing the exploration slider and watching the backlog is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A loop that takes slightly longer than the frame is fine because the buffer is big. (2) A loop that is faster than the frame wastes audio. (3) The ring holds all the audio forever.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level examination requires the learner to relate parts of the system (the producer, the ring, the consumer) and reason about how a small rate difference accumulates. Using the same formula on six timings lets the learner see which one is the borderline case and why.

**Content:**

The model: one audio frame is 2,048 bytes and arrives every 40 ms. The ring holds 9.765625 frames (the depth measured in `03-ring-latency.py`, equal to 40,000 bytes at 8 bytes per sample time: 5,000 sample times, or 0.390625 s). Each pass of the loop takes P milliseconds of work and then reads one frame. If the loop is faster than 40 ms, it waits for the frame.

| # | Time per pass P (ms) | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30 | never | The loop is faster than 40 ms, so it waits for each frame and the backlog stays at zero. |
| 2 | 40 | never | The loop exactly matches the audio rate, so there is no growth. |
| 3 | 45 | 3.56 | Growth 0.125 frames per pass, so it passes 9.77 frames on pass 79, and 79 x 45 ms = 3.56 s. |
| 4 | 50 | 2.0 | Growth 0.25 frames per pass, so it passes 9.77 on pass 40, and 40 x 50 ms = 2.0 s. |
| 5 | 60 | 1.2 | Growth 0.5 frames per pass, so it passes 9.77 on pass 20, and 20 x 60 ms = 1.2 s. |
| 6 | 130 | 0.65 | Growth 2.25 frames per pass, so it passes 9.77 on pass 5, and 5 x 130 ms = 0.65 s. |

For exploration the learner sets P from 10 to 100 ms in steps of 0.1 ms, default 40.0 ms. The sim shows the backlog in frames growing against the capacity of 9.765625 frames.

**Provenance:** The frame size and ring size are the values in `src/kits/study-buddy-base/config.py` (`FFT_SIZE`, `MIC_SAMPLE_RATE`, `MIC_BUFFER_BYTES`). The ring depth of 9.765625 frames comes from a measurement on the test board at 50 ms per pass (the delay stopped growing near 460 ms), and its cause is not confirmed. The model is a simplification, and the sim labels it "model, based on one board's measurement." The 130 ms value is the measured full-screen update time from Chapter 5.

**Rules:** Let T be the larger of P and 40 ms. The backlog after n passes is n x (T / 40 - 1) frames. The first sample is lost at the first whole number n for which the backlog is greater than 9.765625, and the time is n x T. If T equals 40, nothing is ever lost. Times are shown in seconds to two decimal places.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner moves the slider and watches the backlog line rise or stay flat against the capacity line.
2. The learner starts the 6 timings. Timing 1 is shown.
3. The learner types the seconds until the first loss, or "never," and submits.
4. The sim draws the backlog line for that timing and shows the Why text.
5. After timing 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that a loop only 5 ms too slow still loses audio within 3.6 seconds.

**Feedback:** 6 timings, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is <answer>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

**Starting State:** The slider is at 40.0 ms with the backlog flat at zero, and the question "How long can this loop run before audio is lost?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that a frame is 512 samples, 2,048 bytes, and 40 ms; that the microphone ring was created with 40,000 bytes but measured about 9.8 frames (0.4 s) deep; and that a 50 ms pass loses audio after about 2.0 s while a 130 ms pass loses it after about 0.65 s.

docs.text:
1. Circular buffer - Wikipedia - How a ring buffer holds data between a producer and a consumer.
  2. Real-time computing - Wikipedia - Deadlines and why missing one loses data.
  3. machine.I2S - MicroPython documentation - The ibuf ring buffer used by the microphone driver.

docs.title: Bit Depth Quantizer
docs.text:
Run the Bit Depth Quantizer MicroSim Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/bit-depth-quantizer/main.html" width="100%" height="502px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Bit depth sets how many different values each audio sample can take. With n bits there are 2n levels, spread evenly from -1.0 to +1.0. This MicroSim draws one cycle of a sine wave in gray and its quantized version in blue: each point is rounded to the nearest level, so the smooth curve becomes a staircase.

The level count, the step between levels, 2 / (levels - 1), and the largest rounding error, half a step, are all computed from the slider. A sample exactly halfway between two levels rounds up. Move from 1 bit to 16 bits and watch the staircase get finer as the level count doubles with every bit.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Move the Bit depth slider from 1 to 16 bits. Read the level count and the step size under the plot.
  2. Press Start challenges. Type a whole number without commas and press Submit or Enter.
  3. A wrong first answer gets a hint, and you can try once more. After a second wrong answer the sim shows the answer and counts the question as missed.
  4. Press Next question to continue. After question 5 press Show score.

While a challenge question is open, the slider is locked and the level count is hidden, so the answer comes from your own calculation. Mastery is 5 of 5 correct within two attempts each.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will calculate the number of levels available at a given bit depth, and the smallest bit depth that provides a required number of levels.

docs.title: Warm-Up (3 minutes)
docs.text: Ask: "How many different patterns can you make with 1 light switch? With 2? With 3?" Build the doubling table on the board up to 4 switches.

docs.title: Guided Exploration (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Students move the slider one bit at a time from 1 to 8 and record the level count each time.
  2. Ask: "Each extra bit adds how many levels?" Students should see that the count doubles rather than growing by a fixed amount.
  3. At 16 bits, ask why the staircase looks identical to the sine wave.

docs.title: Challenge (7 minutes)
docs.text: Students answer the five challenge questions. For question 5, have them show the two powers of two that bracket 1,000.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Does a higher bit depth make a note's pitch more accurate? What does it improve instead?
  2. Is 8-bit audio "half as good" as 16-bit audio? Compare 256 and 65,536 levels.
  3. The Pico's ADC has 12 bits. How many levels can it report?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The sim records up to two attempts for each of 5 questions. Mastery is 5 of 5 correct. Moving the slider is exploration, not evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Audio bit depth - Wikipedia overview of bit depth, levels and dynamic range.
  2. Quantization (signal processing) - Wikipedia article on rounding samples to levels and quantization error.
  3. Power of two - Wikipedia table of powers of two used in the challenges.

docs.title: Related Resources
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: Sound and Digital Audio
Original specification

Type: microsim sim-id: bit-depth-quantizer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the number of levels available at a given bit depth, and the smallest bit depth that provides a required number of levels, for 5 challenge questions, with all 5 correct within two attempts each.

Prerequisites: bit depth, levels, quantization error, powers of two (all defined in the section "Bit Depth" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 5 challenge questions the learner types a number. An answer is correct when it equals the Answer column in Content exactly. Mastery is 5 of 5 correct, with up to two attempts per question. Moving the bit-depth control and watching the staircase is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Each extra bit adds a fixed number of levels instead of doubling them. (2) A higher bit depth makes the sound's pitch more accurate. (3) 8 bits is half as good as 16 bits.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation of 2 to the power n needs repeated practice with a check. Seeing the staircase get finer as the number of levels doubles gives the learner a mental picture to check the arithmetic against.

Content:

The sim draws one cycle of a sine wave and the staircase of its quantized version. The learner chooses the bit depth for exploration: minimum 1, maximum 16, step 1, unit bits, default 4. The sim shows the number of levels for the chosen bit depth after the learner changes it.

Challenge questions, in this order:

# Question Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 How many levels does 3-bit audio have? 8 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. 2 How many levels does 8-bit audio have? 256 2 to the power 8 is 256. 3 How many levels does the Pico's 12-bit ADC have? 4096 2 to the power 12 is 4,096. 4 How many levels does 16-bit audio have? 65536 2 to the power 16 is 65,536. 5 What is the smallest bit depth with at least 1,000 levels? 10 2 to the power 9 is 512, which is too few, and 2 to the power 10 is 1,024.

Provenance: The levels follow from the formula levels = 2 to the power n given in the chapter. The 12-bit figure is the RP2350 ADC resolution mentioned in the chapter.

Rules: levels = 2 to the power n. The quantized value of a sample x between -1.0 and +1.0 is the nearest of the evenly spaced levels between -1.0 and +1.0, with spacing 2 / (levels - 1). A sample exactly halfway between two levels rounds up. Answers are whole numbers typed without commas.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the bit-depth control from 1 to 16 and watches the staircase get finer and the level count double each step.
  2. The learner starts the challenges and types an answer to question 1.
  3. The sim says whether the answer is correct. After a wrong first answer, the learner may try once more.
  4. After a second wrong answer, the sim shows the answer and the Why text, and the question counts as missed.
  5. After question 5, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that adding one bit always doubles the number of levels.

Feedback: 5 questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ". First incorrect: "Not quite. Think about doubling for each bit. Try again." Second incorrect: "The answer is : ". A running score "n of 5" is shown.

Starting State: The sine wave and its 4-bit staircase are shown with the text "16 levels" and the question "What happens to the staircase as you add bits?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that n bits give 2 to the power n levels, that 16 bits give 65,536 levels, and that each extra bit adds about 6 dB.

docs.title: Embed This MicroSim
docs.text:
Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/chatbot-or-agent-sorter/main.html" width="100%" height="564px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A chatbot answers one message at a time. A personal agent uses tools, works in several steps, acts without being asked at that moment, and comes back for a decision before it changes something that affects you. This MicroSim turns that definition into ten quick decisions.

Each card describes one illustrative behavior, such as "Tells a joke when asked" or "Sends an alert to the student's desk device when a test is one day away." You sort it into Chatbot behavior or Agent behavior. The sim tells you right away whether you were right and gives a one-sentence reason that names the trait involved. Each answered behavior becomes a numbered chip in its correct bin: green when you sorted it correctly, orange when you missed it.

After the tenth behavior, a summary shows your score and lists every behavior you missed, with its correct bin and the reason.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the behavior on the card.
  2. Press Chatbot behavior or Agent behavior. Each behavior gets one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback, then press Next. Next stays disabled until you choose a bin.
  4. After behavior 10, press See results to see your score and the behaviors you missed.
  5. Press Restart to practice the same ten behaviors in a new random order.

The first run uses a fixed order and is the only run that counts toward mastery. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will distinguish chatbot behaviors from personal-agent behaviors by classifying 10 described behaviors, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt (Bloom's Taxonomy: Analyze, verb distinguish).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Students should have read the chapter section What Is a Personal Agent?, which defines personal agent, chatbot, tool, and multi-step work.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 minutes). Ask students to name one app that "talks" to them. Is it a chatbot or an agent? Record their guesses without correcting them.
  2. First run (5 minutes). Students complete the sorter individually. The first run is their evidence of mastery, so they should not restart before finishing.
  3. Rule check (5 minutes). For each missed behavior, students write which of the four agent signs it shows or lacks: uses a tool to act, works in more than one step, acts without being prompted at that moment, or asks for approval before acting.
  4. Practice run (3 minutes). Students press Restart and sort the shuffled behaviors again.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Behaviors 3 and 4 both involve talking. Why is one a chatbot behavior and the other an agent behavior?
  2. Many agents contain a chatbot-style language model inside. Does that make every agent a chatbot? Use the chapter's test: does it only reply, or does it act?
  3. Which of the agent behaviors would you want your Study Buddy to ask permission for first? Why?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any program that talks is an agent. Behaviors 1, 7, and 10 talk but take no action.
  • A chatbot that sounds smart is an agent. Rewriting or summarizing pasted text is still one request and one reply.
  • An agent must be a robot or a physical device. Behavior 6 is software acting on a schedule.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: A student who scores 8 or more on the first run has met the objective. For students below 8, review the missed-behavior list together and ask them to explain each reason in their own words before a practice run.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture
  • Software agent on Wikipedia
  • Chatbot on Wikipedia

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture.

Show the full specification 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** chatbot-or-agent-sorter<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/conversational-ai/tree/main/docs/sims/chat-interface-anatomy<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish chatbot behaviors from personal-agent behaviors by classifying 10 described behaviors, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

**Prerequisites:** personal agent, chatbot, tool, multi-step work (all defined in the section "What Is a Personal Agent?" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 10 behaviors, the learner commits to one of two bins, "Chatbot behavior" or "Agent behavior". A classification is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct. Reading a behavior without committing is not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Any program that talks is an agent. (2) A chatbot that sounds smart is an agent. (3) An agent must be a robot or a physical device.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level distinguishing requires the learner to apply the three traits to new cases rather than recite them. A forced two-way choice on concrete behaviors makes the learner decide which trait is present, and the one-sentence reason after each answer names the trait.

**Content:**

The learner sees the behaviors one at a time in this fixed order:

| # | Behavior shown to the learner | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Answers one typed question, then waits for the next message. | Chatbot behavior | It replies to a single message and takes no further action. |
| 2 | Reads the school calendar, finds a test, and adds a reminder for the night before. | Agent behavior | It uses a tool and acts in several steps without being asked for each one. |
| 3 | Explains what a "TEST:" event is when asked, with no access to any calendar. | Chatbot behavior | It gives information only and takes no action for the person. |
| 4 | Asks "Should I move your study session to 6 pm?" before changing the schedule. | Agent behavior | It comes back for a decision before an action that affects the person. |
| 5 | Rewrites a paragraph that the student pastes in. | Chatbot behavior | One request produces one reply, and the work ends there. |
| 6 | Checks every morning for new due dates and announces them. | Agent behavior | It acts on its own over time on the person's behalf. |
| 7 | Tells a joke when asked. | Chatbot behavior | It produces a reply only. |
| 8 | Sends an alert to the student's desk device when a test is one day away. | Agent behavior | It takes an action through a tool, without being asked at that moment. |
| 9 | Remembers that the student prefers 7 pm reminders and schedules the next reminder for 7 pm. | Agent behavior | It uses what it remembers to take an action on the person's behalf. |
| 10 | Summarizes a news article that the student pastes in. | Chatbot behavior | One request produces one reply, and no action follows. |

**Provenance:** Illustrative behaviors written for this sim from the chapter section "What Is a Personal Agent?". The sim labels them "illustrative".

**Rules:** A behavior belongs in "Agent behavior" when it includes at least one of these: it uses a tool to take an action, it works in more than one step, it acts without being prompted at that moment, or it asks for approval before an action. Otherwise it belongs in "Chatbot behavior". The score is the count of correct classifications, from 0 to 10.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads behavior 1 and chooses a bin.
2. The sim shows whether the choice was correct and the reason from the Why column, then the learner continues to the next behavior.
3. After behavior 10, the sim shows the score and lists each missed behavior with its reason.
4. The learner can restart with the same 10 behaviors in a new random order. Only the first run counts as evidence.

**Feedback:** Ten items, fixed order on the first run, one attempt per item. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite: <Why>". The correct bin is revealed immediately after each answer. A running score "n of 10" is shown after every answer.

**Starting State:** Behavior 1 is shown with the two bins and the question "Is this a chatbot behavior or an agent behavior?"

**Chapter Anchors:** A chatbot answers one message at a time. An agent uses tools, works in several steps, and comes back when it needs a decision.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 14: Streaming Speech, Security, and Network Resilience.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** chunk-heap-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** examine<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will examine 8 upload designs to decide whether each fits in a given free heap and, for those that fit, how many sends it needs, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

**Prerequisites:** 16-bit and 32-bit recording sizes, memoryview slice, chunk, free heap, contiguous block (all defined in this chapter above this block and in Chapter 2).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 cases the learner chooses "fits" or "does not fit", and for a case that fits, types the number of sends. A case is correct when the choice matches the Fits column and, for fitting cases, the number matches the Sends column exactly. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Moving the explorer's sliders is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Sending in chunks makes the recording itself smaller. (2) Joining the header and body is harmless because the recording is already in memory. (3) A bigger free heap total always means a big block is available. (4) Streaming needs the whole recording in memory.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level examination requires the learner to break a design into the blocks it needs and compare them with what is available. Using the same rule on eight designs lets the learner see which designs move the memory problem, rather than remove it.

**Content:**

Four designs are described. In each, S is the length in seconds, R16 is the 16-bit recording size \( S \times 25{,}600 \) bytes, and R32 is the 32-bit size \( S \times 51{,}200 \) bytes.

| Design | Description | Largest memory it needs |
|---|---|---|
| A | Record 16-bit. Join the header and the body into one bytes object, then send it once. | Two blocks of R16 at the same time: \( 2 \times R16 \) in all, the largest single block R16 |
| B | Record 16-bit. Send the header, then send the recording in slices of a chunk size K bytes. | R16 for the recording, plus a small K-byte staging area: \( R16 + K \) in all, the largest single block R16 |
| C | Record 32-bit, convert in place after release, send the first half in slices of K bytes. | R32 for the buffer, plus K: \( R32 + K \) in all, the largest single block R32 |
| D | Stream each 1,024-byte frame as it is converted and keep nothing. | One 1,024-byte staging frame, at any length of speech |

The rule: a case fits when the total memory the design needs is no more than the free heap F minus a reserve of 40,000 bytes, which stands for the code, display, and network buffers. The number of sends is the length divided by the chunk size, rounded up (for design D, the frames of 1,024 bytes).

| # | Design | S (s) | K (bytes) | F (bytes) | Fits | Sends | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | B | 3 | 2,048 | 180,000 | fits | 38 | R16 is 76,800; plus 2,048 is 78,848, under 140,000. 76,800 / 2,048 is 37.5, rounded up to 38. |
| 2 | B | 5 | 2,048 | 180,000 | fits | 63 | R16 is 128,000; plus 2,048 is 130,048, under 140,000. 128,000 / 2,048 is 62.5, rounded up to 63. |
| 3 | A | 5 | not used | 180,000 | does not fit | none | The join needs 128,000 + 128,000 = 256,000, over 140,000. |
| 4 | C | 5 | 2,048 | 180,000 | does not fit | none | R32 is 256,000, over 140,000 by itself. |
| 5 | C | 3 | 2,048 | 260,000 | fits | 38 | R32 is 153,600; plus 2,048 is 155,648, under 220,000. The first half to send is 76,800 bytes: 38 sends. |
| 6 | B | 10 | 2,048 | 260,000 | does not fit | none | R16 is 256,000, over 220,000. |
| 7 | D | 10 | 1,024 | 100,000 | fits | 250 | One 1,024-byte frame needs no recording. 10 s is 256,000 bytes: 256,000 / 1,024 is 250 frames. |
| 8 | B | 5 | 8,192 | 180,000 | fits | 16 | R16 is 128,000; plus 8,192 is 136,192, under 140,000. 128,000 / 8,192 is 15.6, rounded up to 16. |

For exploration the learner sets S from 1 to 10 s in steps of 1 s (default 5), K from 512 to 8,192 bytes in the five sizes of the chapter's table (default 2,048), and F from 100,000 to 260,000 bytes in steps of 10,000 (default 180,000), and sees each design's memory need drawn against the free heap with the reserve.

**Provenance:** The recording sizes follow from the kit's 12,800 samples per second, with 4 bytes per sample for 32-bit words and 2 for 16-bit samples (`config.MIC_SAMPLE_RATE`). The reserve of 40,000 bytes and the free heap values are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative." The learner's own free heap comes from Chapter 2's memory report.

**Rules:** Total need and largest block follow the Largest memory column. A case fits when the total need is at most \( F - 40{,}000 \). Sends are \( \lceil \text{bytes to send} / K \rceil \), where the bytes to send are R16 for designs A and B, R16 (the converted half) for design C, and \( S \times 25{,}600 \) split into 1,024-byte frames for design D. A design that does not fit has no send count.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner moves the three sliders and watches each design's bar against the free heap line.
2. The learner starts the 8 cases. Case 1 is shown.
3. The learner chooses fits or does not fit and, if it fits, types the number of sends.
4. The sim draws the case's memory need against the free heap and shows the Why text.
5. After case 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that designs A and C fail at 5 s where design B fits, and that design D fits at any length.

**Feedback:** 8 cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. It <fits or does not fit><, with N sends if it fits>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

**Starting State:** Design B at 5 s, 2,048 bytes, and 180,000 free is drawn, with the question "Does this fit in the free heap, and how many sends does it need?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that a 5 s recording is 128,000 bytes in 16-bit and 256,000 in 32-bit, that joining the head and body needs a second block as large as the recording, that 2,048-byte chunks make 63 sends for 5 s, and that a WebSocket frame header is 8 bytes.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 16: Configuring the School Agent and Calendar.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** daily-briefing-composer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** apply<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will apply the daily briefing rules to 8 Cedar Ridge events on the morning of Monday, October 19, 2026, by sorting each into the part of the briefing it appears in or "Not mentioned," with at least 7 of the 8 correct.

**Prerequisites:** daily briefing, event category, today's events, next test, due soon, upcoming_days, max_items (all defined in the section "The Daily Briefing and Reminders" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 events, in order, the learner chooses one of four places: Today, Next test, Due soon, or Not mentioned, then submits. A choice is correct when it equals the Answer column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first submission of each event. Changing the date or the settings afterward in exploration is not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The briefing lists every upcoming event. (2) A test on the same day goes under "Next test." (3) A due date 10 days away is "due soon." (4) A test tomorrow is not mentioned because it is not today.

**Instructional Rationale:** Applying rules to cases needs cases that sit on each side of every rule boundary: today versus later, a category the briefing reads versus one it ignores, inside versus outside the window. The learner commits a place for each event before the briefing text is shown, so a misread rule appears as a wrong place.

**Content:**

The settings for the exercise are fixed: today is Monday 2026-10-19, `max_items` = 3, `upcoming_days` = 7. The rules: "Today" holds today's events of category test, due, event, sports, or academic, up to 3. "Next test" is the first test after today and within 7 days. "Due soon" holds due events after today and within 7 days, up to 3. Everything else is "Not mentioned." Events of category no-school do not appear in the briefing.

The 8 events, in order:

| # | Event (title, date, category) | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|-------------------------------|--------|-------------------------|
| 1 | Picture Retake Day, Mon Oct 19, event | Today | It is today and its category is event. |
| 2 | TEST: Algebra II Unit 3 - Quadratics, Tue Oct 20 8:00 AM, test | Next test | It is the first test after today, 1 day away. |
| 3 | DUE: English 10 personal narrative draft, Wed Oct 21, due | Due soon | A due date 2 days away is inside the 7-day window. |
| 4 | DUE: Biology osmosis lab report, Thu Oct 22, due | Due soon | 3 days away, and it is the second due item, within the limit of 3. |
| 5 | Football vs. Eastbrook Eagles, Fri Oct 23, sports | Not mentioned | A sports event is announced only on its own day. |
| 6 | Maker Club: Study Buddy Build Night, Mon Oct 26 3:30 PM, event | Not mentioned | An event on a later day is not in the briefing. It is also 7 days away, at the edge of the window. |
| 7 | TEST: Biology Unit 2 - Genetics, Tue Nov 10 10:02 AM, test | Not mentioned | 22 days away, outside the 7-day window. |
| 8 | End of Quarter 1, Fri Oct 30, academic | Not mentioned | An academic milestone is announced only on its own day. |

After the last event, the sim shows the composed briefing for these rules: "Good morning from Cedar Ridge. Picture Retake Day is today. Location: Library. Your next Algebra II test is tomorrow at 8 AM. English 10 personal narrative draft is due on Wednesday. Biology osmosis lab report is due on Thursday. Griffins aim high!"

**Provenance:** The events and dates are from the real Cedar Ridge calendar (`docs/schools/cedar-ridge-high-school/calendar.ics`). The rules and the final text come from `src/chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/server/compose.py` and are checked by `test_pipeline.py`.

**Rules:** An event is "Today" if its date range includes the briefing date and its category is test, due, event, sports, or academic, counting up to `max_items`. "Next test" is the earliest event of category test with a start date after today and a start before today plus `upcoming_days` days. "Due soon" is events of category due with a start date after today and before today plus `upcoming_days` days, up to `max_items`. For exploration the learner may change the date to any school day of 2026-2027 (weekends and no-school days produce no briefing), `max_items` from 1 to 5 in steps of 1 (default 3), and `upcoming_days` from 1 to 14 in steps of 1 (default 7); the text is rebuilt by the same rules. The mascot line is added last and dropped first if the text would exceed 300 characters.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads the rules and the 8 events, then opens exploration, changes `upcoming_days` and the date, and watches which events enter or leave the briefing.
2. The learner starts the 8 events. Event 1 is shown with the four places.
3. The learner chooses a place and submits.
4. The sim shows the correct place and the Why text, and adds or leaves out the event's sentence in the briefing being built.
5. After event 8, the sim shows the score and the complete briefing. The learner should notice that only 4 of the 8 events are spoken, and that sports and academic events appear only on their own day.

**Feedback:** 8 events, fixed order, one choice each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. This event goes in <answer>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

**Starting State:** The 8 events are listed with the settings (today Monday 2026-10-19, 3 items, 7 days) and the question "Which part of the briefing is this event in?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's briefing for 2026-10-19 is the text shown above, 361 bytes as published; the sim reproduces its wording. The chapter states that the briefing is not sent on weekends or no-school days, and that the mascot line is added last.
