docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 14: Streaming Speech, Security, and Network Resilience.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** retry-backoff-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the longest time a request can take under 8 retry settings, to within 0.05 s, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

**Prerequisites:** timeout, retry, exponential backoff, ceiling, attempt (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 settings the learner types the worst-case total time in seconds. An answer is correct when it is within 0.05 s of the number in the Answer column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Dragging the explorer's controls and watching the timeline is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The wait doubles for ever. (2) The last attempt is followed by a wait. (3) Jitter makes the worst case longer. (4) The waits are the only time a retry costs.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation requires the learner to carry out the worst-case formula on new numbers. Seeing the same attempts laid out on a timeline, with the waits and the timeouts as separate segments, shows what each term in the formula stands for and why the last attempt has no wait after it.

**Content:**

The model: a request makes up to N attempts. Every attempt fails by timing out after T seconds. After each failed attempt except the last, the device waits. The wait after failed attempt k (k = 0 for the first) has a ceiling of \( \min(\text{cap}, \text{base} \times 2^k) \). The worst case is every attempt timing out and every wait taking its full ceiling, so the worst-case total is \( N \times T + \sum_{k=0}^{N-2} \min(\text{cap}, \text{base} \times 2^k) \). With jitter, each actual wait is a random number from 0 up to its ceiling, and never above it.

| # | Base (ms) | Cap (ms) | Attempts N | Timeout T (s) | Answer (s) | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 500 | 8,000 | 4 | 8 | 35.5 | 4 x 8 = 32 s of timeouts, plus waits of 0.5 + 1 + 2 = 3.5 s. |
| 2 | 500 | 8,000 | 3 | 5 | 16.5 | 3 x 5 = 15 s, plus waits of 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 s. |
| 3 | 1,000 | 4,000 | 5 | 3 | 26 | 5 x 3 = 15 s, plus waits of 1 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 11 s: the fourth wait would be 8 s but is capped at 4 s. |
| 4 | 500 | 2,000 | 4 | 2 | 11.5 | 4 x 2 = 8 s, plus waits of 0.5 + 1 + 2 = 3.5 s. |
| 5 | 250 | 8,000 | 6 | 4 | 31.75 | 6 x 4 = 24 s, plus waits of 0.25 + 0.5 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.75 s. |
| 6 | 500 | 8,000 | 1 | 8 | 8 | One attempt has no retry and no wait. |
| 7 | 500 | 8,000 | 7 | 8 | 79.5 | 7 x 8 = 56 s, plus waits of 0.5 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 8 = 23.5 s (the sixth would be 16 s but is capped at 8 s). |
| 8 | 100 | 800 | 4 | 1 | 4.7 | 4 x 1 = 4 s, plus waits of 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.7 s. |

For exploration the learner sets the base from 100 to 1,000 ms in steps of 50 (default 500), the cap from 800 to 8,000 ms in steps of 200 (default 8,000), N from 1 to 7 in steps of 1 (default 4), and T from 1 to 8 s in steps of 1 (default 8), and sees the timeline of attempts and waits with the worst-case total. A switch shows one random jittered run beneath the worst case, labeled "one random run."

**Provenance:** The formula and the default values (500 ms, 8,000 ms, 4 attempts, 8 s) are the chapter's `backoff.py` and `buddy_config.py` settings, and the default row matches `02-backoff-table.py`, which prints 35.5 s. The other settings are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative."

**Rules:** Ceiling of the wait after failed attempt k is \( \min(\text{cap}, \text{base} \times 2^k) \) in milliseconds. There is no wait after the last attempt. Worst-case total in seconds is \( N \times T + (\text{sum of the } N - 1 \text{ ceilings}) / 1000 \). A jittered wait is a whole number of milliseconds from 0 to its ceiling. For N = 1 there are no waits.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner drags the four controls and watches the timeline lengthen or shorten.
2. The learner turns on the "one random run" switch and sees that the jittered run is never longer than the worst case.
3. The learner starts the 8 settings. Setting 1 is shown.
4. The learner types the worst-case total in seconds and submits.
5. The sim draws that setting's timeline and shows the Why text.
6. After setting 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that in settings 3 and 7 the cap makes later waits equal, and that setting 6 has no waits at all.

**Feedback:** 8 settings, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The worst case is <answer> s: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

**Starting State:** The default setting (500 ms, 8,000 ms, 4 attempts, 8 s) is drawn as a timeline with the question "What is the longest this request can take?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that with a base of 500 ms, a cap of 8,000 ms, 4 attempts and an 8 s timeout the longest a request can take is 35.5 s; that the ceilings of the first six retries are 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000 and 8,000 ms; and that with full jitter each wait is a random number from 0 to its ceiling.

docs.title: RGB565 Color Mixer
docs.text:
Run the RGB565 Color Mixer MicroSim Fullscreen

You can include this MicroSim on your website using the following iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/rgb565-color-mixer/main.html" width="100%" height="592px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The round display in the kit stores each pixel in RGB565: 5 bits of red, 6 bits of green, and 5 bits of blue packed into one 16-bit number. This mixer runs the same packing rule as the kit's color565() function in src/kits/study-buddy-base/lib/gc9b72.py:

value = (red & 0xF8) << 8 | (green & 0xFC) << 3 | blue >> 3

For each color strength the sim shows all 8 input bits. The bits that are kept are outlined in the color's own hue, and the low bits that are dropped are grayed and struck out. Below them, the 16 packed bits show where each group lands: red in bits 15 to 11, green in bits 10 to 5, and blue in bits 4 to 0. The sim also shows the hexadecimal value and the two bytes the driver sends, high byte first.

Two swatches sit side by side. The left one is the full 24-bit color you mixed. The right one is the color the display can actually show after the low bits are dropped, so you can see when the difference is visible and when it is not.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Drag the Red, Green, and Blue sliders. The swatches, the kept bits, the 16-bit value, and the hex value all update together. The sim opens on orange (255, 128, 0), which packs to 0xFC00.
  2. Press Start Challenges. Each challenge shows a color and its (R, G, B) numbers. The sliders lock and the bits are hidden.
  3. Type the RGB565 value in hexadecimal (for example F800 or 0xF800; upper or lower case both work) and press Check or the Enter key.
  4. If your first answer is wrong, you get one more try. After a second wrong answer the sim shows the correct value and why. The bits are revealed after each challenge so you can check your work.
  5. After challenge 6 the sim shows your score out of 6. Mastery is 5 of 6. Press Try Challenges Again to repeat, or keep exploring with the sliders.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Learning objective: Students will calculate the 16-bit RGB565 value for six given colors using the packing rule, with at least 5 of 6 correct within two attempts each (Bloom's Taxonomy: Apply).

Audience: High school students building the Open Study Buddy kit (grades 9-12).

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes.

Prerequisites: pixels, binary and hexadecimal numbers, bit masking and shifting (Chapter 5 section "RGB565 Color").

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (3 minutes). With the sim on orange, ask: "Which bits does each color keep?" Have students name the kept groups (5, 6, 5) before touching a slider.
  2. Explore (5 minutes). Students set red to 255 and slowly lower it to 248. The 16-bit value does not change. Then go one step lower to 247. Ask them to explain why using the struck-out bits.
  3. Green gets the extra bit (2 minutes). Repeat with green from 255 down to 252, then 251. Green changes every 4 steps, red and blue every 8.
  4. Challenges (8 minutes). Students work the six challenges, writing each step on paper: mask, shift, combine, convert to hex.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does RGB565 give green 6 bits instead of red or blue?
  2. Gray (110, 110, 110) is not the same 16-bit pattern for each color group. Why do the red and blue groups match but green differ?
  3. The kit sends FC 00 for orange. What would go wrong if the driver sent the low byte first?
  4. How many different colors can RGB565 show, and how many does 24-bit color show?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The challenge score (target 5 of 6 within two attempts each) is the evidence of mastery. Moving the sliders is exploration and is not scored.
  • Exit ticket: "Pack cyan (0, 255, 255) into RGB565 and show each step." (Answer: 0x07FF.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 5: Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size - the RGB565 Color section explains the packing rule used here.
  • High color (Wikipedia) - background on 16-bit color formats, including 5-6-5.
  • Bitwise operation (Wikipedia) - AND masks and bit shifts.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 5: Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** rgb565-color-mixer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-python/tree/main/docs/sims/rgb-color-mixer<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the 16-bit RGB565 value for 6 given colors, using the packing rule, with at least 5 of 6 correct within two attempts each.

**Prerequisites:** pixel, RGB565, bit masking and shifting (all defined in the section "RGB565 Color" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 6 colors the learner types the RGB565 value in hexadecimal. An answer is correct when it equals the RGB565 value column in Content, ignoring upper or lower case and a leading "0x". Mastery is 5 of 6 correct, with up to two attempts per color. Moving the exploration sliders and watching the bits is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) RGB565 stores 8 bits per color. (2) The extra bit goes to blue. (3) The low bits of each color are kept and the high bits are dropped.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation of a bit-packed value needs the learner to follow the masking and shifting rule step by step. Seeing the 16 bits change with the three color strengths gives the learner a way to check the arithmetic.

**Content:**

For exploration, the learner sets red, green, and blue strengths from 0 to 255 in steps of 1 (unit: none, default 255, 128, 0). The sim shows the color, the three kept bit groups (5, 6, and 5 bits), and the 16-bit value in binary and hexadecimal.

Challenge colors, in this order:

| # | Color | (R, G, B) | RGB565 value | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Red | (255, 0, 0) | F800 | Red keeps its top 5 bits (11111) in the top of the number. |
| 2 | Green | (0, 255, 0) | 07E0 | Green keeps its top 6 bits (111111) in the middle. |
| 3 | Blue | (0, 0, 255) | 001F | Blue keeps its top 5 bits (11111) in the bottom. |
| 4 | Yellow | (255, 255, 0) | FFE0 | Red 11111 and green 111111 together make FFE0. |
| 5 | Orange | (255, 128, 0) | FC00 | Green 128 keeps 100000, so the green bits are 0x0400 and red is 0xF800. |
| 6 | Gray | (110, 110, 110) | 6B6D | Red 01101, green 011011, and blue 01101 pack to 0110101101101101. |

**Provenance:** The packing rule is `color565` from `src/kits/study-buddy-base/lib/gc9b72.py`. The values in the table were computed with that function.

**Rules:** value = ((R AND 0xF8) shifted left 8) OR ((G AND 0xFC) shifted left 3) OR (B shifted right 3), with R, G, and B whole numbers from 0 to 255. The result is a number from 0 to 65535 shown as four hexadecimal digits.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner drags the red, green, and blue controls and sees the color, the kept bit groups, and the 16-bit value update together.
2. The learner starts the challenges. Challenge 1 shows the color and its (R, G, B) numbers.
3. The learner types the RGB565 value in hexadecimal and submits.
4. If it is wrong the first time, the learner may try once more. After a second wrong answer the sim shows the correct value and the Why text.
5. After challenge 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that the 16-bit value only changes when a color crosses a multiple of 8 (or of 4 for green).

**Feedback:** 6 challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". First incorrect: "Not quite. Check which bits each color keeps (5, 6, 5). Try again." Second incorrect: "The value is <answer>: <Why>". A running score "n of 6" is shown.

**Starting State:** The mixer shows orange (255, 128, 0) with its bits, and the question "Which bits does each color keep?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that RGB565 uses 5, 6, and 5 bits, has 65,536 colors, and that orange (255, 128, 0) is 0xFC00.

docs.title: Same-Subnet Checker
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 13: Wi-Fi, HTTP, and Connecting to the Agent.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** same-subnet-checker<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate whether two IPv4 addresses are on the same network, given a netmask, in 8 cases, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

**Prerequisites:** IP address, netmask, network address, same network, binary form of a number from 0 to 255 (all defined in this chapter above this block; binary numbers are in Chapter 3).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 cases the learner chooses "same network" or "different networks", then types the network address of the first device. A case is correct when both answers match the Answer columns in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Using the explorer (typing any addresses and watching the binary AND) is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Addresses that start with the same number are always on the same network. (2) A mask can only fall between whole numbers. (3) The all-zeros and all-ones device addresses can be given to a device.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation requires the learner to carry out the mask-and-compare procedure on new numbers. Showing the two addresses and the mask in binary, with the mask's 1 bits highlighted, ties the procedure to what the mask keeps, and asking for the network address as well as the yes/no answer shows the work.

**Content:**

The explorer shows an address, a second address, and a netmask. Each is shown as four numbers and as four groups of 8 bits. The sim computes the network address of each as the bitwise AND of the address and the mask. The two addresses are on the same network when the two network addresses are equal.

| # | First address | Netmask | Second address | Same network? | Network address of the first | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 192.168.1.23 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.1.50 | same | 192.168.1.0 | The mask keeps the first three numbers, and both start 192.168.1. |
| 2 | 192.168.1.23 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.2.50 | different | 192.168.1.0 | The third numbers, 1 and 2, differ and the mask keeps them. |
| 3 | 10.4.7.88 | 255.255.0.0 | 10.4.200.9 | same | 10.4.0.0 | The mask keeps only 10.4, and both start 10.4. |
| 4 | 10.4.7.88 | 255.255.255.0 | 10.4.200.9 | different | 10.4.7.0 | The same two addresses, but this mask also keeps the third number, 7 and 200. |
| 5 | 172.16.5.5 | 255.255.240.0 | 172.16.15.1 | same | 172.16.0.0 | 240 is 11110000, so only the top 4 bits of the third number are kept; 5 and 15 are both 0000. |
| 6 | 172.16.5.5 | 255.255.240.0 | 172.16.16.1 | different | 172.16.0.0 | 16 is 00010000, so its kept bits are 0001, not 0000. |
| 7 | 192.168.1.200 | 255.255.255.128 | 192.168.1.20 | different | 192.168.1.128 | 128 is 10000000: 200 keeps the top bit (1) and 20 keeps 0. |
| 8 | 192.168.1.130 | 255.255.255.128 | 192.168.1.200 | same | 192.168.1.128 | 130 and 200 are both 128 or more, so both keep the top bit 1. |

For exploration the learner can type any two addresses (each number 0 to 255) and choose a netmask from 255.255.255.0, 255.255.255.128, 255.255.240.0 or 255.255.0.0. The default is 192.168.1.23, 255.255.255.0 and 192.168.1.50.

**Provenance:** The arithmetic is the chapter sections "The Netmask" and "The Local Network", and the same cases (1 to 6) are in the table printed by `02-ip-and-subnet.py`. The addresses are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative."

**Rules:** The network address is the bitwise AND of each of the four numbers of the address with the matching number of the mask. Two addresses are on the same network when their network addresses are equal. If the learner types a number outside 0 to 255, the sim ignores the change and keeps the previous value.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner opens the explorer and changes the second address's last number, watching its bits and the kept bits change.
2. The learner changes the netmask from 255.255.255.0 to 255.255.0.0 and notices which cases flip from different to same.
3. The learner starts the 8 cases. Case 1 is shown.
4. The learner chooses same or different, types the first address's network address, and submits.
5. The sim highlights the kept bits of both addresses and shows the Why text.
6. After case 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that cases 3 and 4 use the same two addresses and have opposite answers.

**Feedback:** 8 cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. They are <same or different>, and the network address is <network address>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

**Starting State:** The explorer shows 192.168.1.23 and 192.168.1.50 with 255.255.255.0, with the question "Are these two on the same network?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the netmask keeps the network part of an address, that 255.255.240.0 keeps the top 4 bits of the third number, that 172.16.5.5 and 172.16.15.1 are on the same network under that mask while 172.16.16.1 is not, and that a network with \( h \) host bits has \( 2^h - 2 \) usable addresses.

docs.title: Sampling Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Sampling Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/sampling-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="517px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A microphone input is measured at a fixed sample rate. This MicroSim draws a true sine tone in gray, the sample dots in red, and the wave the dots suggest in blue. When the tone is below the Nyquist limit (half the sample rate) the blue wave matches the true tone. When the tone is above the limit, the dots trace a lower, false tone: the true frequency folds back to sample rate - true frequency.

The blue wave is not drawn by hand. For a tone f above the limit, every sample of sin(2πf t) equals a sample of -sin(2π(fs - f) t), so the sim draws that phase-inverted wave and it passes exactly through every dot. At exactly half the sample rate every sample lands on zero, and the sim says the samples cannot show the tone reliably.

The 12,800 Hz rate is the kit's MIC_SAMPLE_RATE, and 16,000 Hz is the test 05 speaker rate. The other tones and rates are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Move the True frequency slider (100 to 9,000 Hz) and pick a Sample rate. Watch the dots and the blue wave they suggest. The true frequency always stays below the sample rate: picking a lower rate lowers the frequency if needed.
  2. Press Start challenges. Each challenge shows a tone and a sample rate.
  3. Type the apparent frequency in hertz and press Submit or Enter. The sim then shows the samples, the Nyquist limit and the correct answer.
  4. Press Next challenge, and after challenge 6 press Show score.

Each challenge allows one answer, and an answer within 1 Hz counts as correct. Mastery is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will calculate the frequency a sampled tone appears to have, given its true frequency and the sample rate.

docs.title: Warm-Up (3 minutes)
docs.text: Show a video clip of a car wheel that seems to spin backward. Ask why a camera taking pictures at a fixed rate could make a wheel look slow or reversed.

docs.title: Guided Exploration (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. At 12,800 Hz, students move the tone from 1,000 Hz up past 6,400 Hz and watch the blue wave slow down instead of speed up.
  2. Students set the tone to 7,000 Hz and confirm the chapter's example: it appears at 5,800 Hz.
  3. Students change the sample rate to 16,000 Hz and note that the same tone is now captured correctly.

docs.title: Challenge (7 minutes)
docs.text: Students complete the six challenges. Ask them to write the folding calculation for each answer before they submit.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Does a tone above the Nyquist limit disappear, get quieter, or turn into something else?
  2. Why would a recording device filter out high frequencies before sampling?
  3. Is a higher sample rate always better? When does it stop helping?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The sim records 6 first-attempt answers. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct within 1 Hz. Moving the controls is exploration, not evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem - Wikipedia article on the sample rate needed to capture a signal.
  2. Aliasing - Wikipedia article on how high frequencies fold into false low ones.
  3. Nyquist frequency - Wikipedia article on the half-sample-rate limit.

Original specification

Type: microsim sim-id: sampling-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/sampling-parameter-explorer Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the frequency a sampled tone appears to have, given its true frequency and the sample rate, for 6 challenge tones, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: sampling, sample rate, frequency, Nyquist limit, aliasing (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 challenge tones the learner types the apparent frequency in hertz before the sim shows it. An answer is correct when it is within 1 Hz of the Apparent frequency column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Changing the tone and the sample rate and watching the dots is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A tone above half the sample rate disappears. (2) A tone above half the sample rate is recorded at its true frequency but quietly. (3) A higher sample rate always sounds better regardless of the sound's frequency.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs the learner to use the folding rule on new numbers. Committing a number first, and then seeing the sampled dots form a wave of a different frequency, shows that the lost tone reappears as a false one.

Content:

The sim shows one true sine wave, its sample dots, and the wave the dots suggest. The folding rule used for the apparent frequency is given in the Rules field.

Challenge tones, in this order:

# True frequency (Hz) Sample rate (Hz) Nyquist limit (Hz) Apparent frequency (Hz) Why (shown as feedback) 1 1,000 12,800 6,400 1,000 1,000 is below 6,400, so it is captured correctly. 2 6,000 12,800 6,400 6,000 6,000 is just below the limit, so it is captured correctly. 3 7,000 12,800 6,400 5,800 7,000 is above 6,400, so it folds to 12,800 - 7,000 = 5,800. 4 9,000 12,800 6,400 3,800 9,000 is above 6,400, so it folds to 12,800 - 9,000 = 3,800. 5 3,000 4,000 2,000 1,000 3,000 is above 2,000, so it folds to 4,000 - 3,000 = 1,000. 6 5,000 8,000 4,000 3,000 5,000 is above 4,000, so it folds to 8,000 - 5,000 = 3,000.

Exploration controls: true frequency from 100 to 9,000 Hz in steps of 100 Hz, default 1,000 Hz; sample rate chosen from 4,000, 8,000, 12,800 and 16,000 Hz, default 12,800 Hz.

Provenance: The 12,800 Hz and 16,000 Hz rates are the kit's MIC_SAMPLE_RATE and test 05 RATE. The other tones and rates are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative."

Rules: The Nyquist limit is the sample rate divided by 2. For a true frequency f and sample rate fs, if f <= fs / 2 the apparent frequency equals f. If fs / 2 < f <= fs, the apparent frequency is fs - f. The challenges use only frequencies that satisfy one of those two cases (no frequency equals exactly fs / 2 or fs). In exploration, the true frequency is limited to values below the sample rate: if the learner picks a sample rate that is not above the current frequency, the frequency is lowered to the largest allowed value below the rate. When f equals fs / 2 exactly, the sim shows the message "at the Nyquist limit: the samples cannot show this tone reliably" instead of an apparent frequency.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores: changes the true frequency and the sample rate and watches the dots and the wave they suggest.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. Challenge 1 shows a true frequency and a sample rate.
  3. The learner types the apparent frequency in hertz and submits.
  4. The sim shows the dots and the suggested wave for that tone, with the correct answer and the Why text.
  5. After challenge 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that tones 3 to 6 reappeared at lower frequencies, never at higher ones.

Feedback: 6 challenges, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The apparent frequency is Hz: ". The correct answer is revealed immediately after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The explorer is shown at 1,000 Hz and 12,800 Hz with the question "What wave do these dots suggest?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the kit microphone rate is 12,800 Hz with a Nyquist limit of 6,400 Hz, and that a 7,000 Hz tone sampled at 12,800 Hz appears at 5,800 Hz.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 16: Configuring the School Agent and Calendar.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** school-time-utc-converter<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the UTC time of 8 school-local times, including 3 that fall at a daylight-saving change, with at least 7 of the 8 exactly right.

**Prerequisites:** UTC, time zone, daylight saving time, offset, CDT, CST, EDT, a time that does not exist, a time that happens twice (all defined in the section "Time Zones and Daylight Saving" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 local times, in order, the learner types the UTC time as hours and minutes (24-hour clock) and the UTC date, then submits. An answer is correct when both the time and the date equal the Answer column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first submission of each item. Using the exploration clock before the items is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The offset from UTC is the same all year. (2) A time that does not exist is an error. (3) A time that happens twice has no answer. (4) The same wall-clock time in two cities is the same instant.

**Instructional Rationale:** Calculating with offsets requires the learner to first decide which offset is in force on a given date, and the edge cases force the learner to apply a stated rule rather than a memorized offset. Committing a number before the answer is shown exposes the wrong-offset habit.

**Content:**

The two rules for awkward times, always shown: (1) a local time that does not exist is read with the offset in force before the gap; (2) a local time that happens twice is read as its first occurrence. The zone rules for America/Chicago: CDT is UTC minus 5 hours from the second Sunday in March at 2:00 AM until the first Sunday in November at 2:00 AM; CST is UTC minus 6 hours the rest of the year. For America/New_York the offsets are EDT UTC minus 4 and EST UTC minus 5, on the same dates.

The 8 items, in order:

| # | Local time and zone | Answer (UTC) | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---------------------|--------------|-------------------------|
| 1 | Tue 2026-10-20 08:00, America/Chicago | 2026-10-20 13:00 | October 20 is before the first Sunday in November, so CDT applies: 8 + 5 = 13. |
| 2 | Tue 2026-12-01 08:00, America/Chicago | 2026-12-01 14:00 | December is CST: 8 + 6 = 14. The same wall-clock hour is one hour later in UTC than in October. |
| 3 | Sun 2026-11-01 01:30, America/Chicago | 2026-11-01 06:30 | 1:30 AM happens twice that morning. Rule 2 takes the first, which is CDT: 1:30 + 5 = 6:30. |
| 4 | Sun 2026-11-01 02:30, America/Chicago | 2026-11-01 08:30 | After the clocks fall back at 2:00 AM CDT the zone is CST, and 2:30 AM happens once: 2:30 + 6 = 8:30. |
| 5 | Sun 2027-03-14 01:30, America/Chicago | 2027-03-14 07:30 | Before the 2:00 AM jump it is still CST: 1:30 + 6 = 7:30. |
| 6 | Sun 2027-03-14 02:30, America/Chicago | 2027-03-14 08:30 | 2:30 AM does not exist that day. Rule 1 uses the offset from before the gap, CST: 2:30 + 6 = 8:30. |
| 7 | Sun 2027-03-14 03:30, America/Chicago | 2027-03-14 08:30 | After the jump it is CDT: 3:30 + 5 = 8:30, the same instant as item 6. |
| 8 | Tue 2026-10-20 09:00, America/New_York | 2026-10-20 13:00 | New York is on EDT: 9 + 4 = 13. It is the same instant as item 1: the same instant is a different wall-clock time in a different zone. |

**Provenance:** The zone rules are the published US daylight-saving rules for these zones, and the answers were computed with Python's `zoneinfo` in `src/chapters/16-school-agent-calendar/server/test_pipeline.py`, which checks items 1 to 7 and item 8's offset.

**Rules:** UTC time = local time minus the zone's offset (offset is negative west of Greenwich, so local time plus the number of hours behind). Which offset applies depends on the date and the zone's rule. The UTC date may differ from the local date when the sum passes midnight. Rules 1 and 2 above decide the nonexistent and repeated local times.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner opens the exploration clock, picks a zone and a local date and time, and sees the UTC time, the offset in force, and a note when the time does not exist or happens twice.
2. The learner starts the 8 items. Item 1 is shown with an empty answer.
3. The learner types the UTC date and time and submits.
4. The sim shows the correct UTC time, the offset used, and the Why text.
5. After item 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that items 6 and 7 give one instant for two different local times.

**Feedback:** 8 items, fixed order, one submission each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The UTC time is <answer>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

**Starting State:** The exploration clock shows America/Chicago, 2026-10-20 08:00, with the question "What time is this in UTC?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that 8:00 AM on Oct 20, 2026 in Chicago is 13:00 UTC and on Dec 1, 2026 is 14:00 UTC, that 2:30 AM on 2027-03-14 does not exist and is read with the offset from before the gap, and that 1:30 AM on 2026-11-01 happens twice and the first is taken.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When a tone does not complete a whole number of cycles in the 512-sample frame, its energy leaks into neighboring bins. Multiplying the samples by the Hann window, w[i] = 0.5 - 0.5 cos(2 pi i / 512), tames the leakage but always spreads a peak over about three bins.

The chart shows bins 30 to 50 as a percentage of the loudest bin, with a dashed line at 10%. The sim counts every bin from 0 to 255 at or above that line. In explore mode you move a tone of amplitude 1,000 between 900 and 1,100 Hz and switch the window. In the quiz you predict, for six tones, which window gives fewer bins above 10%, then see both spectra side by side. The sim computes a real 512-point DFT and reproduces the counts printed by 04-leakage-hann.py.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
The MicroSim opens in its starting state and nothing moves until you act.

  • Start the 6 tones / Back to explore: Switch between exploring and the quiz.
  • Prediction menu and Submit: Choose No window, Hann window or The same. One attempt per tone.
  • Next tone / See score: Move on after the feedback.
  • Window menu and Tone slider: Explore only: pick the window; move the tone from 900 to 1,100 Hz in steps of 6.25 Hz.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will compare the spectra of 6 test tones taken with no window and with the Hann window, and choose for each the window that gives the narrower peak, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Bloom's Taxonomy level: Analyze (compare)

docs.title: Audience and Duration
docs.text: High school students (grades 9-12) building the Open Study Buddy; about 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: frequency bin, spectral leakage, windowing, Hann window, magnitude spectrum (all defined in this chapter above the block).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Count the dark bars at 1,000 Hz and 1,012.5 Hz with each window. Write the four counts in a table.
  2. Guided practice (5 min): For tones 1 and 2, decide whether the tone sits on a bin center before predicting.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Complete all six tones. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text: (1) A window always makes the peak narrower. (2) Leakage only happens to loud tones. (3) A tone exactly on a bin leaks.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Does a window always make the peak narrower? When does it not?
  2. Where does a tone have to sit for the worst leakage without a window?
  3. Does a quieter tone leak less? Why does the percentage scale answer this?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The quiz inside the MicroSim is the evidence of mastery: each item is scored on the first attempt only, the correct answer and its reason are shown after every submission, and the final screen reports the score against the mastery threshold.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
Full specification from Chapter 9 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** spectral-leakage-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** compare<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will compare the spectra of 6 test tones taken with no window and with the Hann window, and choose for each the window that gives the narrower peak, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

**Prerequisites:** frequency bin, spectral leakage, windowing, Hann window, magnitude spectrum (all defined in this chapter above the block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 6 tones the learner sees the tone's frequency and its bin number, predicts which window ("No window", "Hann window", or "The same") gives fewer bins with at least 10% of the loudest bin's magnitude, and submits before the two spectra are drawn. A choice is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Moving the exploration slider is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A window always makes the peak narrower. (2) Leakage only happens to loud tones. (3) A tone exactly on a bin leaks.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level comparison requires the learner to relate where a tone sits relative to the bins to how a window changes the picture. Predicting before the spectra are drawn forces a decision based on that relationship. The six tones include two on-bin cases where the window does not help, which exposes the first misconception.

**Content:**

The model is a sine wave of amplitude 1,000 sampled at 12,800 Hz for 512 samples. The "no window" spectrum is the magnitude of the 512-point DFT of the samples. The "Hann window" spectrum is the same after multiplying the samples by w[i] = 0.5 - 0.5 cos(2 pi i / 512). The sim counts bins 0 to 255 whose magnitude is at least 10% of the largest magnitude in that spectrum.

| # | Tone (Hz) | Bin | Bins at least 10%, no window | Bins at least 10%, Hann | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,000 | 40.00 | 1 | 3 | No window | The tone is exactly on a bin, so there is no leakage to remove, and the window adds a three-bin peak. |
| 2 | 1,006.25 | 40.25 | 5 | 3 | Hann window | The tone is a quarter bin off center, so the plain spectrum leaks into 5 bins and Hann holds it to 3. |
| 3 | 1,012.5 | 40.50 | 10 | 4 | Hann window | Halfway between bins is the worst case without a window: 10 bins. |
| 4 | 1,018.75 | 40.75 | 5 | 3 | Hann window | A quarter bin off center on the other side, the mirror image of tone 2. |
| 5 | 1,037.5 | 41.50 | 10 | 4 | Hann window | Another halfway case, between bins 41 and 42. |
| 6 | 1,050 | 42.00 | 1 | 3 | No window | Exactly on bin 42, so the window can only widen the peak. |

For exploration the learner moves a tone slider from 900 Hz to 1,100 Hz in steps of 6.25 Hz (default 1,000 Hz) and chooses the window, and the sim draws the magnitude of bins 30 to 50 for the chosen window.

**Provenance:** The counts in the table are produced by `src/chapters/09-signal-processing-fft/04-leakage-hann.py` and a variant of it using the same code and the same FFT, for the tones 1,000, 1,006.25, 1,012.5, 1,018.75, 1,037.5, and 1,050 Hz. The sim computes the spectra with the same formulas and must reproduce the table.

**Rules:** Count bins k from 0 to 255 with magnitude >= 0.1 x the largest magnitude. The "Answer" is the window with the smaller count; if the counts are equal the answer is "The same" (no challenge has equal counts). Slider: min 900, max 1,100, step 6.25, default 1,000, unit Hz.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner moves the slider with each window and watches the peak and the skirt of small bins around it.
2. The learner notices that on bin centers (1,000 Hz and 1,050 Hz) the plain spectrum has a single spike.
3. The learner starts the 6 tones. Tone 1 is shown with its bin number.
4. The learner chooses a window and submits.
5. The sim draws both spectra, highlights the bins counted, and shows the Why text.

**Feedback:** 6 tones, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. <Why>". The two spectra and the counts are revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

**Starting State:** The slider is at 1,000 Hz with the plain spectrum drawn as one spike and the question "Which window makes this peak narrower?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that a tone on a bin center has 1 loud bin with no window and 3 with Hann, that 1,006.25 Hz gives 5 and 3, and that 1,012.5 Hz gives 10 and 4.

docs.text:
1. Spectral leakage - Wikipedia - Why off-bin tones spread across many bins.
  2. Hann function - Wikipedia - The window formula used by the kit.
  3. Window function - Wikipedia - How windows trade peak width for leakage.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Faster code is not always better code. Each 40 ms audio frame leaves 30 ms for the audio work after a 10 ms display reserve, and the right implementation is the simplest one whose worst-case pass time fits that limit: plain Python first, then viper, then inline assembly. If even assembly is too slow, the work itself must shrink.

The bar at the top splits one frame into the audio-work limit and the display reserve. Below it, three bars show the worst-case time of each option against the limit (dashed green) and the budget (gray). In explore mode you set the budget, reserve and three times. In the quiz you recommend an option, or None fits, for six scenarios. All times are illustrative, not measurements of the kit.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
The MicroSim opens in its starting state and nothing moves until you act.

  • Start the 6 scenarios / Back to explore: Switch between the sliders and the quiz.
  • Recommendation menu and Submit: Choose Plain Python, Viper, Assembly or None fits. One attempt per scenario.
  • Next scenario / See score: Move on after the feedback.
  • Budget, Reserve, Plain, Viper and Asm sliders: Explore only: budget 10 to 80 ms (step 5), reserve 0 to 20 ms (step 5), times 1 to 300 ms.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will recommend, for 6 scenarios, the simplest implementation whose worst-case pass time fits within the frame budget minus the display reserve, or state that none fits, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Bloom's Taxonomy level: Evaluate (recommend)

docs.title: Audience and Duration
docs.text: High school students (grades 9-12) building the Open Study Buddy; about 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: frame budget, display reserve, worst-case pass time, viper code, inline assembly, performance trade-offs (all defined in this chapter above the block).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Starting from scenario 1's numbers, raise the reserve until Viper stops fitting. Note the reserve at which it changes.
  2. Guided practice (5 min): For each scenario, write limit = budget - reserve first, then check the options from the top down.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Complete all six scenarios. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text: (1) The fastest implementation is always the best choice. (2) An implementation that fits on average fits the deadline. (3) Assembly is always needed for real-time audio.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. In scenario 2 the fastest option was not the right one. Why?
  2. Why does the average pass time not decide whether an option fits?
  3. What should you do when no option fits?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The quiz inside the MicroSim is the evidence of mastery: each item is scored on the first attempt only, the correct answer and its reason are shown after every submission, and the final screen reports the score against the mastery threshold.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
Full specification from Chapter 10 
Type: microsim
**sim-id:** speedup-chooser<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** recommend<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will recommend, for 6 scenarios, the simplest implementation whose worst-case pass time fits within the frame budget minus the display reserve, or state that none fits, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

**Prerequisites:** frame budget, display reserve, worst-case pass time, viper code, inline assembly, performance trade-offs (all defined in this chapter above the block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each scenario the learner chooses one of "Plain Python", "Viper", "Assembly", or "None fits" and submits. A choice is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Changing the numbers in the exploration panel is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The fastest implementation is always the best choice. (2) An implementation that fits on average fits the deadline. (3) Assembly is always needed for real-time audio.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluate-level recommendation requires the learner to apply a stated criterion to evidence and justify the choice. The scenarios put a boundary case (an implementation that fits by exactly zero margin), a case where the simplest option already fits, and a case where nothing fits, so the learner cannot recommend by habit.

**Content:**

The numbers in this activity are **illustrative** and are not measurements of the kit. Each scenario gives the frame budget, the display reserve, and the worst-case pass time of three implementations, all in milliseconds. The complexity order from simplest to hardest is Plain Python, Viper, Assembly. The fitting limit is the budget minus the reserve; an implementation fits when its worst-case time is less than or equal to the limit.

| # | Budget (ms) | Reserve (ms) | Limit (ms) | Plain Python | Viper | Assembly | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 40 | 10 | 30 | 120 | 6 | 4 | Viper | Plain Python is over the limit; viper and assembly both fit, and viper is the simpler. |
| 2 | 40 | 10 | 30 | 18 | 5 | 3 | Plain Python | Plain Python already fits, so any faster option costs readability for nothing. |
| 3 | 40 | 10 | 30 | 90 | 34 | 12 | Assembly | Viper at 34 ms is over the 30 ms limit; assembly at 12 ms fits. |
| 4 | 40 | 10 | 30 | 200 | 80 | 45 | None fits | Even assembly at 45 ms is over the limit, so the work itself must be reduced. |
| 5 | 20 | 5 | 15 | 60 | 14 | 7 | Viper | Viper at 14 ms is within the 15 ms limit, so assembly is not needed. |
| 6 | 40 | 10 | 30 | 31 | 12 | 9 | Viper | Plain Python at 31 ms is just over the limit of 30 ms; viper at 12 ms fits. |

For exploration the learner sets the budget (10 to 80 ms, step 5, default 40), the reserve (0 to 20 ms, step 5, default 10), and the three times (1 to 300 ms, step 1, defaults 90, 20, 10), and the sim shows which options fit.

**Provenance:** The scenario numbers are illustrative and invented for this activity. The 40 ms budget and 10 ms reserve are the values used in the chapter section "The Real-Time Constraint and the Frame Overrun". The sim labels all times "illustrative, not measured."

**Rules:** limit = budget - reserve. An option fits when its time <= limit. The answer is the first option that fits in the order Plain Python, Viper, Assembly; if none fits the answer is None fits. Budget: min 10, max 80, step 5, default 40, unit ms. Reserve: min 0, max 20, step 5, default 10, unit ms. Times: min 1, max 300, step 1, unit ms.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner changes the numbers in the exploration panel and watches which options fit.
2. The learner notices that raising the reserve can make a fitting option stop fitting.
3. The learner starts the 6 scenarios. Scenario 1 is shown.
4. The learner chooses a recommendation and submits.
5. The sim shows the limit, which options fit, the correct answer, and the Why text.

**Feedback:** 6 scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is <answer>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

**Starting State:** The exploration panel shows scenario 1's numbers with the limit of 30 ms and the three options marked fits or does not fit, and the question "Which is the simplest option that fits?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the audio work gets 30 ms of the 40 ms frame after a 10 ms display reserve, that the simplest approach that passes timing verification on the worst pass is the right one, and that the numbers in this activity are illustrative.

docs.text:

  2. Inline assembler for Thumb2 architectures - MicroPython documentation - Writing assembly functions in MicroPython.
  3. Real-time computing - Wikipedia - Why the worst case, not the average, sets the deadline.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Open Study Buddy device on your desk is an agent terminal: it gives the agent ears, a voice, and a face, but not its brain. The brain is the buddy server, which runs on a school computer and is not part of the desk device. This MicroSim shows the five kit parts of the terminal and the buddy server as a network diagram in two groups, "Agent terminal (the desk device)" and "School network".

In Explore mode, hover over or click a part to read its job. Clicking a part also highlights every connection to it and lists what travels along each one. Notice that four parts connect only to the Pico, and only the Pico connects to the buddy server, over Wi-Fi.

In Quiz mode, the sim shows one job description at a time and you click the part that does that job. The correct part turns green, a wrong click turns orange, and the feedback repeats the part's job.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start in Explore. Hover over a part to read its job, then click it to see its connections.
  2. Answer the Check yourself question: which part must the Pico talk to over Wi-Fi? Press Show answer to check.
  3. Press Quiz. Read the job description and click the matching part in the diagram. Each question gets one attempt.
  4. Press Next question after each answer. After question 6, press See results to see your score and any missed parts.
  5. Press Restart quiz to try again, or Explore to go back to exploring.

Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Quiz mode hides the job text on hover, so the quiz measures what you remember.

When the page is opened full screen, you can also drag and zoom the diagram. Inside the textbook page, use the navigation buttons at the bottom of the diagram.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will identify the job of each of the five kit parts and of the buddy server by matching six described jobs to the correct part, with at least 5 of 6 correct (Bloom's Taxonomy: Remember, verb identify).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Students should have read the chapter section The Open Study Buddy Device, including the table of five kit parts.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes). Students click each of the six parts and read its job and connections.
  2. Check yourself (1 minute). Students answer the Wi-Fi question before pressing Show answer.
  3. Quiz (4 minutes). Students complete the six-question quiz without switching back to Explore.
  4. Trace a request (5 minutes). Starting at the microphone, students name every part a spoken question passes through until the answer comes out of the speaker.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the speaker need an amplifier? What would happen if the Pico tried to drive the speaker directly?
  2. The buddy server is not part of the desk device. What are two benefits of putting the brain on a separate computer?
  3. Which single part would you replace to upgrade the agent's brain? Which parts would stay the same?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The speaker and the amplifier are the same thing. The node is named "MAX98357A amplifier and speaker" because the amplifier turns digital audio numbers into sound that the speaker plays.
  • The buddy server is part of the desk device. It sits in the separate "School network" group.
  • The Pico sends sound straight to the display. The Pico sends text and pictures to the display and audio numbers to the speaker.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: A student who scores 5 or 6 on the quiz has met the objective. For students below 5, the results screen lists each missed part with its job text for review.

docs.text:

  • Raspberry Pi Pico series documentation from Raspberry Pi
  • I²S on Wikipedia

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture.

Show the full specification 
Type: graph-model
**sim-id:** study-buddy-architecture-explorer<br/>
**Library:** vis-network<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/bioinformatics/tree/main/docs/sims/profile-hmm-architecture<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Remember<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** identify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will identify the job of each of the five kit parts and of the buddy server by matching six described jobs to the correct part, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

**Prerequisites:** Open Study Buddy device, agent terminal, buddy server, and the five kit parts (all defined in the section "The Open Study Buddy Device" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** In quiz mode the sim shows one job description and the learner clicks the part that does that job. A click is correct when it matches the Correct part column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering and clicking in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The speaker and the amplifier are the same thing. (2) The buddy server is part of the desk device. (3) The Pico sends sound straight to the display.

**Instructional Rationale:** Remember-level identification needs retrieval, so the learner first explores each part and then retrieves the matching part from a job description. Showing the connections reveals which parts talk to the Pico and which talk across the network, which is the structure the chapter describes.

**Content:**

Six nodes, in two groups. The group "Agent terminal (the desk device)" contains five nodes, and the group "School network" contains one node. Each node shows this text when hovered or clicked:

| Node | Group | Job text revealed |
|---|---|---|
| Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | Agent terminal | Runs the terminal program, reads the microphone and buttons, drives the display and speaker, and talks to the buddy server over Wi-Fi. |
| Round color display | Agent terminal | Shows the clock, the agent's words, and status as a 360 by 360 pixel round picture. |
| INMP441 microphone | Agent terminal | Turns sound into digital numbers that the Pico can read. |
| MAX98357A amplifier and speaker | Agent terminal | Turns digital audio numbers into sound that the student hears. |
| Mode, Up, and Down buttons | Agent terminal | Let the student change modes, move through menus, and adjust values by hand. |
| Buddy server | School network | Receives requests, decides on a reply, and sends it back. It runs on a school computer and is not part of the desk device. |

Five edges. The meaning of each edge is shown when either of its two nodes is selected:

| From | To | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| INMP441 microphone | Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | Sends digital sound numbers to the Pico. |
| Mode, Up, and Down buttons | Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | Send button presses to the Pico. |
| Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | Round color display | Sends text and pictures to show. |
| Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | MAX98357A amplifier and speaker | Sends digital audio numbers to play. |
| Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W | Buddy server | Sends requests and receives replies over Wi-Fi on the school network. |

Quiz questions, in this fixed order:

| # | Job description shown | Correct part |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Turns sound into digital numbers. | INMP441 microphone |
| 2 | Turns digital audio numbers into sound the student hears. | MAX98357A amplifier and speaker |
| 3 | Shows the clock and the agent's words as a round picture. | Round color display |
| 4 | Runs the terminal program and connects to Wi-Fi. | Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W |
| 5 | Lets the student change modes and adjust values by hand. | Mode, Up, and Down buttons |
| 6 | Decides on a reply and sends it back, from a school computer. | Buddy server |

**Provenance:** From the chapter section "The Open Study Buddy Device" and the table of five kit parts there. The sim labels the quiz wording "written for this sim".

**Rules:** A quiz answer is correct when the clicked node equals the Correct part. The score is the number of correct answers, from 0 to 6. Selecting a node in explore mode highlights that node and every edge connected to it.

**Learner Activity:**

1. In explore mode, the learner hovers or clicks each of the six nodes to read its job text.
2. The learner selects a node and sees its connected edges and their meanings.
3. The learner answers the question: "Which part must the Pico talk to over Wi-Fi?" (answer: the buddy server).
4. The learner switches to quiz mode and clicks the matching part for each of the six job descriptions.
5. After question 6 the sim shows the score and lists each missed part with its job text.

**Feedback:** Six questions, fixed order, one attempt per question. Correct: "Correct: <job text>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The part that does this is <correct part>: <job text>". The correct part is revealed immediately after each answer, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

**Starting State:** All six nodes and five edges are visible with no node selected, in explore mode, with the instruction "Click a part to learn its job."

**Chapter Anchors:** The device has five groups of parts. The buddy server is not part of the desk device. The terminal talks to the buddy server over Wi-Fi on the school network.

docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 12: Wake-Word Detection.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** template-score-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the template score of 4 small windows by mean subtraction, unit normalization and a dot product, within 0.02 of the correct value in at least 3 of the 4.

**Prerequisites:** feature, window, mean subtraction, unit normalization, dot product score, template (all defined in this chapter above the block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 4 challenge windows the learner types a score before the sim reveals it. A score is correct when it is within 0.02 of the Score column in Content. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Stepping through the worked window in exploration is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A louder or stronger window scores higher. (2) A steady offset in a band changes the score. (3) A negative score means "no similarity" instead of "the opposite pattern". (4) The order of the frames does not matter.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation needs a procedure with a checkable answer. The windows are small enough (3 frames, 2 bands) to calculate by hand, and four challenges are chosen so that each breaks one of the misconceptions.

**Content:**

All windows have 3 frames and 2 bands. Each frame is written (band 0, band 1). The template is already mean-subtracted and length 1: (-0.5, 0.5), (0, 0), (0.5, -0.5). The sim labels all windows "synthetic".

The worked window, used in exploration: E = (10, 2), (10, 4), (10, 6). Band means 10 and 4. After subtraction: (0, -2), (0, 0), (0, 2). Length 2.83. Dot with the template -2.00. Score -0.71.

| # | Window | Band means | After subtraction | Length | Dot | Score | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|--------|------------|--------------------|--------|-----|-------|-------------------------|
| 1 | W1: (3, 9), (4, 8), (5, 7) | 4, 8 | (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, -1) | 2.00 | 2.00 | 1.00 | Subtracting the band means leaves exactly the template's shape, so the angle is 0. |
| 2 | W2: (2, 12), (4, 10), (6, 8) | 4, 10 | (-2, 2), (0, 0), (2, -2) | 4.00 | 4.00 | 1.00 | Twice the strength, same shape: normalizing divides by 4 and gives the template, so strength does not matter. |
| 3 | W3: (5, 7), (4, 8), (3, 9) | 4, 8 | (1, -1), (0, 0), (-1, 1) | 2.00 | -2.00 | -1.00 | The same band movements in the opposite order are the opposite pattern, so the score is -1. |
| 4 | W4: (3, 6), (4, 8), (6, 7) | 4.33, 7 | (-1.33, -1), (-0.33, 1), (1.67, 0) | 2.58 | 1.00 | 0.39 | Only partly the same shape: the dot product is 1.00 but the length is 2.58, so the score is 1.00 / 2.58. |

**Provenance:** Synthetic windows written for this sim; the arithmetic matches the chapter's toy-window sections and was checked with Python.

**Rules:** Band mean = sum of that band's values over the 3 frames, divided by 3. After subtraction = value - band mean. Length = square root of the sum of squares of the 6 subtracted numbers. Dot = sum over the 6 entries of subtracted value times template value. Score = dot divided by length, or 0 if the length is below 0.000001. Scores are shown to 2 decimals and compared with a tolerance of 0.02.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner steps through the worked window E in three stages: mean subtraction, normalization, dot product. At each stage the sim shows the numbers. The learner should notice that the band that never moves (band 0 of E) contributes nothing.
2. The learner starts the 4 challenges. Window W1 is shown with the template.
3. The learner types the score and submits.
4. The sim shows the three stages with their numbers and the Why text.
5. After challenge 4, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that W1 and W2 differ in strength and colouring but score the same, and that W3 has the same numbers as W1 in a different order.

**Feedback:** 4 challenges, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The score is <score>: <Why>". The score is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 4" is shown.

**Starting State:** The worked window E is shown before any stage, with the question "What does this window score against the template?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that W1 and W2 score 1.00, W3 scores -1.00, W4 scores 0.39, and that the template is (-0.5, 0.5), (0, 0), (0.5, -0.5).

docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 17: Privacy, Safety, and Responsible Listening.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** threat-model-sorter<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** prioritize<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will prioritize 10 classroom threats into the correct fix order using each threat's likelihood, impact, and effort to fix, with at least 8 of 10 threats in the correct position.

**Prerequisites:** threat model, asset, actor, attack surface, likelihood, impact, risk score, effort to fix (all defined in the section "The Threat Model" above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner arranges all 10 threats in order and submits once. A threat is in the correct position when its position equals the Fix position column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 in the correct position. Changing the likelihood and impact of the example threat in exploration is not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The most technical-sounding threat is always the most important. (2) Likelihood alone decides priority. (3) Equal scores mean the order does not matter. (4) A threat caused by our own bug is not a real threat.

**Instructional Rationale:** Prioritizing at the Evaluate level means choosing an order against stated criteria and defending it. Giving the learner the three ratings and one tie-break rule makes the criteria explicit, so the activity checks judgment applied to criteria rather than memory of the table.

**Content:**

The rule: the risk score is likelihood times impact. Threats are ordered by risk score from highest to lowest. Among threats with equal scores, the lower effort comes first. Among threats with equal score and equal effort, the lower threat number comes first.

The 10 threats, shown in this scrambled order, with their ratings (likelihood and impact from 1 to 3, effort from 1 easy to 3 hard):

| Threat | Description | Likelihood | Impact | Effort | Score | Fix position | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T7 | Always-on listening turned on without approval | 1 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 9 | Score 3, effort 1, and its number is lower than T10's, so it comes ninth. |
| T2 | Eavesdropping on an unencrypted HTTP link | 2 | 3 | 2 | 6 | 5 | Score 6 with effort 2: after the three effort-1 threats and T1, before T9. |
| T10 | Someone else's voice triggers the device | 3 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 10 | Score 3 ties with T7 and effort ties too, so the higher number goes last. |
| T4 | secrets.py committed to git | 2 | 3 | 1 | 6 | 2 | Score 6 with effort 1; its number is higher than T3's. |
| T9 | A cloud vendor keeps recordings | 2 | 3 | 3 | 6 | 6 | Score 6 with the highest effort, so it is last of the score-6 group. |
| T1 | Microphone left open with no indicator | 2 | 3 | 2 | 6 | 4 | Score 6 with effort 2: after the effort-1 threats, before T2. |
| T6 | Server logs keep audio or transcripts | 3 | 2 | 1 | 6 | 3 | Score 6 with effort 1; its number is higher than T4's. |
| T5 | Prompt injection in a calendar title | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 7 | Score 4 is below every score-6 threat; effort 2 and number 5 put it before T8. |
| T3 | Exposed MQTT broker | 2 | 3 | 1 | 6 | 1 | Score 6 with effort 1 and the lowest number among them, so it is first. |
| T8 | Lost or stolen device | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 8 | Score 4 and effort 2 tie with T5, so the higher number goes after it. |

**Provenance:** The ratings are the judgments in `src/chapters/17-privacy-responsible-listening/tools/threat_model.py` and the chapter table "The Threat Model". The sim labels them "reasoned judgments for a classroom, not statistics."

**Rules:** Score = likelihood x impact, from 1 to 9. Order by score descending, then effort ascending, then threat number ascending. The correct order is therefore unique. The sim counts how many threats are in the position given in the Fix position column.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner explores one example threat and changes its likelihood and impact between 1 and 3; the score updates at once.
2. The learner is shown the 10 threats in the scrambled order and the ordering rule.
3. The learner arranges them from first to fix to last to fix and submits.
4. The sim reveals the correct order, marks each threat as correctly or wrongly placed, and shows the Why text for each wrongly placed threat.
5. The sim shows the score "n of 10". The learner should notice that six threats tie at 6, so effort decided their order.

**Feedback:** One submission of 10 placements. Correct placement: the threat is marked correct. Wrong placement: "Not quite. <Threat> belongs in position <n>: <Why>". The correct order is revealed after the submission, and the score is shown.

**Starting State:** The 10 threats are shown in the scrambled order with their ratings visible and the question "Which threat should you fix first, and why?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the ratings are judgments, that six of the ten threats tie at a score of 6, that effort breaks ties, and that the first three to fix are T3, T4, and T6.

docs.title: Threshold Trade-Off Explorer
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 12: Wake-Word Detection.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** threshold-tradeoff-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** judge<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge which detection threshold, if any, meets stated limits on false rejects and false accepts in 4 scenarios, choosing the correct threshold or "none" in at least 3 of 4.

**Prerequisites:** detection threshold, score, false accept, false reject, threshold trade-off (all defined in this chapter above the block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 4 scenarios the learner chooses one threshold from the table in Content, or "none", before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Answer column. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Moving the threshold control and watching the two error rates in exploration is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A higher threshold is always safer. (2) There is always a threshold that satisfies both limits. (3) A false-accept rate per attempt is the same as per hour.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluate-level judgment means deciding against criteria, so each scenario states limits and the learner must test candidate thresholds against them. Scenario 3 has no valid answer, which makes the learner judge rather than pick the middle option.

**Content:**

The sim shows two score distributions as histograms: 1,000 scores for "Hey Pico" and 1,000 for other sounds, and a threshold line. All scores are synthetic and labelled "synthetic". For each threshold the sim shows the false-reject percentage (wake scores below the threshold) and the false-accept percentage (other scores at or above it).

| Threshold | False rejects | False accepts |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| 0.50 | 0.0% | 16.6% |
| 0.55 | 0.1% | 9.1% |
| 0.60 | 0.8% | 5.3% |
| 0.65 | 3.5% | 2.4% |
| 0.70 | 11.2% | 0.8% |
| 0.75 | 26.2% | 0.5% |
| 0.80 | 49.3% | 0.1% |
| 0.85 | 74.3% | 0.0% |
| 0.90 | 90.1% | 0.0% |

Scenarios, in this order. Among the thresholds that meet every limit, the answer is the one with the smallest sum of the two percentages; if no threshold meets every limit, the answer is "none".

| # | Scenario | Limits | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|----------|--------|--------|--------------------------|
| 1 | A quiet bedroom where missing the phrase is annoying | False rejects at most 5% | 0.65 | 0.50 to 0.65 meet the limit; 0.65 has the fewest false accepts of them (2.4%). |
| 2 | A busy classroom where a false wake-up is disruptive | False accepts at most 1% | 0.70 | 0.70 and higher meet the limit; 0.70 has the fewest false rejects of them (11.2%). |
| 3 | A demo that must almost never miss and almost never wake by mistake | False rejects at most 10% and false accepts at most 1% | none | At 0.65 false accepts are 2.4% (too many) and at 0.70 false rejects are 11.2% (too many). No threshold meets both; the detector needs to be better, not retuned. |
| 4 | A shared class device with a patient user | False rejects at most 25% and false accepts at most 1% | 0.70 | 0.70 gives 11.2% and 0.8%. 0.75 has false rejects of 26.2%, which is over the limit. |

**Provenance:** The scores are synthetic: 1,000 "Hey Pico" scores drawn near mean 0.80 with standard deviation 0.08 (capped at 1.0) and 1,000 other scores near mean 0.35 with standard deviation 0.15, from the fixed-seed generator (seed 77) in `src/chapters/12-wake-word-detection/01-detector-math-test.py`. The percentages in the table are that script's output.

**Rules:** False reject = wake score < threshold. False accept = other score >= threshold. The threshold control has the range 0.50 to 0.90, step 0.05, default 0.70, unit score. Percentages are shown to 1 decimal. The scenario answer is chosen as stated in Content.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner moves the threshold and watches the two histograms' tails and the two percentages. The learner should notice that the two numbers move in opposite directions.
2. The learner starts the 4 scenarios. Scenario 1 is shown with its limits.
3. The learner chooses a threshold or "none" and submits.
4. The sim marks the threshold on the histograms, shows both percentages at the chosen value and at the answer, and shows the Why text.
5. After scenario 4, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that scenario 3 cannot be solved by moving the threshold.

**Feedback:** 4 scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <Why>". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is <answer>: <Why>". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 4" is shown.

**Starting State:** The threshold is at 0.70 with both histograms visible and the question "How many of each error would you accept?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's trade-off table has the same 9 rows. It states that 0.70 gives 11.2% false rejects and 0.8% false accepts.

docs.title: Time and Frequency Domain Viewer
docs.text:
Run the Time and Frequency Domain Viewer MicroSim Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/open-study-buddy/sims/time-and-frequency-domain-viewer/main.html" width="100%" height="577px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The same sound can be drawn two ways. The time domain plot shows the waveform: how the signal changes over a 20 ms window. The frequency domain bar chart shows the ingredients: one bar for each sine component, placed at its frequency, with height equal to its amplitude.

This MicroSim builds a sound from two sine components that you control and draws both views together. The bars are measured, not copied: the sim runs a discrete Fourier transform (DFT) on the 20 ms waveform. Every frequency used is a multiple of 50 Hz, so each component lands exactly on a DFT bin and the measured height equals the component amplitude. If you set both components to the same frequency they add together into one taller bar, just as they would in a real spectrum.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Move Freq 1, Amp 1, Freq 2 and Amp 2. Watch both views change at the same time.
  2. Set one amplitude to 0 and notice that its bar disappears.
  3. Press Start challenges. Each challenge shows a spectrum and three waveforms, A, B and C, drawn on the same vertical scale.
  4. Press A, B or C. The sim marks the matching waveform in green, marks a wrong pick in red, and explains the answer.
  5. Press Next challenge, and after challenge 6 press Show score.

Each challenge allows one pick. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will interpret a frequency-domain bar chart by choosing, for 6 challenge sounds, the time-domain waveform that has the same frequencies and amplitudes.

docs.title: Warm-Up (3 minutes)
docs.text: Play a single steady beep, then two notes at once. Ask: "How would you draw each sound as a list of ingredients?"

docs.title: Guided Exploration (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Students set Amp 2 to 0 and move Freq 1. Ask: "What happens to the bar, and what happens to the waveform?"
  2. Students change Amp 1 only. Ask the same question.
  3. Students set both components to 200 Hz and explain why there is only one bar, at height 1.5.

docs.title: Challenge (7 minutes)
docs.text: Students complete the six challenges. After each wrong pick, ask them to name which property (position or height) they misread.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Do taller bars mean higher pitches? What does bar height mean?
  2. Are the two views showing different sounds?
  3. A sound with two tones shows two bars. Why does its waveform look like one wiggly line instead of two separate waves?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The sim records 6 first-attempt picks. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Using the sliders is exploration, not evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Frequency domain - Wikipedia article comparing time-domain and frequency-domain views.
  2. Discrete Fourier transform - Wikipedia article on the calculation used to measure the bars.
  3. Spectrum analyzer - Wikipedia article on instruments that display a frequency-domain view.

docs.title: Related Resources
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: Sound and Digital Audio
Original specification

Type: microsim sim-id: time-and-frequency-domain-viewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/spectrum-analyzer/tree/main/docs/sims/waveform-types Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret a frequency-domain bar chart by choosing, for 6 challenge sounds, the time-domain waveform that has the same frequencies and amplitudes, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: time domain, frequency domain, frequency, amplitude (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 challenges the learner is shown a frequency-domain bar chart and picks one of three time-domain waveforms. A pick is correct when it matches the Correct choice column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Using the sliders in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Taller bars mean higher pitches. (2) The two views show different sounds. (3) A sound with two tones must show two separate waves in the time view.

Instructional Rationale: Interpreting a spectrum requires connecting bar position to pitch and bar height to amplitude. Choosing among waveforms that differ in exactly one of those properties makes the learner decide which property each bar encodes.

Content:

Each sound is the sum of sine components, written (frequency in Hz, amplitude on a scale of 0 to 1). The sim draws the bars for the spectrum and the waveform for the time-domain choices from these lists.

# Spectrum shown (components) Choice A Choice B Choice C Correct choice Why (shown as feedback) 1 (200, 1.0) (200, 1.0) (400, 1.0) (200, 0.5) A The bar is at 200 Hz and full height. 2 (400, 1.0) (200, 1.0) (400, 1.0) (400, 0.5) B The bar position gives the frequency: 400 Hz. 3 (200, 0.5) (200, 1.0) (400, 0.5) (200, 0.5) C The bar height gives the amplitude: half. 4 (200, 1.0) and (600, 0.5) (200, 1.0) (200, 1.0) and (600, 0.5) (600, 1.0) and (200, 0.5) B Two bars mean two components, with the heights shown. 5 (300, 0.75) and (900, 0.75) (300, 0.75) and (900, 0.75) (300, 0.75) (900, 0.75) and (300, 0.25) A Both bars are the same height, at 300 and 900 Hz. 6 (100, 1.0), (300, 0.5) and (500, 0.25) (100, 1.0), (300, 0.25) and (500, 0.5) (100, 0.25), (300, 0.5) and (500, 1.0) (100, 1.0), (300, 0.5) and (500, 0.25) C The bars fall in height from left to right: 1.0, 0.5, 0.25.

Exploration controls: two components, each with frequency from 100 to 1,000 Hz in steps of 50 Hz (defaults 200 Hz and 600 Hz) and amplitude from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.25 (defaults 1.0 and 0.5). Both views update together as the learner changes them.

Provenance: All components are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative."

Rules: A time-domain waveform is the sum of its components, each a sine wave of its frequency and amplitude, plotted over a 20 ms window. The spectrum has one bar per component, placed at its frequency, with height proportional to its amplitude. A component with amplitude 0 has no bar.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores: changes the frequency and amplitude of each component and sees both views change at the same time.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. Challenge 1 shows a spectrum and three waveforms.
  3. The learner picks one waveform.
  4. The sim shows whether the pick is correct, marks the matching waveform, and shows the Why text.
  5. After challenge 6, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that bar position is frequency and bar height is amplitude.

Feedback: 6 challenges, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. ". The correct choice is revealed right after each pick, and a running score "n of 6" is shown.

Starting State: The two views are shown with the default components and the question "Which bars belong to which part of the wave?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that bar position is frequency and bar height is amount, that a steady beep is one bar, and that two notes at once are two bars.
